text: Your body contains about 37.2 trillion cells, and roughly 3.8 million of them are replaced every second.
The human nose can detect over 1 trillion different scents, far more than the previously estimated 10,000.
Your brain uses about 20% of your total energy, despite making up only about 2% of your body weight.
Humans share about 60% of their DNA with bananas and about 98.7% with chimpanzees.
Tibetan people have a gene variant (EPAS1) inherited from Denisovans that helps them thrive at high altitudes with low oxygen.
Humans are bioluminescent — we emit visible light, but it's about 1,000 times weaker than what our eyes can detect.
The human nose can detect over one trillion distinct scents, far more than previously thought.
Your bones are about five times stronger than steel of the same density, but they remain light enough for movement.
The Bajau people of Southeast Asia have evolved genetically larger spleens, allowing them to free-dive to depths of 70 meters.
The adult human body has 206 bones, but babies are born with around 270–300 bones — many fuse together during childhood and adolescence.
The human heart beats about 100,000 times per day and pumps approximately 2,000 gallons of blood through about 60,000 miles of blood vessels.
The small intestine, despite its name, is about 20 feet (6 meters) long — three times the length of the large intestine — and is where most nutrient absorption takes place.
The human body produces about 25 million new cells every second — roughly the same number as cells destroyed to maintain equilibrium.
There are four major blood types — A, B, AB, and O — determined by antigens on red blood cells; type O negative is the universal donor because it lacks antigens that trigger rejection.
The brain contains about 86 billion neurons, each forming up to 10,000 synaptic connections — creating a network of roughly 100 trillion connections in total.
The liver is the only internal organ capable of complete regeneration — it can regrow to its full size even if up to 75% is removed.
Human skin is the body's largest organ, covering about 21 square feet (2 square meters) in adults and accounting for about 15% of body weight.
The human eye can distinguish approximately 10 million different colors, though individuals vary due to differences in photoreceptor distribution and neural processing.
The human gut microbiome contains 10–100 trillion microorganisms — outnumbering human cells — and plays key roles in immunity, metabolism, and even mood regulation.
The average adult has about 5 liters of blood, which makes a complete circuit of the body in roughly 60 seconds — faster during exercise.
The human immune system produces antibodies specific to roughly 10 billion different antigens, giving us the ability to recognize and fight an almost unlimited range of pathogens.
Muscle makes up about 40% of body weight in a typical adult, and the human body has over 600 skeletal muscles working together to produce every movement.
The strongest muscle relative to its size in the human body is the masseter (jaw muscle), capable of exerting a biting force of over 200 pounds.
Humans are one of the few mammals born with almost entirely undeveloped brains — a newborn's brain is only about 25% of its adult size, reaching 90% by age 5.
The human cornea is the only tissue in the body with no blood vessels — it gets oxygen directly from the air and nutrients from the tears and aqueous humor.
The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the human body, capable of withstanding forces up to 30 times body weight.
The human stomach produces a new protective mucus lining every two weeks — otherwise the stomach's hydrochloric acid (strong enough to dissolve iron) would digest itself.
During deep sleep, the brain's glymphatic system activates to flush out toxic waste products — including amyloid-beta proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease.
The human fingernails grow about 3–4 mm per month — about four times faster than toenails — and nails grow faster on the dominant hand.
Chronic stress shrinks the hippocampus — the brain's memory center — explaining why prolonged anxiety impairs learning and memory formation.
The human body contains enough carbon to make about 9,000 pencils, enough iron to make a 3-inch nail, and enough fat to make seven bars of soap.
The human body replaces its entire surface layer of skin roughly every 27 days — shedding about 30,000–40,000 dead skin cells per hour.
The vagus nerve — the body's longest cranial nerve — connects the brain to the heart, lungs, and gut, and plays a central role in the 'rest and digest' parasympathetic response.
Teeth are the only part of the human body that cannot repair themselves — once adult enamel is destroyed, the body cannot regenerate it.
The human body has two types of sweat glands: eccrine glands (cooling) all over the body, and apocrine glands (triggered by stress/emotion) concentrated in the armpits and groin.
An adult human produces about 1–1.5 liters of saliva daily — essential for digestion, lubrication, and the antimicrobial protection of the oral cavity.
The human kneecap (patella) is the largest sesamoid bone in the body — a bone embedded within a tendon that protects the knee joint and improves the leverage of the quadriceps muscle.
The human body contains about 100,000 miles (160,000 km) of nerve fibers — enough to wrap around Earth's equator four times.

Crying for emotional reasons (as opposed to irritants) produces tears with higher levels of stress hormones like ACTH and leucine-enkephalin — suggesting tears may help the body excrete stress chemicals.
The human spinal cord is only about 18 inches (45 cm) long in adults — yet it carries all nerve signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
The human body's fastest reflex — the eye-blink reflex — takes just 40 milliseconds to complete, driven by the trigeminal and facial nerve pathways.
Human hair grows about 6 inches (15 cm) per year on average, with each strand having a lifespan of 2–7 years before falling out and being replaced.
The appendix, long dismissed as vestigial, is now believed to serve as a 'safe house' for beneficial gut bacteria — repopulating the intestine after diarrheal illnesses.
Bone marrow produces about 200 billion red blood cells every day — a red blood cell lives for about 120 days before being broken down mainly by the spleen.
The human eye's retina contains approximately 120 million rod cells (for dim light/motion) and 6 million cone cells (for color and detail).
Humans are the only mammals that cannot breathe and swallow simultaneously as adults — the larynx descends in the throat during childhood, enabling complex speech but increasing choking risk.
The human cochlea, a snail-shaped organ in the inner ear, contains about 15,000–20,000 tiny hair cells that convert sound vibrations into electrical signals sent to the brain.
The placenta during pregnancy acts as a temporary organ that produces hormones, exchanges nutrients and oxygen between mother and fetus, and provides immune protection.
Insulin, a hormone produced by the pancreatic beta cells, is critical for glucose uptake by cells — without it, blood sugar rises to dangerous levels, as in type 1 diabetes.
The human body has about 5 million hair follicles — the same number as chimpanzees — but human hair is far finer, which is why we appear much less hairy.
The prefrontal cortex — responsible for planning, decision-making, and impulse control — is not fully developed until age 25, explaining why risk-taking peaks in adolescence.
Neurons in the brain fire electrical signals at speeds of up to 268 mph (431 km/h), while slower unmyelinated nerve fibers transmit pain signals at only 1 mph.
The human body contains about 3 billion base pairs of DNA in each cell — if the DNA from a single cell were stretched out, it would be about 2 meters long.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body has about 1,000 different species of bacteria on its skin alone — most are harmless or beneficial, forming a protective microbiome that crowds out pathogens.

Kissing recruits up to 34 facial muscles and transfers over 80 million bacteria between partners in a 10-second kiss, according to research from the Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research.
The human large intestine (colon) absorbs most of the water from digested food — processing about 1.5 liters per day — which is why dehydration causes constipation.
Sweat itself is odorless — body odor arises when bacteria on the skin break down compounds in apocrine sweat into short-chain fatty acids and thioalcohols.
The thyroid gland in the neck regulates metabolism by producing thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) — hormones that control how fast cells use energy.
The human body can survive about 3 weeks without food but only 3 days without water — the kidneys alone require about 1 liter of water daily just to filter waste.
Telomeres — protective caps on chromosomes — shorten with each cell division, acting as a biological clock; when they become critically short, cells stop dividing, contributing to aging.
Humans have three tiny bones (ossicles) in the middle ear — the malleus, incus, and stapes — the smallest bones in the body, yet responsible for transmitting sound vibrations.
The stomach's pH of 1.5–3.5 is acidic enough to dissolve metals — among its jobs is breaking down tough fibrous materials and killing many ingested pathogens.
REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, is associated with memory consolidation — the brain replays and sorts experiences from the day.
The human kidney filters about 50 gallons (190 liters) of blood daily, producing just 1–2 liters of urine — concentrating waste products more than 100-fold.
Brown fat, found mainly in newborns and in small deposits in adults, burns energy to generate heat — researchers are studying it as a target for obesity treatment.
The pineal gland, a pea-sized structure deep in the brain, produces melatonin — the hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle in response to light and dark cycles.
A sneeze forces air out of the body at speeds of up to 100 mph (160 km/h) — even faster than a cough — and can release up to 40,000 droplets.
The human heart begins beating about 22 days after conception, long before the brain is developed — making it the first functional organ formed during embryonic development.
Mitochondria — the organelles that produce cellular energy (ATP) — have their own separate DNA, believed to be the remnant of a ancient bacterial symbiosis billions of years ago.

The adrenal glands, sitting atop the kidneys, release adrenaline (epinephrine) in seconds during a threat, triggering the fight-or-flight response: raised heart rate, dilated pupils, and redirected blood flow.
The human tongue has about 10,000 taste buds, each containing 50–100 taste receptor cells that are replaced roughly every 10 days.
Hiccups are caused by an involuntary contraction of the diaphragm — the same nerve (phrenic) that triggers breathing; the longest recorded hiccup attack lasted 68 years.
About 8% of the human genome consists of retroviral DNA — remnants of ancient viral infections that became permanently integrated into human chromosomes millions of years ago.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Serotonin, often called the 'happy hormone,' is produced mostly in the gut (about 95%) rather than the brain — one reason gut health strongly influences mood.
During pregnancy, fetal cells cross the placental barrier and can persist in the mother's body for decades — a phenomenon called fetal microchimerism that may benefit maternal health.
The human eye has a 'blind spot' where the optic nerve exits the retina — but the brain fills in this gap seamlessly, so we never notice it in normal vision.
The human body produces heat so efficiently that in one hour a resting adult generates enough heat to bring half a liter of water to a boil.
Cartilage has no blood supply of its own and gets nutrients by diffusion from surrounding tissues — which is why it heals so poorly after injury compared to bone.
Goosebumps are caused by tiny muscles (arrector pili) at the base of each hair follicle contracting — an evolutionary remnant from ancestors who raised fur to appear larger or conserve warmth.
Babies in the womb can taste foods that the mother eats — flavor compounds pass through the amniotic fluid, and studies show infants later prefer tastes they encountered before birth.
The human body replaces most of its atoms over a period of several years — only neurons in certain parts of the brain, tooth enamel, and lens cells may last a lifetime.
The lymphatic system drains about 2–4 liters of interstitial fluid back into the bloodstream daily — it is also the primary route through which immune cells patrol the body's tissues.
Humans are one of only a handful of species that experience menopause — the permanent end of reproductive capacity — which is thought to benefit offspring by freeing older females for childcare.
The aorta, the body's main artery, is about the width of a garden hose — yet it carries oxygenated blood from the heart to almost every organ in the body.
Humans have both fast-twitch and slow-twitch muscle fibers — fast-twitch for powerful short bursts (sprinting), slow-twitch for sustained endurance (marathon running).
Oxytocin, released by the posterior pituitary gland, promotes bonding, trust, and affection — nicknamed the 'love hormone,' it surges during childbirth, breastfeeding, and physical touch.
The human body has two lungs but they are not equal — the right lung has three lobes and is larger, while the left lung has two lobes and is smaller to accommodate the heart.
The human olfactory bulb, which processes scent, is directly connected to the hippocampus and amygdala — explaining why smells so powerfully evoke memories and emotions.
Humans are born with a diving reflex — when the face is submerged in cold water, heart rate slows and blood is redirected to vital organs, a survival response shared with marine mammals.
The human pancreas produces about 1–1.5 liters of digestive enzymes per day, including amylase, lipase, and proteases that break down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
The iris — the colored part of the eye — contains a unique pattern of crypts, ridges, and furrows that is more individual than a fingerprint, used in biometric identification.
The immune system's T cells 'remember' pathogens they have encountered, allowing faster, stronger responses on reinfection — the biological basis for both natural immunity and vaccines.
The human body has roughly 10 times more microbial cells than human cells — but since microbial cells are far smaller, they represent only about 1–3% of body mass.
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body — 99% of it is stored in bones and teeth, with the remaining 1% critical for muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and blood clotting.
The human body stores about 2,000 calories of glycogen in the muscles and liver — roughly enough for 90 minutes of intense exercise before the body must turn to fat reserves.
The human body has four chambers in the heart — left and right atria (upper) and left and right ventricles (lower) — with the left ventricle doing the most work as it pumps blood to the entire body.
The human body's total surface area of the alveoli in the lungs is about 70 square meters — roughly the area of a tennis court — providing enormous capacity for gas exchange.
Dopamine, associated with reward and pleasure, also plays a critical role in movement — its depletion in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease, leading to tremor and rigidity.
Fingertips have the highest density of touch receptors (Meissner's corpuscles) in the entire body, enabling humans to detect textures with a resolution of just 13 micrometers.
Babies are born with a rooting reflex — turning toward anything that strokes their cheek — an automatic feeding behavior that disappears by about 4 months as voluntary control develops.
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver — releasing it into the small intestine to help digest fats; the body can function normally without it after removal.
Platelet cells in the blood are incredibly fast: within seconds of a cut, platelets gather at the wound site and begin forming a clot, stopping blood loss.
The human body contains more than 200 different cell types — from neurons and red blood cells to hepatocytes and osteoblasts — each expressing different subsets of the same genetic blueprint.
Laughter activates the nucleus accumbens (reward center) and releases endorphins — studies show that laughter can reduce pain perception, lower cortisol, and enhance immune function.

Humans have a unique ability to run long distances in heat that few other animals can match — a form of persistence hunting possible because of bipedalism, sweat glands, and the ability to breathe independently of stride.

The blood-brain barrier is a selective filtering membrane formed by tightly packed cells lining brain capillaries — protecting the brain from pathogens and toxins while allowing essential nutrients through.
Vitamin D is actually a hormone, not a vitamin — it is synthesized in the skin from cholesterol when exposed to UV light and regulates calcium absorption, immune function, and gene expression.
Human birth weight roughly triples in the first year of life — the fastest relative growth rate of any primate during that period.
The human spleen acts as a blood reservoir — it stores about 8 fl oz (240 mL) of red blood cells and contracts during intense exercise or hemorrhage to release them into circulation.
The human retina processes about 10 million bits of information per second, but only about 10,000 bits per second actually reach conscious awareness — the rest is filtered by the thalamus.
The human body has a total of 12 pairs of ribs — 7 'true' ribs connect directly to the sternum, 3 'false' ribs connect indirectly, and 2 'floating' ribs attach only to the spine.
Newborns have a 'sucking blister' on their lips — a callus that develops in the womb and helps them latch and feed efficiently from birth.
The human hypothalamus, deep in the brain, regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and emotions — acting as the control center for the entire autonomic nervous system.
The human body loses about 1% of bone density per year after age 40 — weight-bearing exercise and calcium intake are the most effective ways to slow this decline.
Humans have roughly 500 lymph nodes distributed throughout the body — they filter lymph fluid and host the immune cells that identify and destroy pathogens.
The liver performs over 500 functions including detoxification, protein synthesis, glycogen storage, hormone metabolism, and production of bile — making it the body's largest internal organ.

Human saliva contains a painkiller called opiorphin that is up to 6 times more potent than morphine — though only present in tiny amounts, it may partly explain why oral wounds heal faster than skin wounds.
The brain's amygdala processes fear and emotional memories — people with damaged amygdalae feel no fear response, even to genuinely dangerous situations.
White blood cells (leukocytes) are the soldiers of the immune system — there are five main types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils, each with distinct roles.
Humans are the only primates with whites of the eyes (sclerae) — which may have evolved to allow others to follow our gaze, facilitating complex social communication.
The human pituitary gland, no larger than a pea, produces at least eight hormones including growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, and prolactin — earning it the title 'master gland' of the endocrine system.
Human DNA is about 99.9% identical between any two people — the 0.1% difference accounts for all visible and invisible biological variation between individuals.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body has a 'second brain' in the gut — the enteric nervous system contains over 500 million neurons that can function independently of the brain and communicate via the vagus nerve.
Bone is a living tissue constantly being remodeled — osteoblasts build new bone while osteoclasts break it down; the entire adult skeleton is replaced approximately every 10 years.
The average adult human brain weighs about 3 pounds (1.4 kg) and consumes approximately 11 watts of power — equivalent to a dim light bulb.
Humans and most primates are trichromats — possessing three types of color-sensitive cone cells — whereas many birds and fish are tetrachromats with four cone types, seeing ultraviolet light.
The prostate gland in males wraps around the urethra and produces fluid that makes up about 30% of semen volume — it tends to enlarge with age, often restricting urine flow.
The human body's fastest signal — myelinated A-fibers — conduct nerve impulses at up to 120 m/s (270 mph); myelination allows dramatically faster signaling than unmyelinated fibers.
The human stomach can expand from about 75 mL when empty to approximately 1 liter after a normal meal, and up to 4 liters after an exceptionally large meal.
About 70% of the human immune system resides in the gut — specifically in gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) — which is why diet and microbiome health profoundly affect immunity.
The human body has about 30,000 genes — far fewer than researchers expected before the Human Genome Project; the number is only twice that of a fruit fly.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Breast milk contains over 700 species of bacteria and hundreds of human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) that specifically feed beneficial gut bacteria in infants, shaping their microbiome.
The human Achilles tendon can withstand loads of up to 12 times body weight during running — yet it is the most commonly ruptured tendon in the body.
The biological clock (circadian rhythm) is driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus — a cluster of about 20,000 neurons that synchronize to the 24-hour day/night cycle.
Humans shed and regrow their entire outer layer of skin (epidermis) about every 27 days — over a lifetime this amounts to about 105 pounds of shed skin.

The glottis — the opening between the vocal cords — produces sound by rapidly opening and closing as air passes through; trained singers can control its vibrations to produce notes of extraordinary range.

Babies born before 37 weeks (premature) have lungs that lack sufficient surfactant — a soap-like substance needed to keep air sacs open; synthetic surfactant therapy has dramatically improved survival.
The iris color is determined by the amount of melanin pigment — more melanin produces brown eyes, less produces blue or green, and the color can continue to change slightly through childhood.
Human breast tissue contains receptors for cortisol and adrenaline, explaining why psychological stress and anxiety can affect breast density and are linked to higher breast cancer risk.
The human body contains about 0.2 milligrams of gold — distributed through the blood and other tissues — though at current prices, it amounts to only a fraction of a cent.
Muscle memory is a real biological phenomenon — repeated motor skills strengthen specific neural pathways in the cerebellum, making the movements automatic and less mentally demanding over time.
Pain is a complex perception, not just a signal — the same tissue damage produces different pain experiences depending on expectations, attention, emotional state, and past experiences.
The eardrum (tympanic membrane) is so thin — just 0.1 mm — that it can vibrate in response to sounds as faint as 10 decibels, equivalent to the rustling of leaves.

Human breast milk dynamically changes composition — even during a single feeding, the fat content rises as feeding progresses, and the protein and immune factor content shifts based on the baby's age and needs.
The inner ear's vestibular system detects linear acceleration and rotation in six directions — providing the brain with its sense of balance and spatial orientation.
During pregnancy, a woman's blood volume increases by 40–50% — the body manufactures extra red blood cells and plasma to supply oxygen and nutrients to the growing fetus.
The corpus callosum — a bundle of about 200 million nerve fibers — connects the left and right hemispheres of the brain and allows them to share information and coordinate tasks.
Epigenetic changes — modifications that turn genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence — accumulate throughout life and are influenced by diet, stress, exercise, and environment.
The human knee is the largest and most complex joint in the body — four bones, four ligaments, and two C-shaped cartilage pads (menisci) must work in precise coordination for normal movement.
Sleep deprivation impairs the immune system so severely that even one sleepless night can reduce natural killer cell activity by 70%, increasing vulnerability to infections and cancer.
The human body contains about 2–3 grams of zinc — concentrated in muscles, bones, skin, and the prostate — essential for DNA synthesis, wound healing, and immune function.
Natural killer (NK) cells are immune cells that patrol the body for infected or cancerous cells — they can trigger cell death within minutes of detecting an abnormal target.
The human diaphragm is the primary muscle of breathing — it contracts about 20,000 times per day, with each contraction expanding the chest cavity to draw air into the lungs.
Chronic inflammation — low-level immune activation without infection — is linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's, and many cancers, making it a key target in preventive medicine.
Human breast milk contains antibodies (particularly IgA) that coat the gut lining of newborns, providing passive immunity against pathogens the mother has encountered.
The human body's primary energy currency is ATP (adenosine triphosphate) — each molecule is recycled up to 500–750 times per day, with the body producing its own weight in ATP daily.
Humans are one of very few animals capable of voluntarily controlling their breathing — a unique adaptation that allowed the fine breath control required for complex speech and singing.
The human body generates enough electrical activity that some people can charge small devices with their warmth — skin surface temperature averages 91°F (33°C) and radiates infrared heat.
The tendons and ligaments of the foot function as springs — they store and release elastic energy with each step, making human walking and running about 50% more efficient.

Humans are highly dependent on sleep, spending about a third of their lives unconscious — during this time the brain consolidates memories, the body repairs tissues, and hormones like growth hormone are released.
The human lung contains about 300 million alveoli, each surrounded by capillaries — the combined surface area is about the size of half a tennis court.
An average human produces about 1 million sperm cells per second from puberty onward — over a lifetime, a male can produce over a trillion sperm.
The human pineal gland was called the 'seat of the soul' by Descartes — today we know it primarily regulates melatonin secretion, coordinating the body's internal clock with environmental light.
The placenta produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) — the hormone detected by pregnancy tests — within days of implantation, signaling the body to maintain the pregnancy.
Human hands contain 27 bones — 8 carpals in the wrist, 5 metacarpals in the palm, and 14 phalanges in the fingers — more bones per unit area than almost any other part of the body.

The human body can sense pain in virtually every tissue except the brain itself — neurosurgeons can operate on awake patients without causing brain pain, which is why brain tumors go unnoticed until they press on other structures.
Laughter is contagious because the brain has mirror neurons that automatically activate when we see or hear laughing — a social glue mechanism that deepens bonding and group cohesion.
Human tears contain lysozyme — an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls — making them a first line of antimicrobial defense in the eye.
Osteoporosis affects about 200 million people worldwide — it causes bones to become porous and fragile, with hip fractures being a leading cause of disability and death in the elderly.

The human body's inflammation response can raise core temperature by up to 4°C (7°F) during severe illness — a fever that creates a hostile environment for pathogens while accelerating immune responses.
The human ear can detect frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz — though this range narrows with age, particularly at the high-frequency end.
The brain's hippocampus — critical for forming new long-term memories — can generate new neurons throughout adulthood, a process called neurogenesis, particularly in response to exercise.
Proprioception — the sense of where your body parts are in space without looking — is often called the 'sixth sense' and relies on receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.
The human larynx descended into the throat during evolution, enabling the complex vowel sounds needed for language — no other animal's anatomy allows the same range of speech sounds.
The average person blinks 15–20 times per minute — mostly automatically — which amounts to about 10 million blinks per year, keeping the cornea moist and clear.
The human body produces about 20–40 liters of gas in the intestines every day through bacterial fermentation — most is absorbed, with only about 1–2 liters expelled.

Hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, turns bright red when oxygenated and dark red/purple when deoxygenated — veins look blue due to how skin absorbs different wavelengths of light.
Human fingertips can detect surface variations as small as 13 nanometers — about 100 times finer than the width of a human hair — giving us extraordinary sensitivity for fine motor tasks.
Humans lose about 50–100 hairs per day as part of normal hair cycling — each follicle independently cycles through growth (anagen), regression (catagen), and rest (telogen) phases.
The average person produces about 3–5 pounds (1.4–2.3 kg) of stool per week, 75% of which is water and the remaining 25% is bacteria, fiber, and dead cells.
Cortisol — the 'stress hormone' produced by the adrenal glands — follows a daily rhythm, peaking about 30 minutes after waking, helping mobilize energy for the demands of the day.

The lens of the human eye thickens and flattens (accommodation) to focus at different distances — this flexibility declines with age, causing presbyopia (difficulty focusing on near objects) in most people after 40.
Each kidney contains about 1 million tiny filtering units called nephrons — together they can filter about 200 liters of blood per day, producing just 1–2 liters of concentrated urine.
The human placenta is fully formed by the end of the first trimester and secretes estrogen and progesterone — hormones that maintain pregnancy and prepare the body for lactation.

Blood pressure is measured as two numbers — systolic (maximum, during a heartbeat) over diastolic (minimum, between beats); normal is under 120/80 mmHg, with values above 130/80 classified as hypertension.

The gut-brain axis — bidirectional communication between the enteric and central nervous systems via the vagus nerve and gut hormones — means gut bacteria can directly influence anxiety, mood, and stress response.
The human skull consists of 22 bones — 8 form the neurocranium (protecting the brain) and 14 form the viscerocranium (face) — most of which fuse completely by early adulthood.
Humans experience four distinct sleep stages cycling every 90 minutes: N1 (light sleep), N2 (true sleep), N3 (deep slow-wave sleep), and REM — a full night provides 4–6 complete cycles.
The human body has no organ for storing vitamin C — all excess is excreted in urine, which is why daily intake from food is essential to prevent scurvy.
Capillaries — the smallest blood vessels — are so narrow that red blood cells must line up single file to pass through them; their walls are only one cell thick to allow gas exchange.

The human brain has a region called Broca's area (in the left frontal lobe) dedicated to speech production — damage to it causes Broca's aphasia, where patients understand language but cannot speak fluently.
Endorphins — the body's natural opioids — are released by exercise, laughter, and even spicy food, binding to the same receptors as morphine to reduce pain and induce feelings of euphoria.
The human immune system's first line of defense includes physical barriers — skin, mucus, cilia, and stomach acid — before any immune cell activation is needed.
Human fetal cells during pregnancy can migrate to the mother's brain and liver and persist for decades — researchers found fetal cells in mother's brains up to 27 years after birth.
Human sweat is primarily water, but also contains electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride), lactic acid, urea, and ammonia — the salty taste comes from sodium chloride.
The human body has a remarkable ability to detect the taste of fat — a sixth taste (oleogustus) beyond sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami — through specific taste receptor cells.
The heart's electrical conduction system — the sinoatrial (SA) node, atrioventricular (AV) node, and Purkinje fibers — generates and coordinates heartbeat without input from the brain.
Humans are one of very few animals that experience adolescence — a prolonged developmental period between childhood and adulthood characterized by brain rewiring, especially in the prefrontal cortex.

Iron is the most common mineral deficiency in the world — it is essential for hemoglobin production, and deficiency causes anemia, fatigue, and impaired cognitive function, affecting over 1 billion people.

The surface of the small intestine is covered with finger-like projections called villi, each lined with even smaller microvilli (the 'brush border') — increasing the absorptive area to about 250 square meters.
Humans can detect low concentrations of the chemical geosmin — the earthy smell of rain on dry soil — at just 5 parts per trillion, indicating deep evolutionary sensitivity to rainfall.
Humans are the only primates with a chin — its evolution is debated, but theories include a structural byproduct of jaw reduction, a role in withstanding chewing forces, or a role in mate selection.
The human body contains about 2.5 grams of iron — most in hemoglobin, some stored in the liver as ferritin, and the rest in muscles as myoglobin, the protein that gives red meat its color.
Cartilage in embryos is largely replaced by bone during a process called ossification — but some cartilage persists in adults at joint surfaces, the ear, nose, and trachea.
The human brain's cerebellum — the 'little brain' at the base of the skull — contains more neurons than the rest of the brain combined, though they are smaller and differently organized.
Human nails are made of keratin — the same protein as hair and the outer layer of skin — and grow about 0.1 mm per day, slightly faster in summer and on the dominant hand.

Humans have a 'superpower' in pattern recognition — the brain dedicates an entire region (the fusiform face area) specifically to recognizing faces, able to process and distinguish thousands of individuals.
The human immune system includes about 2 trillion lymphocytes circulating in the blood and lymph — each programmed with receptors that recognize a unique molecular target.

Humans are among the longest-lived mammals relative to body size — a combination of large brains, social cooperation, and medicine has pushed average life expectancy past 70 years in most of the world.

Fascia is a continuous sheet of connective tissue made of collagen that surrounds and links every muscle, organ, nerve, and blood vessel in the body. Unlike tendons and ligaments, fascia forms an uninterrupted three-dimensional web that transmits mechanical tension across the entire body.

The thoracolumbar fascia is a broad diamond-shaped sheet in the lower back that connects the latissimus dorsi, gluteus maximus, and deep spinal muscles, effectively linking the upper and lower limbs through a single connective-tissue structure.

The lymphatic system is a one-way drainage network of vessels, nodes, and organs that returns interstitial fluid to the bloodstream, absorbs dietary fat from the gut, and hosts immune cells. Unlike blood, lymph has no pump — it moves by muscle contractions, breathing, and one-way valves.

The body contains approximately 600–700 lymph nodes arranged in clusters at the neck, armpits, groin, and around abdominal organs. Nodes filter lymph and act as staging areas where T and B lymphocytes encounter antigens and mount immune responses.

The thyroid gland produces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), hormones that regulate metabolism in virtually every cell. Even a small imbalance in thyroid output can affect body temperature, heart rate, weight, mood, and cognitive function.

The adrenal glands sit atop each kidney and have two distinct zones: the outer cortex secretes steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens), while the inner medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine in the 'fight-or-flight' stress response.

The pituitary gland, about the size of a pea, is called the 'master gland' because its hormones control the thyroid, adrenal glands, gonads, and growth. It is divided into the anterior lobe (which produces six major hormones) and the posterior lobe (which stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin).

The hypothalamus, a small brain region just above the brainstem, serves as the command center linking the nervous and endocrine systems. It monitors blood chemistry and body temperature and directs the pituitary to release or inhibit hormones accordingly.

There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves that emerge directly from the brain rather than the spinal cord; they supply sensation and motor control to the head and neck, and cranial nerve X (the vagus) extends all the way to the abdomen.

The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) is unique because its axons run directly from smell receptors in the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb without a relay in the thalamus, giving olfaction a more direct pathway to the limbic system and memory than any other sense.

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is the largest cranial nerve and provides sensory innervation to the entire face, scalp, and mouth, as well as motor control to the chewing muscles. Trigeminal neuralgia, a stabbing facial pain from nerve irritation, is described as one of the most severe pains known to medicine.

source.name: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The spinal cord is about 45 cm long in adults and runs from the brainstem to the first or second lumbar vertebra, after which the nerves continue as the cauda equina — meaning 'horse's tail' in Latin. It contains 31 pairs of spinal nerves organized into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal segments.

Gray matter in the spinal cord forms a butterfly-shaped core where interneurons and motor neurons process and relay signals; surrounding white matter consists of myelinated axon tracts carrying signals up to the brain (sensory) and down from the brain (motor).

The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes all nerves outside the brain and spinal cord and is divided into the somatic nervous system (voluntary movement and sensation) and the autonomic nervous system (involuntary regulation of organs, glands, and blood vessels).

Proprioception — the sense of body position and movement — is mediated by mechanoreceptors in muscles (muscle spindles), tendons (Golgi tendon organs), and joints. It allows you to touch your nose with eyes closed and is often called the 'sixth sense.'

Muscle spindles are stretch-sensitive receptors embedded within skeletal muscles. When a muscle is suddenly stretched, spindle afferents trigger the stretch reflex — a monosynaptic spinal reflex that contracts the muscle to resist the stretch, as seen when a doctor taps your knee tendon.

The vestibular system, housed in the inner ear's bony labyrinth, senses head movement and position using three semicircular canals (for rotational acceleration) and two otolith organs — the utricle and saccule — for linear acceleration and gravity.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Hair cells in the vestibular system have tiny stereocilia that bend when fluid in the semicircular canals moves. Bending one direction opens ion channels (depolarizing the cell and increasing nerve firing); bending the other direction closes them, giving the brain a precise readout of rotational direction.

Humans can taste five basic taste qualities: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory). Each is detected by specialized taste receptor cells on taste buds, with bitter having the most receptor gene variants — over 25 TAS2R genes — likely an evolutionary defense against toxins.

A sixth taste, fat (oleogustus), has been proposed and is now gaining acceptance; specialized receptors (CD36 and GPR120) on taste cells detect free fatty acids, which may explain the particular appeal of fatty foods beyond their texture alone.

The olfactory epithelium in the nasal cavity contains about 6–10 million olfactory receptor neurons, each expressing just one of the ~400 functional odorant receptor types in humans. Combinations of activated receptors create the neural code for a specific smell.

Olfactory receptor neurons are among the only neurons in the adult nervous system that continuously regenerate throughout life; they have a lifespan of only 30–60 days and are replaced from basal stem cells in the epithelium.

Pain signals travel to the brain via two main fiber types: fast A-delta fibers (myelinated, producing sharp immediate pain) and slow C fibers (unmyelinated, producing dull aching or burning pain). This is why an injury often produces a sharp first pain followed by a deeper, lingering second pain.

The gate control theory of pain proposes that non-painful input (like rubbing an injury) can 'close the gate' in the spinal cord dorsal horn, reducing pain signals ascending to the brain. This mechanism explains why rubbing a bumped elbow provides real, if temporary, relief.

Wound healing occurs in four overlapping stages: hemostasis (clotting, within minutes), inflammation (redness and swelling, hours to days), proliferation (new tissue formation, days to weeks), and remodeling (scar maturation, weeks to over a year).

During the proliferative phase of wound healing, fibroblasts migrate into the wound and deposit type III collagen to form granulation tissue; this is later replaced by stronger type I collagen in the remodeling phase, though scar tissue never fully regains the tensile strength of unwounded skin.

Bone remodeling is a continuous lifelong process in which osteoclasts resorb old or damaged bone and osteoblasts deposit new bone matrix. In a healthy adult, about 10% of the entire skeleton is replaced each year through this cycle.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: Bone remodeling is tightly coupled to mechanical loading: bones subjected to greater stress become denser, while bones that are unloaded (as in long-duration spaceflight or bed rest) lose mineral density rapidly. This principle underlies both weight-bearing exercise for osteoporosis prevention and the bone loss challenge of space travel.

There are three types of cartilage in the human body: hyaline cartilage (smooth, covering joint surfaces), elastic cartilage (flexible, found in the ear and epiglottis), and fibrocartilage (tough, found in intervertebral discs and the knee menisci). None contains blood vessels, so it heals poorly after injury.

Tendons connect muscle to bone and consist primarily of densely packed parallel collagen type I fibers, making them strong in tension but relatively inextensible. The Achilles tendon — the largest in the body — must withstand forces up to 12 times body weight during running.

Ligaments connect bone to bone across joints and are composed of dense irregular connective tissue with more elastin than tendons, allowing some stretch. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in the knee primarily resists anterior translation of the tibia and internal rotation — explaining why ACL tears are common in pivoting sports.

Synovial fluid is a viscous, egg-white-like fluid secreted by the synovial membrane lining joint capsules. It lubricates joint surfaces, reducing friction to near zero, and delivers nutrients to avascular hyaline cartilage. Its viscosity comes from long-chain hyaluronic acid molecules.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a clear, colorless fluid produced by the choroid plexus in the brain's ventricles. It cushions the brain and spinal cord, removes metabolic waste, and regulates intracranial pressure; roughly 500 mL is produced daily, with the full volume of about 150 mL replaced four times per day.

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by tight junctions between endothelial cells of brain capillaries, supported by astrocytic end-feet. It blocks most large and hydrophilic molecules from entering brain tissue, protecting the neural environment — but also making it one of the biggest obstacles in treating brain diseases.

The glymphatic system — a waste-clearance network unique to the brain — uses channels around blood vessels to flush cerebrospinal fluid through brain tissue during sleep, removing metabolic byproducts including amyloid-beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication highway linking the enteric nervous system (the gut's own 100-million-neuron network) with the central nervous system via the vagus nerve, hormones, and gut bacteria metabolites. About 90% of serotonin in the body is produced in the gut, not the brain.

The enteric nervous system (ENS) is so complex it can function independently of the brain and spinal cord — coordinating peristalsis, enzyme secretion, and blood flow throughout the gut even after the vagus nerve is severed. This autonomy earned it the nickname 'the second brain.'

Circadian rhythms are driven at the molecular level by an interlocking transcription-translation feedback loop involving the CLOCK and BMAL1 proteins, which activate Period (PER) and Cryptochrome (CRY) genes; PER and CRY proteins accumulate and then inhibit CLOCK/BMAL1, completing a ~24-hour cycle in every cell.

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus is the master clock that synchronizes peripheral clocks in every organ. It receives direct light input from intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin, which is most sensitive to blue light (~480 nm).

Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression that do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Key mechanisms include DNA methylation (silencing genes by adding methyl groups to cytosines) and histone modification (acetylation or methylation of histone proteins that package DNA, altering how tightly DNA is coiled and thus how accessible it is to transcription).

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Epigenetic marks accumulate with age in a characteristic pattern that can be used to estimate biological age — so-called 'epigenetic clocks' such as Horvath's clock can predict chronological age from methylation patterns across thousands of CpG sites with an accuracy of a few years.

Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG in humans) that cap and protect chromosome ends. With each cell division they shorten slightly because DNA polymerase cannot replicate the very end of a linear chromosome; when telomeres become critically short, the cell enters senescence or apoptosis.

Telomerase is the enzyme that adds telomere repeats back onto chromosome ends, counteracting erosion. It is highly active in stem cells, germ cells, and most cancer cells (allowing unlimited division), but largely inactive in differentiated adult cells — making telomere shortening a key component of cellular aging.

Adult stem cell niches are specialized microenvironments that maintain stem cells in an undifferentiated, self-renewing state. Examples include the bone marrow niche for hematopoietic stem cells, the intestinal crypt base for intestinal stem cells, and the hair follicle bulge for skin stem cells.

Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in bone marrow give rise to all blood cell types — red cells, platelets, and every variety of white cell — through a hierarchy of progressively committed progenitors. A single HSC transplant can fully reconstitute the immune and blood systems of an irradiated recipient.

The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is the longest cranial nerve, running from the brainstem through the neck, chest, and abdomen to innervate the heart, lungs, and most abdominal organs. It carries about 80% sensory (afferent) fibers, meaning most vagal communication is from the body to the brain, not the other way around.

The autonomic nervous system is divided into the sympathetic ('fight-or-flight') and parasympathetic ('rest-and-digest') branches. They have opposing effects on most target organs: for example, the sympathetic system increases heart rate and dilates airways, while the parasympathetic system slows the heart and stimulates digestion.

The lymphatic system plays a critical role in fat absorption: lacteals — specialized lymph capillaries in intestinal villi — absorb fat-rich chylomicrons from digested food and transport them as a milky fluid called chyle into the thoracic duct, which drains into the bloodstream at the left subclavian vein.

The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ and serves as a blood filter, removing aged red blood cells and circulating pathogens. It also stores a reserve of monocytes — white cells that rush to sites of inflammation — and platelets. The spleen can be removed without fatal consequences, but the patient becomes more susceptible to certain bacterial infections.

The thymus, located in the upper chest, is where T lymphocytes mature. It is largest relative to body size in infancy and involutes (shrinks and is replaced by fat) after puberty, but small functional remnants persist throughout life. This shrinkage is one reason immune responses weaken with age.

Cortisol follows a pronounced circadian rhythm, peaking within the first 30–45 minutes after waking (the 'cortisol awakening response') then declining through the day. This morning surge prepares the body for the day's metabolic demands by mobilizing glucose, suppressing inflammation, and sharpening cognition.

Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex that regulates blood pressure and electrolyte balance by promoting sodium retention and potassium excretion in the kidney's collecting duct. Its release is controlled by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), a key target for antihypertensive drugs.

Growth hormone (GH), secreted by the pituitary, stimulates growth, cell reproduction, and regeneration. Most GH is released in pulses during deep (slow-wave) sleep, which is one reason adequate sleep is essential for children's development and for adult tissue repair.

Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland in response to darkness, signals to the body that it is night-time and prepares it for sleep. Blue-spectrum light from screens suppresses melatonin secretion more powerfully than longer-wavelength light, which is why nighttime screen use can delay sleep onset.

The pancreas is a dual-function organ: its exocrine portion secretes digestive enzymes into the small intestine, while its endocrine islets of Langerhans secrete insulin (from beta cells) and glucagon (from alpha cells) directly into the bloodstream to regulate blood glucose.

Parathyroid hormone (PTH), from four tiny parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid, is the main regulator of calcium in the blood. It acts on bone (stimulating resorption to release calcium), kidneys (reducing calcium excretion and activating vitamin D), and the gut (increasing calcium absorption via vitamin D).

Nociceptors — the sensory receptors for pain — are free nerve endings found in skin, muscles, joints, and viscera. Unlike other sensory receptors, they do not adapt to prolonged stimulation; persistent pain keeps signaling, which is why chronic inflammation or injury continues to hurt.

Referred pain occurs when pain from an internal organ is perceived at a different body surface location due to convergence of visceral and somatic afferent signals in the spinal cord. Classic examples include cardiac pain felt in the left arm and jaw, and gallbladder pain felt in the right shoulder.

Bone is a composite material of collagen fibers (providing tensile strength and flexibility) and hydroxyapatite crystals (calcium phosphate mineral providing compressive strength). This combination gives bone a strength-to-weight ratio comparable to reinforced concrete.

Compact (cortical) bone forms the dense outer shell of most bones and is organized into cylindrical units called osteons (Haversian systems), each with a central canal carrying blood vessels. Cancellous (spongy) bone fills the interior with a porous lattice that is lightweight while resisting stress from multiple directions.

The intervertebral discs act as shock absorbers between vertebrae and consist of a tough outer annulus fibrosus (concentric rings of fibrocartilage) and a gel-like inner nucleus pulposus (rich in water and proteoglycans). They lose water content with age, reducing disc height and contributing to back pain and reduced spinal flexibility.

The human foot contains 26 bones, 33 joints, and over 100 muscles, tendons, and ligaments — roughly one-quarter of all the bones in the body. The arch system of the foot (medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, and transverse) acts as a spring that stores and returns elastic energy with each step.

source.name: American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society

text: Stem cells in the intestinal epithelium divide every 3–5 days to continuously replace the lining of the small intestine, which is fully renewed every 5–7 days. These intestinal stem cells sit in the base of crypts and are identified by expression of the Lgr5 marker.

Cellular senescence is a state in which damaged cells permanently stop dividing but resist apoptosis (programmed death). Senescent cells secrete inflammatory signals (the 'senescence-associated secretory phenotype'), and their accumulation with age is now recognized as a key driver of aging-related tissue dysfunction.

The cornea of the eye has no blood vessels (it is avascular) and receives oxygen directly from the air and from the aqueous humor. This transparency-enabling feature also means the cornea is immune-privileged and can be transplanted without blood-type matching, making corneal transplants the most frequently performed human transplant.

The lens of the eye is made of crystallin proteins packed into lens fiber cells that lack nuclei and organelles to maximize transparency. Because lens cells do not turn over, the proteins at the lens core were synthesized in embryonic life and must remain stable for a lifetime — making the lens proteins among the oldest in the body.

The retina is a light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing about 120 million rod photoreceptors (for low-light, achromatic vision) and 6 million cone photoreceptors (for color and detail in bright light). Cones are densely packed in the fovea centralis, where visual acuity is highest.

The human ear's cochlea converts mechanical sound vibrations into neural signals via about 15,500 hair cells arranged along the basilar membrane. High-frequency sounds maximally displace the membrane near the base; low-frequency sounds displace it near the apex — a spatial frequency map called tonotopy.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) vibrates in response to sound waves and transmits those vibrations through three tiny ossicles — the malleus, incus, and stapes. The stapes, the smallest bone in the body at roughly 3 mm, connects to the oval window of the cochlea.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Platelets are small anucleate cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes in bone marrow. When a blood vessel is injured, platelets adhere to exposed collagen via von Willebrand factor, become activated, and aggregate to form a primary platelet plug — the first step in hemostasis — before the coagulation cascade reinforces it with fibrin.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The coagulation cascade is a chain of enzymatic reactions involving clotting factors (mostly serine proteases) that ultimately convert soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. It has two initiating pathways — the extrinsic (tissue factor) and intrinsic (contact activation) — that converge at Factor X to produce thrombin.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are biconcave discs lacking a nucleus or mitochondria, optimized for carrying oxygen via hemoglobin. Their unusual shape maximizes surface area for gas exchange and gives them the flexibility to squeeze through capillaries narrower than their own diameter.

The heart's electrical system begins at the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium — the natural pacemaker — which fires about 60–100 times per minute at rest. The signal travels to the atrioventricular (AV) node, then through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to coordinate ventricular contraction.

Sweat glands come in two types: eccrine glands, distributed across most body skin and producing watery sweat for thermoregulation, and apocrine glands, found in armpits and groin and opening into hair follicles. Body odor comes not from apocrine sweat itself but from bacteria metabolizing its fatty-acid and protein-rich secretions.

The human kidney filters about 180 liters of blood plasma per day, yet produces only 1–2 liters of urine, meaning over 99% of the filtered volume is reabsorbed. The nephron — the kidney's functional unit — accomplishes this via sequential active and passive transport along the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, and collecting duct.

The loop of Henle creates a concentration gradient in the kidney medulla through a countercurrent multiplier mechanism, allowing the kidney to produce urine much more concentrated than blood plasma — up to 1,200 mOsm/kg, about four times the plasma concentration. This capacity is crucial for water conservation.

The diaphragm is the dome-shaped primary muscle of breathing. When it contracts and flattens, it increases thoracic volume and decreases pressure, drawing air into the lungs (inspiration). Relaxation allows the chest to recoil, expelling air. Diaphragm fatigue limits endurance exercise capacity.

Surfactant is a phospholipid-protein mixture secreted by type II pneumocytes in the lungs that reduces surface tension in alveoli, preventing them from collapsing during exhalation. Premature infants lacking surfactant develop respiratory distress syndrome; synthetic surfactant therapy has dramatically reduced infant mortality.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system where the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs at about one-sixth the pressure of the systemic circulation. This low pressure minimizes fluid leakage into the alveoli, which would impair gas exchange.

The liver performs over 500 distinct metabolic functions, including detoxifying drugs and alcohol, synthesizing clotting factors and plasma proteins, metabolizing carbohydrates, fats, and amino acids, and storing glycogen and fat-soluble vitamins. It receives dual blood supply — oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich blood from the portal vein.

Myelin, the insulating sheath wrapped around axons by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS), dramatically increases nerve conduction velocity by allowing saltatory conduction — the electrical signal jumps between gaps in the myelin called nodes of Ranvier rather than propagating continuously. Myelinated fibers can conduct at over 100 m/s.

Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cells in the brain and perform numerous functions: they regulate the chemical environment of synapses, maintain the blood-brain barrier, provide metabolic support to neurons, and participate in neural circuit modulation. They are increasingly recognized as active participants in information processing.

Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells, derived from yolk-sac progenitors rather than bone marrow. They constantly survey their environment with mobile processes, prune synapses during development, clear debris, and mount inflammatory responses — but chronic microglial activation is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

The neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber. The neurotransmitter acetylcholine is released, binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, and triggers an action potential that leads to muscle contraction via calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Muscle contraction follows the sliding filament theory: thick myosin filaments use ATP to pull thin actin filaments inward, shortening the sarcomere. This cross-bridge cycle repeats as long as calcium and ATP are present, generating force and movement at the microscopic level that powers every voluntary action.

The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is the body's central stress-response system. In response to stress, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which signals the pituitary to secrete ACTH, which in turn drives cortisol release from the adrenal cortex. Chronic HPA activation is linked to anxiety, depression, and immune suppression.

Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is thermogenic fat found especially around the neck and upper back in adults. Unlike white fat, BAT is packed with mitochondria containing uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which dissipates the proton gradient as heat rather than synthesizing ATP — helping newborns and cold-adapted adults generate body heat without shivering.

Leptin, a hormone secreted by white adipose tissue in proportion to fat stores, signals to the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure. Leptin resistance — where the brain fails to respond to leptin signals — is now considered a central mechanism in obesity, explaining why simply having high leptin does not prevent overeating.

The placenta is a temporary organ created during pregnancy that forms from both maternal and fetal cells. It transfers oxygen and nutrients from mother to fetus, removes fetal waste products, and produces hormones (including hCG, estrogen, and progesterone) that maintain pregnancy — making it the only organ that is both a fetal and a maternal structure simultaneously.

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests. It is produced by the developing embryo immediately after implantation and signals the corpus luteum to continue producing progesterone, preventing menstruation and sustaining the pregnancy until the placenta takes over hormone production around week 10.

The human genome contains approximately 3.2 billion base pairs of DNA, but only about 1.5% encodes proteins. The vast majority of the genome — once dismissively called 'junk DNA' — includes regulatory sequences, non-coding RNAs, repetitive elements, and evolutionary relics, much of which has since been found to have functional roles.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Alternative splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple different proteins by combining exons in different patterns. The human genome has ~20,000 protein-coding genes, yet the proteome contains well over 100,000 distinct proteins — largely because most genes are alternatively spliced.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short (~22 nucleotide) non-coding RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression by binding to complementary sequences in messenger RNA, causing degradation or translation inhibition. Over 2,000 miRNA genes have been identified in humans, and each miRNA can regulate hundreds of target genes.

The complement system is a cascade of plasma proteins that forms part of innate immunity. It can be activated by antibody-antigen complexes (classical pathway), bacterial surfaces (lectin pathway), or spontaneous hydrolysis (alternative pathway), ultimately punching pores in bacterial membranes (membrane attack complex) and flagging pathogens for phagocytosis.

Natural killer (NK) cells are innate immune lymphocytes that recognize and destroy virus-infected cells and tumor cells without prior sensitization. They detect the absence of self-MHC-I molecules — a signal that the cell is infected or cancerous — making them a first-response surveillance system against cancer.

Autophagy — literally 'self-eating' — is a cellular recycling process in which damaged organelles and misfolded proteins are enclosed in a double membrane vesicle (autophagosome) and delivered to lysosomes for degradation. Autophagy is upregulated during fasting and is essential for cellular homeostasis and longevity.

The proteasome is a large protein complex that degrades ubiquitin-tagged proteins. Ubiquitin — a small 76-amino-acid protein — is attached to proteins earmarked for disposal; the proteasome then unfolds and chops them into peptides. This system regulates protein turnover, cell cycle progression, and the immune response.

The human microbiome is not just in the gut: distinct microbial communities colonize the skin (about 1,000 species), oral cavity, lungs, urogenital tract, and eyes. Disruptions to these communities are linked to eczema, asthma, periodontal disease, urinary tract infections, and other conditions.

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) — particularly butyrate, propionate, and acetate — are produced when gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber. Butyrate is the primary fuel for colonocytes (colon cells), stimulates regulatory T-cell development, and has anti-inflammatory effects; low fiber intake reduces SCFA production and is linked to inflammatory bowel disease.

The human body has about 45 miles (72 km) of nerves, ranging from the thick sciatic nerve (~2 cm diameter) to tiny unmyelinated C fibers thinner than a micron. Peripheral nerves can regenerate after injury at a rate of roughly 1 mm per day — meaning recovery from a severe nerve cut can take months to years.

The deep fascia forms the muscular compartments of the limbs. In compartment syndrome, swelling after injury raises pressure within these closed fascial sheaths, compressing blood vessels and nerves. Without emergency fasciotomy to release the pressure, permanent muscle and nerve damage can occur within hours.

Plantar fasciitis — inflammation of the plantar fascia connecting the heel to the toes — is the most common cause of heel pain, affecting about 2 million people per year in the US. The plantar fascia bears up to 14% of the total load during walking and stores elastic energy to support the foot arch.

The skin's dermis is largely composed of an extracellular matrix of collagen and elastin fibers embedded in proteoglycans, all produced by dermal fibroblasts. Elastin gives skin its ability to snap back after stretching; with age, elastin degrades and cross-links accumulate, causing wrinkles and sagging.

Melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis produce melanin through a pathway starting with tyrosine and the enzyme tyrosinase. Each melanocyte serves about 36 surrounding keratinocytes, donating melanin-filled vesicles (melanosomes) that cap the keratinocyte nucleus to protect DNA from UV radiation.

Keratinocytes are born in the basal layer of the epidermis and migrate outward over ~4 weeks, progressively filling with keratin, losing their organelles, and flattening to form the tough, waterproof stratum corneum before shedding. This constant renewal replaces the entire skin surface roughly every month.

The hair follicle is a complex mini-organ that cycles through growth (anagen), regression (catagen), and rest (telogen) phases. Scalp hairs remain in anagen for 2–7 years, which is why scalp hair can grow very long, while eyelash hairs have a short anagen of just 30–45 days.

During the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle, estrogen stimulates the endometrium to thicken. After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum further prepares it for implantation. If fertilization does not occur, progesterone drops, the endometrium sheds (menstruation), and the cycle restarts.

Sperm cells are about 50 micrometers long (about half a millimeter) and can survive 3–5 days inside the female reproductive tract. They undergo capacitation — a series of biochemical changes — after entering the reproductive tract, which is required before they can fertilize an egg.

The acrosome reaction is a key fertilization event in which enzymes stored in the cap of the sperm head (the acrosome) are released to digest through the zona pellucida — the glycoprotein layer surrounding the egg — enabling the sperm to fuse with the egg membrane.

Neural tube defects (like spina bifida) occur when the embryonic neural tube fails to close during the third to fourth week of gestation. Adequate folic acid (vitamin B9) before and during early pregnancy reduces the risk by up to 70%, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended for all people of childbearing age.

Apoptosis is programmed cell death executed by proteases called caspases. It is essential for development (sculpting fingers by eliminating webbing, removing neurons that fail to make proper connections), immune tolerance (deleting self-reactive T cells), and tumor suppression. Unlike necrosis, it produces neat cell fragments that are silently phagocytosed without inflammation.

The cell cycle has built-in checkpoints (G1, S, G2-M) where surveillance proteins verify that DNA is undamaged and replication is complete before allowing the cell to proceed. The tumor-suppressor protein p53 is a key checkpoint regulator; mutations in the TP53 gene occur in over half of all human cancers.

Stem cells in the bone marrow include not only hematopoietic stem cells but also mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which can differentiate into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, adipocytes, and fibroblasts. MSCs also have immunosuppressive properties that are being explored in therapies for autoimmune diseases and graft-versus-host disease.

Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are adult cells reprogrammed back to an embryonic-like pluripotent state by introducing four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc). This 2006 discovery by Shinya Yamanaka, which earned him the 2012 Nobel Prize, opened the door to patient-specific stem cells without embryo destruction.

The mitochondrion has its own circular genome (mtDNA), a remnant of an ancient bacterial endosymbiont. Human mtDNA contains 37 genes and is inherited exclusively from the mother, making it a valuable tool for tracing maternal lineage and studying human migration out of Africa.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body produces approximately 25 trillion red blood cells, and about 2 million new ones are made every second in the bone marrow. Old red cells (after ~120 days) are destroyed primarily in the spleen, and their heme is broken down to bilirubin — the pigment that gives bruises their yellow color and urine its yellow tint.

The nitric oxide (NO) molecule is a gaseous signaling compound produced by endothelial cells from arginine by the enzyme eNOS. It diffuses into vascular smooth muscle and causes relaxation and vasodilation, regulating blood pressure. Nitroglycerin, used to treat angina since the 1870s, works by being converted to NO in the body.

The lymphatic system has no central pump, but lymph flow is assisted by contractions of smooth muscle in lymph vessel walls, one-way lymphatic valves, skeletal muscle contractions, respiratory pressure changes, and pulsation of adjacent arteries. Manual lymphatic drainage massage leverages these mechanisms to reduce lymphedema.

The stomach secretes about 2–3 liters of gastric juice per day, containing hydrochloric acid (pH ~1.5–2) and pepsin. The extreme acidity activates pepsinogen to pepsin for protein digestion and kills most ingested bacteria. Stomach epithelial cells are protected by a thick mucus layer and are rapidly replaced every 3–5 days.

The small intestine is about 6 meters long in adults and is lined with finger-like villi each covered in microvilli (together called the brush border), which increase absorptive surface area to roughly 250 square meters — about the size of a tennis court. The small intestine absorbs most nutrients, water, and minerals from digested food.

Peristalsis is the wave-like muscular contraction that propels food through the digestive tract. It is coordinated by the enteric nervous system and occurs in the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and colon. Antiperistalsis — reverse waves — drives vomiting when the brainstem activates the vomiting center.

Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, emulsifies dietary fats into smaller droplets to increase the surface area for lipase enzymes. Bile salts are derived from cholesterol and are recycled via enterohepatic circulation — reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver, completing 6–10 circuits per day.

Glycolysis — the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate — occurs in the cytoplasm and produces a net gain of 2 ATP. The citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria then extract up to 30–32 more ATP per glucose molecule through electron transport and chemiosmosis.

Ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, acetone) are produced by the liver from fatty acids when carbohydrate availability is low. The brain, which normally runs almost exclusively on glucose, can derive up to 75% of its energy from ketones during prolonged fasting or a ketogenic diet, reducing its glucose requirement.

The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is a hormonal cascade that regulates blood pressure and fluid balance. Reduced kidney perfusion triggers renin release, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE then converts it to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that also drives aldosterone release. ACE inhibitors and ARBs block this system and are among the world's most prescribed blood pressure drugs.

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone produced by the kidney in response to low oxygen levels (hypoxia). It stimulates bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. Athletes who train at altitude naturally boost EPO; synthetic EPO is used medically for anemia and is also a banned performance-enhancing drug.

The somatosensory cortex is organized as a 'homunculus' — a distorted map of the body surface, with disproportionately large areas devoted to the hands, lips, and tongue, which have the highest density of sensory receptors. The motor cortex has a corresponding motor homunculus with similar enlargements for fine motor regions.

Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the strengthening of a synaptic connection after repeated stimulation and is considered the primary cellular mechanism of learning and memory. It requires NMDA receptor activation and results in insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane, increasing the response to future signals.

The hippocampus is critical for forming new episodic and spatial memories. The famous patient H.M., who had both hippocampi surgically removed to treat epilepsy, could no longer form new explicit memories, though older memories and procedural skills were intact — demonstrating the hippocampus's specific role in memory consolidation.

Sleep has two main types that alternate through the night in ~90-minute cycles: non-REM sleep (divided into three stages from light to deep) and REM (rapid eye movement) sleep. Deep non-REM sleep is critical for physical restoration and memory consolidation; REM sleep is associated with vivid dreaming and emotional processing.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is the most anterior part of the frontal lobe and is the seat of executive functions: planning, decision-making, impulse control, and working memory. The PFC is the last brain region to fully mature, not completing myelination until the mid-20s, which explains adolescent impulsivity.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: The amygdala, an almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe, processes emotional significance and is central to the fear response. It can trigger the fight-or-flight response faster than the prefrontal cortex can consciously evaluate a threat — a 'low road' pathway that provides rapid but sometimes inaccurate threat assessment.

Dopamine is a neurotransmitter with multiple roles: it mediates reward and motivation (mesolimbic pathway), voluntary movement (nigrostriatal pathway), and the regulation of the pituitary (tuberoinfundibular pathway). Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease; excessive dopamine signaling is linked to schizophrenia.

Serotonin (5-HT) is a neurotransmitter synthesized from the amino acid tryptophan. In the brain it regulates mood, sleep, and appetite; in the gut it coordinates intestinal movements. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most prescribed antidepressants, and work by blocking serotonin's reabsorption at synapses.

GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, counterbalancing glutamate's excitatory effects. Benzodiazepines (like diazepam) and alcohol enhance GABA receptor activity, producing sedation, anxiolysis, and muscle relaxation. Disrupted GABA signaling is implicated in epilepsy, anxiety disorders, and insomnia.

Neuroplasticity — the brain's ability to reorganize by forming new synaptic connections — continues throughout life. Adult neurogenesis (birth of new neurons) occurs in the hippocampal dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb; physical exercise and environmental enrichment promote it, while chronic stress suppresses it.

Broca's area (left inferior frontal gyrus) is essential for speech production and grammar processing; Wernicke's area (left posterior superior temporal gyrus) is critical for language comprehension. Damage to Broca's causes halting, effortful speech; damage to Wernicke's produces fluent but meaningless speech — two distinct aphasia syndromes.

The kidneys regulate blood pH through bicarbonate reabsorption, hydrogen ion secretion, and ammonia production. Even small deviations from the normal arterial pH of 7.35–7.45 can be life-threatening — pH below 7.2 impairs cardiac function, and above 7.6 causes neuromuscular excitability (tetany) and seizures.
