Vitamin D is technically a prohormone rather than a vitamin. Skin converts a cholesterol precursor to vitamin D3 using UVB radiation; the liver then converts it to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and the kidney produces the active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), which regulates calcium absorption and immune function.

The tongue has about 10,000 taste buds, each containing 50–150 taste receptor cells with a lifespan of only 10–14 days — they are among the shortest-lived sensory cells in the body. Taste perception declines with age partly because taste bud numbers decrease and replacement slows.

Proprioceptive signals from muscle spindles are processed in the cerebellum, which compares intended movement (from the motor cortex) with actual movement feedback and sends corrective signals. Cerebellar damage causes ataxia — jerky, uncoordinated movements — because the error-correction loop is broken.

The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) stabilizes the visual image on the retina during head movement by producing an eye rotation equal and opposite to the head rotation. It operates with remarkably short latency (~7 ms) — far faster than visually guided eye movements — because it uses a simple three-neuron arc.

The blood type system includes not only the ABO system but also the Rh factor (positive or negative) and over 30 other blood group systems (Kell, Duffy, Kidd, Lewis, etc.) — making each person's blood antigen profile unique. Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative mother and Rh-positive fetus can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn.

The lymph nodes are connected in chains and clusters along lymph vessels; the thoracic duct — the largest lymphatic vessel — collects lymph from the lower body and left side of the upper body and empties it into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper quadrant.

The sinoatrial (SA) node's spontaneous pacing rate is about 100 beats per minute, but resting heart rate is typically 60–80 bpm because the parasympathetic nervous system (via the vagus nerve) continuously slows it. Highly trained endurance athletes can have resting heart rates below 40 bpm due to elevated vagal tone.

Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. At rest it is about 5 L/min; during intense exercise a trained athlete's heart can pump over 40 L/min — an 8-fold increase. This is achieved by increasing both heart rate and stroke volume (via greater venous return and more forceful contraction).

The periosteum is the fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of bones (except at joint surfaces). It contains osteoprogenitor cells essential for bone repair and is richly innervated — making fractures so painful. Bones grow in width by periosteal appositional growth, while length increases at epiphyseal growth plates.

The epiphyseal growth plate (physis) at the ends of long bones is a zone of hyaline cartilage where bone lengthening occurs in children and adolescents. Growth plates close (ossify) after puberty under the influence of estrogen (in both sexes), which is why girls, who experience earlier estrogen surges, typically stop growing taller earlier than boys.

Hyaluronic acid is a glycosaminoglycan found throughout the body's extracellular matrix — in synovial fluid, skin, the vitreous humor of the eye, and connective tissue. One gram can hold up to 6 liters of water, giving connective tissues turgor and cushioning. It is also widely used in dermatology and orthopedics.

The Golgi apparatus is a stack of membrane-bound cisternae that sorts, modifies, and packages proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum for secretion, delivery to organelles, or insertion into the plasma membrane. It adds carbohydrate chains to proteins (glycosylation) that are critical for cell recognition, immune function, and receptor binding.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and the hydroxyl radical are byproducts of aerobic metabolism. In small amounts they act as signaling molecules; in excess they damage DNA, lipids, and proteins. The body deploys antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) to neutralize them.

The hypothalamus regulates body temperature through both heat-production mechanisms (shivering thermogenesis, brown fat activation, vasoconstriction) and heat-loss mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation, behavioral cooling). Pyrogens — molecules released during infection — reset the hypothalamic thermostat upward to produce fever, which enhances immune function.

The corneal reflex — blinking when something approaches the eye — is mediated by the trigeminal nerve (afferent, sensing the stimulus) and the facial nerve (efferent, closing the eyelid). It is used to test brainstem integrity in unconscious patients; its absence can indicate brainstem damage.

The pupillary light reflex — constriction of the pupil in response to bright light — involves the optic nerve (CN II) carrying the afferent signal and the oculomotor nerve (CN III) carrying the parasympathetic constriction signal. Importantly, it is consensual — both pupils constrict when one eye is illuminated.

Nociceptive pain signals ascending to the brain synapse in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, then cross to the opposite side and ascend in the spinothalamic tract to the thalamus, which relays them to the somatosensory cortex (conscious localization) and limbic system (emotional suffering component of pain).

Endorphins are endogenous opioid peptides released by the hypothalamus and pituitary gland in response to pain, stress, or vigorous exercise. They bind the same receptors as morphine, producing analgesia and euphoria — the 'runner's high' is partly attributed to endorphin release, though recent research also implicates endocannabinoids.

Phagocytosis is the process by which neutrophils and macrophages engulf and destroy pathogens and cellular debris. After engulfing a target into a phagosome, they fuse it with lysosomes containing digestive enzymes and reactive oxygen species. Neutrophils — the most abundant white blood cells — are usually the first responders to infection.

MHC (major histocompatibility complex) molecules — called HLA in humans — are cell-surface proteins that present peptide fragments to T lymphocytes. MHC class I (on all nucleated cells) presents peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells; MHC class II (on antigen-presenting cells) presents to CD4+ helper T cells. MHC diversity makes organ transplant matching difficult.

Antibodies (immunoglobulins) have a Y-shaped structure with two heavy and two light chains linked by disulfide bonds. The variable regions at the tips of the Y form the antigen-binding site (Fab region); the constant Fc region determines the antibody class (IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, IgD) and its effector functions.

Breast milk contains immunoglobulin A (IgA), lactoferrin, lysozyme, and oligosaccharides that act as prebiotics, collectively conferring passive immunity and shaping the infant gut microbiome. Colostrum — the first milk — is especially rich in IgA and immune factors, explaining why even brief breastfeeding has measurable health benefits.

The average adult produces about 1.5 liters of saliva per day. Saliva contains amylase (beginning starch digestion), lysozyme and IgA (antimicrobial protection), mucins (lubrication), and bicarbonate (neutralizing acid). Dry mouth (xerostomia) dramatically increases the risk of dental cavities.

Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, rating 5 on the Mohs scale — harder than steel. It is 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite crystallites) with no cells or collagen, and unlike bone it cannot self-repair. Once enamel is lost to acid erosion or abrasion, it is gone permanently.

Cartilage has no blood supply — it relies on diffusion of nutrients from synovial fluid or perichondrium. This is why cartilage injuries heal so poorly: without a vascular inflammatory response, the repair process is severely limited. Fibrocartilage scar tissue, which forms in some cartilage defects, lacks the biomechanical properties of hyaline cartilage.

The Achilles tendon stores elastic strain energy during the loading phase of running and releases it during push-off, acting as a biological spring. This mechanism reduces metabolic energy expenditure by about 35% compared to running on a rigid foot, and explains why having compliant tendons is an advantage for long-distance running.

Interoception is the sense of the internal state of the body — hunger, thirst, heartbeat, bladder fullness, temperature, and pain. Recent neuroscience frames interoception as a key driver of emotion and subjective feeling; the insula cortex is the primary interoceptive cortex and is activated during both physical discomfort and emotional distress.

The human body contains about 206 bones in adulthood, down from roughly 270–300 at birth because many bones fuse during development. Babies have more cartilage and separate bony elements (for example, the skull has several plates to allow passage through the birth canal) that fuse through childhood.

Fascia contains its own mechanoreceptors (Ruffini endings, Pacinian corpuscles) and free nerve endings, meaning it contributes to proprioception, interoception, and pain. Myofascial pain syndrome — characterized by trigger points of hyperirritable muscle-fascia — is thought to arise from disrupted motor end plates combined with sensitized fascial receptors.

The lymphatic system clears macromolecules, immune cells, and lipids from tissues that blood capillaries cannot remove. In cancer, tumor cells can enter lymphatic vessels and be trapped in sentinel lymph nodes — the first nodes a tumor drains to. Sentinel node biopsy helps surgeons determine if cancer has spread without removing all regional nodes.

The thyroid gland's follicles store thyroid hormone precursor (thyroglobulin) in a colloid gel, providing a 2–3 month reserve of hormone. Iodine deficiency prevents synthesis of T3 and T4; the pituitary then secretes excess TSH to stimulate the thyroid, causing it to enlarge into a goiter.

Oxytocin, the 'bonding hormone,' is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It promotes uterine contractions during labor, milk ejection during breastfeeding, and social bonding, trust, and reduced anxiety in both sexes. Synthetic oxytocin (Pitocin) is one of the most widely used drugs in obstetrics to induce or augment labor.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) is released from the posterior pituitary when blood osmolarity rises or blood volume falls. It acts on the collecting ducts of the kidney to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, dramatically increasing water reabsorption and concentrating urine. Alcohol suppresses ADH, which is why alcohol consumption leads to increased urination and dehydration.

The immune system distinguishes self from non-self through central and peripheral tolerance mechanisms. In the thymus, T cells that react strongly against self-peptides are eliminated (negative selection). Failures of tolerance lead to autoimmune diseases, of which over 80 distinct conditions have been identified in humans.

Mast cells are immune cells found in connective tissue, especially near blood vessels and under skin and mucosal surfaces. They contain granules filled with histamine, heparin, and other mediators. When triggered by IgE antibodies binding allergens, they degranulate rapidly — causing the redness, swelling, and itch of allergic reactions and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis.

The colon absorbs water and electrolytes from indigestible food residues to form feces, reducing the roughly 1.5 liters of liquid reaching the large intestine daily to about 150 mL of stool. Gut bacteria ferment remaining fiber, producing gas (mainly CO2, methane, and hydrogen) as a byproduct.

The liver synthesizes most plasma proteins, including albumin (the most abundant, maintaining blood osmotic pressure), clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, XI, XII), and acute-phase proteins that rise sharply during infection and inflammation (fibrinogen, C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A).

Brown adipose tissue is most active in infants (who cannot shiver) and in adults exposed to cold. In 2009, PET-CT scans confirmed that metabolically active brown fat persists in adults, primarily in the supraclavicular region. Its discovery has renewed interest in activating BAT as a potential treatment for obesity and metabolic syndrome.

Ghrelin, known as the 'hunger hormone,' is secreted mainly by the stomach and rises before meals, signaling hunger to the hypothalamus. After bariatric surgery (gastric bypass), ghrelin levels drop dramatically and remain low, partly explaining the strong appetite suppression seen after the procedure beyond simple stomach restriction.

The cornea accounts for about 65–75% of the eye's total refractive power; the lens provides the remaining 25–35% and fine-tunes focus. In presbyopia, the lens gradually stiffens with age, reducing its ability to change shape (accommodate) for near vision — typically becoming noticeable around age 40–45.

The thalamus, sometimes called the 'relay station of the brain,' is a paired egg-shaped structure in the center of the brain that forwards almost all sensory information (except olfaction) to the appropriate cortical areas. It also regulates consciousness and alertness; damage to specific thalamic nuclei can cause permanent unconsciousness.

The basal ganglia — a group of nuclei including the striatum, globus pallidus, and substantia nigra — are critical for action selection, habit formation, and procedural learning. They operate via 'direct' (go) and 'indirect' (no-go) pathways to facilitate desired movements and suppress unwanted ones. Their dysfunction underlies Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease.

The corpus callosum — a thick band of about 200–250 million axons — connects the two cerebral hemispheres, allowing them to coordinate and share information. Severing it (split-brain surgery) can control severe epilepsy but reveals that the two hemispheres have largely independent consciousness, each unaware of what the other perceives.

Oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system myelinate up to 50 axon segments each, whereas peripheral Schwann cells myelinate only one segment each. This difference is why CNS axon regeneration after injury is much poorer than PNS regeneration — oligodendrocytes and CNS myelin debris produce inhibitory signals that block regrowth.

The enteroendocrine cells scattered throughout the gut epithelium are the body's largest endocrine system by cell number. They sense luminal contents (nutrients, bacteria, pH) and release peptide hormones including GLP-1, GIP, CCK, and PYY, which coordinate digestion, insulin secretion, satiety, and gut motility.

The skin microbiome of the axilla (armpit) is dominated by Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species, which produce volatile fatty acids and sulfur compounds from apocrine sweat — the actual chemical basis of body odor. The composition of the axillary microbiome, which varies between individuals, explains why body odor smells different from person to person.

Telomere length in white blood cells correlates inversely with biological age and the risk of age-related diseases. Chronic psychological stress, smoking, obesity, and sedentary behavior accelerate telomere shortening, while regular exercise and a healthy diet are associated with longer telomeres and slower cellular aging.

X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) occurs in every female cell at around day 16 of embryonic development: one of the two X chromosomes is randomly silenced by coating it with XIST RNA and adding repressive histone marks. The resulting patchwork of maternally and paternally active X chromosomes means females are genetic mosaics.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon in which certain genes are expressed from only one parental chromosome. The IGF2 gene (insulin-like growth factor 2) is only expressed from the paternal allele; CDKN1C is only expressed from the maternal allele. Disruption of imprinting causes Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes depending on which parental copy is deleted.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The lymph capillaries (initial lymphatics) are blind-ended tubes with loosely overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way flap valves, allowing interstitial fluid, large proteins, and cells to enter but not flow back. They collect this lymph and pass it through progressively larger collecting vessels and lymph nodes.

The human circadian clock has a natural period slightly longer than 24 hours (about 24.2 hours), and daily light exposure — especially morning light — resets it to stay synchronized with the solar day. Shift work and transmeridian travel cause 'circadian misalignment,' which increases the risk of metabolic disease, cancer, and cardiovascular problems.

source.name: NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences

text: The interstitium — the fluid-filled space between cells throughout the body — was formally proposed as a new organ in 2018. It consists of collagen bundles and hyaluronic acid–filled spaces that form a pressurized shock-absorbing network and may serve as a highway for cancer metastasis.

The number of synapses in the human brain peaks in early childhood — roughly 15,000 synapses per neuron around age 2 — then is pruned back through adolescence to approximately 7,000 per neuron in adulthood. This synaptic pruning, guided by activity (use-it-or-lose-it), sharpens neural circuits; abnormal pruning is implicated in autism and schizophrenia.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: The blood-brain barrier is not uniform: the circumventricular organs (area postrema, median eminence, subfornical organ, etc.) deliberately lack a tight BBB so the brain can sample blood-borne hormones and molecules directly. The area postrema is the vomiting trigger zone that responds to blood-borne toxins — which is why many poisons cause nausea.

DNA is packed into the nucleus with remarkable efficiency: the roughly 2 meters of DNA in each human cell is compressed about 10,000-fold into a nucleus just 6 micrometers in diameter. This is achieved through hierarchical wrapping: DNA around histone octamers (nucleosomes), which coil into 30-nm fibers, then into loops attached to a protein scaffold.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Transposons — mobile genetic elements sometimes called 'jumping genes' — make up about 45% of the human genome. While most are silenced by epigenetic mechanisms, some remain active and their mobilization contributes to somatic mutations in aging and cancer. Transposons have also been a major driver of evolutionary innovation throughout our genome's history.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The CRISPR-Cas9 system — derived from bacterial immune memory — allows precise editing of any DNA sequence in living cells. Since its adaptation for human cells was demonstrated in 2013, it has been used to investigate gene function, develop disease models, and treat sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia in clinical trials with durable results.

Fibrosis — the abnormal accumulation of connective tissue after repeated injury or inflammation — can impair organ function in the liver (cirrhosis), lungs (pulmonary fibrosis), kidneys, and heart. Activated myofibroblasts are the key cells that deposit excessive collagen in fibrosis; they originate from fibroblasts, pericytes, and epithelial cells undergoing EMT.

The corneal endothelium is a single layer of cells on the inner corneal surface that actively pumps water out of the cornea to keep it dehydrated and transparent. Corneal endothelial cells do not regenerate in adults; their density declines from ~3,500 cells/mm² at birth to about 2,000/mm² by old age, and if density falls below ~500/mm², corneal clarity fails.

Stem cell exhaustion — the decline in stem cell number and function with age — is one of the hallmarks of aging. Aged hematopoietic stem cells become biased toward producing myeloid (innate immune) cells at the expense of lymphoid (adaptive immune) cells, contributing to the weakened adaptive immunity and increased inflammation seen in old age.

The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (primarily cortisol) under ACTH stimulation, while the zona glomerulosa produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) regulated by angiotensin II. The zona reticularis produces weak androgens (DHEA) that serve as precursors for peripheral conversion to estrogen and testosterone.

The concept of 'inflammaging' — chronic, low-grade sterile inflammation that increases with age — is now central to geroscience. It is driven by accumulating senescent cells, mitochondrial dysfunction producing ROS, gut microbiome dysbiosis, and declining immune regulation. Inflammaging underlies many age-related diseases including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and neurodegeneration.

The superficial fascia (hypodermis) beneath the skin contains subcutaneous fat, blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves. It is distinct from the deeper investing fascia of muscles. Its thickness and composition varies dramatically by body region, sex, and nutritional status, and it serves as an energy reservoir, thermal insulator, and mechanical shock absorber.

The lymphatic system develops from veins during embryogenesis; most lymphatic endothelial cells originate from a subset of cardinal vein cells expressing the transcription factor Prox1. Defects in lymphatic development cause primary lymphedema — permanent limb swelling — because lymph cannot drain.

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient countries. It is an autoimmune condition in which T cells and anti-thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) progressively destroy thyroid tissue. It is far more common in women than men, with a female-to-male ratio of about 7:1.

The pineal gland, long called the 'seat of the soul' by Descartes, is now known to be primarily a melatonin-secreting neuroendocrine gland. Unlike most brain structures it lacks a blood-brain barrier (being outside it) and is highly calcified in adults — visible on skull X-rays — though calcification does not impair its function.

The abducens nerve (CN VI) has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve, traveling from the brainstem to the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. Because of this long path, it is the cranial nerve most vulnerable to compression from raised intracranial pressure, making lateral gaze palsy an early sign of brain herniation.

The facial nerve (CN VII) not only controls facial expression muscles but also carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, provides parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal and salivary glands, and gives sensation to a small ear region. Bell's palsy — sudden unilateral facial weakness — results from facial nerve inflammation, most commonly after viral infection.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: Conduction velocity in nerve fibers depends on both myelination and fiber diameter. The fastest nerve fibers (Aα, myelinated, large diameter) conduct at over 70 m/s and carry proprioception and motor signals; the slowest (C fibers, unmyelinated, smallest diameter) conduct at only 0.5–2 m/s and carry slow pain, temperature, and autonomic signals.

Dermatomes are regions of skin innervated by a single spinal nerve root. The dermatome map is clinically important: a shingles rash follows a single dermatome (because the varicella-zoster virus reactivates in one dorsal root ganglion), and dermatomal sensory loss localizes a herniated disc or spinal cord lesion.

The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) contain calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths (or otoconia) embedded in a gelatinous matrix atop hair cells. Linear acceleration and gravity shift the heavy crystals, bending hair cells and signaling head tilt or linear motion. Dislodged otoliths cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Type II taste receptor cells (detecting sweet, bitter, and umami) communicate with gustatory neurons not via classical synapses but by releasing ATP through hemichannel proteins. This atypical synaptic mechanism means taste receptor cells can signal broadly to multiple nerve fibers simultaneously.

Supertasters — individuals with a higher density of fungiform papillae and taste buds — experience taste more intensely than average, particularly bitterness. About 25% of people are supertasters, and they tend to dislike bitter foods like coffee, grapefruit, and cruciferous vegetables. The ability to taste the bitter compound PROP (6-n-propylthiouracil) is a classic supertaster test.

The olfactory bulb processes odor signals and sends them directly to the piriform cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex — all parts of the limbic system involved in emotion and memory. This direct limbic connection explains why smells are uniquely powerful triggers of emotional memories compared to other sensory stimuli.

Central sensitization occurs when repeated or intense nociceptive input 'winds up' spinal dorsal horn neurons, making them more responsive to subsequent stimuli. It is the mechanism behind hyperalgesia (increased pain to normally painful stimuli) and allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli) seen in chronic pain conditions like fibromyalgia.

The inflammatory phase of wound healing is orchestrated by platelet-derived growth factors (PDGF) and cytokines that recruit neutrophils (first 24–48 hours) then macrophages (from day 2). Macrophages are essential for clearing debris and transitioning the wound from inflammation to repair — wounds in macrophage-depleted animals heal poorly.

Wnt signaling is a conserved pathway critical for stem cell maintenance, tissue renewal, and embryonic development. It regulates intestinal stem cell identity, hair follicle cycling, and bone formation; aberrant Wnt activation is one of the most common oncogenic events in colorectal cancer, driving uncontrolled intestinal stem cell proliferation.

Notch signaling is a cell-to-cell communication pathway that controls cell fate decisions throughout development and tissue homeostasis. It often works opposite to Wnt: in the intestinal crypt, Wnt promotes stem cell identity while Notch determines whether a cell becomes an absorptive enterocyte or a secretory goblet cell.

Osteocytes — former osteoblasts embedded in bone matrix — are the most abundant bone cells (90–95% of all bone cells) and serve as mechanosensors. They detect mechanical strain through their extensive network of cytoplasmic processes running through tiny channels (canaliculi), and signal osteoblasts and osteoclasts to adjust bone mass accordingly.

Sclerostin, a protein secreted by osteocytes, inhibits Wnt signaling in osteoblasts and thus suppresses bone formation. Antibodies blocking sclerostin (romosozumab) have been developed as an osteoporosis treatment that simultaneously increases bone formation and decreases resorption — a dual action not achieved by previous drugs.

Elastic cartilage contains a dense network of elastic fibers in addition to type II collagen, giving it flexibility and the ability to return to its original shape after deformation. It is found in the auricle of the ear, epiglottis, and Eustachian tube — all places where flexibility without brittleness is needed.

Tendons are attached to bone by a region called the enthesis (or osteotendinous junction), where tendon fibers insert into bone through a transitional zone of fibrocartilage that gradually mineralizes. Enthesopathy — enthesis inflammation — is the hallmark of spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis.

The knee menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges that deepen the tibial socket, distribute compressive load across a larger area, absorb shock, and stabilize the joint. They are about 70% water and their circumferential collagen fibers resist 'hoop stresses' — radial tears that split the meniscus like an unrolling spring.

Synovial joints are lined with a synovial membrane that produces synovial fluid. In rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune attack causes synovial membrane proliferation into an invasive 'pannus' that releases proteases eroding cartilage and bone. Anti-TNF biologics that block inflammatory cytokines have transformed management of this disease since the late 1990s.

The CSF circulates from the lateral ventricles through the foramen of Monro to the third ventricle, then through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and exits into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord. CSF is primarily reabsorbed by arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses, though recent research also implicates meningeal lymphatics.

Hydrocephalus — accumulation of CSF within the skull — occurs when CSF production exceeds absorption. In obstructive hydrocephalus, a blockage in the ventricular system prevents flow; in communicating hydrocephalus, absorption is impaired. Treatment involves surgically implanting a shunt to drain excess CSF into the abdominal cavity.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: P-glycoprotein (P-gp) on brain capillary endothelial cells actively pumps many drugs back out of the brain before they can accumulate, contributing to the blood-brain barrier's resistance to pharmacological treatment. Many cancer drugs and HIV antiretrovirals are P-gp substrates, which is why treating brain tumors and HIV encephalitis is so challenging.

The gut-brain axis communicates through three parallel channels: the vagus nerve (neural), gut hormones like GLP-1 and CCK (endocrine), and immune molecules like cytokines (immune). Gut bacteria further modulate this axis by producing neurotransmitter precursors, short-chain fatty acids, and direct neuroactive metabolites.

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) — transferring gut microbiome from a healthy donor to a recipient — is a highly effective treatment for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, with success rates over 90%. It is being investigated for a growing list of conditions including inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic syndrome, and even neurological conditions.

Clock genes are expressed not only in the brain but in virtually every peripheral tissue — liver, pancreas, muscle, adipose, and immune cells all run their own molecular clocks. Eating at irregular times can desynchronize peripheral clocks from the central SCN clock, impairing glucose metabolism and contributing to metabolic disease even when total calorie intake is unchanged.

Time-restricted eating (TRE) — confining all food intake to a 6–10 hour window each day — synchronizes peripheral clocks with the light-dark cycle, improves insulin sensitivity, reduces blood pressure, and promotes weight loss in metabolic studies. These benefits appear partly independent of calorie restriction.

DNA methylation at CpG islands in gene promoters is typically associated with silencing, while methylation in gene bodies can correlate with active transcription. TET enzymes oxidize methyl groups on DNA to initiate active demethylation, allowing gene expression to be dynamically regulated in response to signals.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Histone acetylation, added by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and removed by deacetylases (HDACs), loosens chromatin structure and generally activates transcription. HDAC inhibitors are used as cancer drugs because many tumors silence tumor suppressor genes via excessive deacetylation; blocking HDACs reopens the chromatin and restores suppressor gene expression.

Telomere length is maintained in germ cells and most stem cells by telomerase, but also by an alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway used by about 10–15% of cancers. ALT relies on homologous recombination between telomeres and produces characteristic long, heterogeneous telomeres. ALT-positive tumors are resistant to telomerase inhibitors.

Neural crest cells are a transient embryonic cell population that migrate from the dorsal neural tube to give rise to a remarkable range of structures: peripheral neurons and glia, adrenal medulla cells, melanocytes, craniofacial cartilage and bone, and smooth muscle of the aorta. Their broad fate has led them to be called a 'fourth germ layer.'

Gap junctions are protein channels (connexins) that directly connect the cytoplasms of adjacent cells, allowing ions, small metabolites, and signaling molecules to pass between cells. In the heart, gap junctions between cardiomyocytes allow the electrical impulse to propagate rapidly as a functional syncytium, enabling a coordinated heartbeat.

The lymphatics in the brain (dural meningeal lymphatics) were discovered in 2015. These vessels run along the dural sinuses and drain immune cells and waste from the CNS into cervical lymph nodes. Their impaired function with aging correlates with reduced amyloid clearance — linking poor lymphatic drainage to Alzheimer's disease risk.

Slow-wave sleep (SWS), characterized by high-amplitude, low-frequency brain waves, is when the glymphatic system is most active and the brain's extracellular space expands by about 60%, greatly increasing convective flow of CSF to flush metabolic waste. Sleep deprivation reduces glymphatic clearance and increases amyloid accumulation after just one night.

Anosmia — loss of smell — is associated with early neurodegenerative diseases including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, sometimes appearing years before motor or cognitive symptoms. This is because olfactory neural pathways connect directly to brain regions affected early in these diseases, making olfactory testing a potential early biomarker.

Mechanoreceptors in the skin include Meissner's corpuscles (sensitive to light touch and texture, concentrated in fingertips), Pacinian corpuscles (sensitive to vibration and deep pressure), Merkel's discs (sensitive to pressure and shape), and Ruffini endings (sensitive to skin stretch). Their differential distribution explains the exquisite touch sensitivity of the fingertips.

Cholesterol is essential for cell membrane fluidity and integrity and is the precursor for all steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. Despite its bad reputation, the body synthesizes about 70–80% of its cholesterol endogenously (mainly in the liver), with diet accounting for only 20–30%. Statins reduce cardiovascular risk by inhibiting the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase).

The Hayflick limit refers to the finite number of times normal human somatic cells can divide — approximately 50–70 divisions — after which they enter replicative senescence due to critically short telomeres. This concept, proposed by Leonard Hayflick in 1961, refuted the prevailing belief that cells were immortal in culture.

Exosomes are nano-sized vesicles (30–150 nm) released by most cell types that carry proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (including miRNAs) from their cell of origin. They mediate intercellular communication and are being intensely studied as disease biomarkers (cancer-derived exosomes in blood) and as drug delivery vehicles.

Interferons are signaling proteins secreted by cells in response to viral infection. Type I interferons (IFN-α/β) trigger an antiviral state in neighboring cells, upregulating hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes that block viral replication. They also activate natural killer cells and dendritic cells, bridging innate and adaptive immunity.

T regulatory cells (Tregs, CD4+FOXP3+) suppress excessive immune responses and maintain self-tolerance by secreting anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and directly suppressing effector T cells. Their loss causes catastrophic multi-organ autoimmunity; conversely, tumors exploit Tregs to evade immune destruction, which is why Treg-targeting is a cancer immunotherapy strategy.

Checkpoint inhibitor drugs (such as anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 antibodies) block inhibitory signals that tumors use to shut down T cell responses. By releasing these 'brakes,' they can unleash the immune system to destroy cancer. They have revolutionized treatment of melanoma, lung cancer, and other malignancies, producing durable remissions in some patients.

The renin enzyme is stored as prorenin in juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney's afferent arterioles. It is released when blood pressure falls, renal perfusion decreases, or sympathetic tone increases — making these cells integrated blood pressure sensors that launch the RAAS cascade within seconds.

The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase that, when insulin binds, activates intracellular signaling cascades (PI3K-Akt and MAPK pathways) to promote glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis, and lipid storage. In type 2 diabetes, these signaling pathways become desensitized (insulin resistance) even though insulin levels are high.

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is an incretin hormone released by L-cells in the distal gut after eating. It stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and reduces appetite. GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) mimic these effects and are now first-line treatments for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

The sarcomere — the basic contractile unit of skeletal muscle — is bounded by Z-discs from which actin thin filaments extend toward the center, where they interdigitate with myosin thick filaments anchored at the M-line. A resting sarcomere is about 2.2 micrometers long; it can shorten to 1.6 micrometers during contraction.

Slow-twitch (type I) muscle fibers are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin (red color), fatigue slowly, and are specialized for aerobic endurance. Fast-twitch (type IIx) fibers have fewer mitochondria, contract more powerfully and quickly, and fatigue rapidly. An intermediate type (IIa) has properties of both. Elite endurance athletes have predominantly type I fibers; sprinters have more type IIx.

Muscle hypertrophy after resistance training is primarily driven by mechanical tension on the sarcomere, which activates the mTORC1 signaling pathway via mechanosensitive kinases. mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to increase ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis, adding myofibrils to existing muscle fibers.

Bone marrow occupies the internal cavities of most bones. In children, nearly all marrow is red (hematopoietically active); with age, red marrow retreats to flat bones (pelvis, sternum, vertebrae, skull) and is replaced by yellow (fatty) marrow in the limbs. In severe anemia or chronic need, yellow marrow can revert to red.

The human eye's blind spot — where the optic nerve exits the retina (optic disc) — has no photoreceptors. Yet we don't notice it because the brain fills in the gap using surrounding information. The blind spot is about 15° from the fovea; each eye's blind spot is compensated for by the opposite eye's field of view in binocular vision.

Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex are among the largest neurons in the brain, with dendrites branching like an elaborate tree confined to a single plane. Each Purkinje cell receives input from one climbing fiber (from the inferior olive) and up to 200,000 parallel fibers (from granule cells), integrating an enormous amount of motor information.

Substance P is a neuropeptide released at pain synapses in the spinal cord that amplifies and prolongs pain signaling. It works alongside glutamate to activate NMDA receptors, contributing to central sensitization. Capsaicin — the active compound in chili peppers — initially activates and then desensitizes TRPV1 nociceptors, which is why repeated capsaicin application reduces pain.

Bone marrow adipocytes (fat cells) are not passive fillers — they secrete adiponectin and other factors that regulate hematopoietic stem cell behavior, and they expand in obesity and aging in ways that displace hematopoietic tissue and may impair immune function and bone health.

Fibronectin is a large extracellular matrix glycoprotein that acts as a molecular bridge, binding collagen, heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and cell-surface integrins simultaneously. It guides cell migration during wound healing, embryogenesis, and immune surveillance. Tumor cells hijack fibronectin binding to migrate and invade tissues.

The human olfactory system can detect some odorants at concentrations as low as parts per trillion. The sensitivity varies dramatically between compounds: humans can smell the sulfur compound ethanethiol (added to natural gas) at about 1 part per billion, while some musks require concentrations in the parts-per-million range.

The bone-derived hormone osteocalcin, secreted by osteoblasts, regulates not only bone mineralization but also whole-body metabolism — it promotes insulin secretion, improves insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat, reduces fat mass, and in animal studies appears to improve cognitive function and muscle endurance with exercise.

Muscle-secreted signaling proteins called myokines — released during contraction — have systemic effects on fat, liver, brain, and bone. The myokine irisin stimulates adipose tissue to produce more heat and promotes neuroplasticity; IL-6 from working muscle reduces insulin resistance and inflammation. These discoveries reveal muscle as an endocrine organ.

Adipose tissue secretes adipokines — signaling molecules including adiponectin, leptin, resistin, and visfatin — that regulate appetite, insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and cardiovascular function. Obese individuals tend to have high leptin (but with resistance) and low adiponectin; increasing adiponectin is considered a key target for metabolic disease treatment.

The human knee is the largest and most complex joint in the body, stabilized by four main ligaments (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL), two menisci, and multiple muscles and bursae. The quadriceps muscle exerts a force up to 6 times body weight on the patellofemoral joint during activities like stair climbing, explaining why patellofemoral pain is so common.

Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell niches are closely associated with blood vessels (sinusoids), and stem cell dormancy is maintained by low oxygen (hypoxic) microenvironments and signals from endothelial and perivascular cells. These niches protect stem cells from oxidative damage and regulate their activation during stress or injury.

The axon initial segment (AIS) is the specialized region of a neuron near the cell body where action potentials are initiated. The AIS has the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels in the cell and acts as a gate: only inputs strong enough to depolarize the AIS to threshold will propagate as an action potential down the axon.

The lymph nodes contain germinal centers where B cells undergo rapid proliferation, somatic hypermutation of their antibody genes, and selection for higher-affinity antibodies — a Darwinian process called affinity maturation. Germinal center reactions are essential for producing the high-affinity, class-switched antibodies that protect us from pathogens and vaccines.

Autophagy declines with age, contributing to the accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles that characterizes aged cells. Caloric restriction and exercise both upregulate autophagy, which is thought to be one reason these interventions extend healthspan across many organisms. Rapamycin, an mTOR inhibitor, enhances autophagy and extends lifespan in model organisms.

The cornea can store donor tissue in a preservation solution (Optisol) at 4°C for up to 14 days before transplantation. Because the corneal endothelium does not regenerate, the key criterion for donor suitability is endothelial cell density (>2,000 cells/mm²). Corneal banks process and test donors 24/7 to ensure fresh tissue is available for surgeons.

Intraocular pressure (IOP) is maintained by the balance between aqueous humor production (by the ciliary body) and drainage (through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal). Elevated IOP is the main risk factor for glaucoma — progressive optic nerve damage leading to irreversible vision loss. Prostaglandin analogs, beta-blockers, and alpha-agonists reduce IOP to protect the optic nerve.

Chromatin remodeling complexes (such as SWI/SNF) use ATP hydrolysis to physically reposition or eject nucleosomes, exposing or hiding DNA regulatory sequences. Mutations in SWI/SNF subunits occur in about 20% of all human cancers, making it one of the most commonly mutated chromatin regulators in cancer — demonstrating the critical importance of epigenetic control in tumor suppression.

The placenta expresses an enzyme called indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) that degrades tryptophan, depleting it locally and suppressing maternal T cell responses against the fetus. This is one of several immune tolerance mechanisms that prevent the mother's immune system from rejecting the genetically foreign fetus.

Meiosis, the cell division producing eggs and sperm, involves two sequential divisions (meiosis I and II) that reduce the chromosome number from 46 to 23. During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments in a process called crossing over (recombination), shuffling parental alleles and generating genetic diversity in offspring.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are RNA transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides that do not encode proteins. Over 16,000 have been identified in humans. They regulate gene expression by acting as scaffolds for chromatin-modifying complexes, decoys for transcription factors, and organizers of nuclear domains. Xist, which mediates X-chromosome inactivation, is the best-characterized lncRNA.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The ECM of cartilage contains aggrecan — a large proteoglycan that traps water by its highly negatively charged glycosaminoglycan side chains (chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate). This entrapped water creates a turgor pressure that gives cartilage its ability to resist compressive loads. Aggrecan is destroyed in osteoarthritis before collagen is lost.

The heart valves operate passively — they open and close in response to pressure differences, requiring no nervous or muscular control. The atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) are held by chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles; these tether the valve leaflets to prevent prolapse into the atria during ventricular contraction.

Alveolar macrophages are lung-resident phagocytes that patrol the air-exchange surfaces, ingesting inhaled particles, microbes, and apoptotic cells. They maintain an anti-inflammatory tone to prevent excessive reactions to harmless inhaled materials, while simultaneously being ready to launch inflammation against pathogens. Tobacco smoke impairs their function, increasing susceptibility to lung infection.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The lymphocyte recirculation pattern is precise: naïve T and B cells enter lymph nodes through high endothelial venules (HEVs) using L-selectin and chemokine receptors, and leave via efferent lymphatics if they don't encounter antigen. Memory and effector lymphocytes switch adhesion molecule profiles to home to peripheral tissues — gut-homing lymphocytes express α4β7 integrin; skin-homing cells express CLA.

The human gut contains more immune cells than any other organ — about 70–80% of all immune cells reside in the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), including Peyer's patches in the small intestine. The GALT must simultaneously tolerate trillions of commensal bacteria and dietary antigens while remaining vigilant against pathogens.

Calcitonin is secreted by C-cells (parafollicular cells) of the thyroid gland in response to high blood calcium, and it opposes PTH by inhibiting osteoclast activity and increasing renal calcium excretion. While essential in fish and reptiles, its role in humans appears minor; thyroidectomy rarely causes calcium problems despite eliminating calcitonin.

The cerebral cortex is organized into six horizontal layers (I–VI), each with distinct cell types, input-output connections, and functions. Layer IV receives sensory input from the thalamus; layer V sends output to the spinal cord and brainstem; layer II/III connects cortical areas. This laminar organization allows parallel processing of information streams.

The default mode network (DMN) is a set of brain regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus, hippocampus) that are active during rest and mind-wandering but suppressed during focused external tasks. The DMN is involved in self-referential thinking, prospection, and social cognition; its dysfunction is a feature of depression, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer's disease.

The blood pH is kept within a narrow range (7.35–7.45) by three buffer systems: the bicarbonate-carbonic acid system (the most important, regulated by both the lungs and kidneys), plasma proteins (including hemoglobin), and phosphate buffers. The lungs respond to pH changes within seconds to minutes; the kidneys take hours to days but provide the most powerful correction.

The enteric nervous system (ENS) contains all the major neurotransmitters found in the CNS — including dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, and nitric oxide — organized into two plexuses: the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's) controlling gut motility and the submucosal plexus (Meissner's) regulating secretion and blood flow.

The prostate gland produces most of the fluid (60–70%) in semen, including zinc, citrate, and proteolytic enzymes such as PSA (prostate-specific antigen). PSA liquefies the semen clot after ejaculation, freeing sperm to swim. Elevated serum PSA is used as a screening marker for prostate cancer, though it has high false-positive rates.

Progeria (Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome) is caused by a point mutation in the LMNA gene, producing a truncated form of lamin A called progerin that destabilizes the nuclear lamina. Affected children age 7–8 times faster than normal, dying of cardiovascular disease at an average age of 14, demonstrating the critical link between nuclear architecture and aging.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Werner syndrome, caused by mutations in a RecQ helicase gene (WRN), produces accelerated aging in adults and dramatically increases cancer risk. WRN helicase participates in DNA replication and repair; its loss causes genomic instability, premature telomere shortening, and senescence — establishing DNA repair as a cornerstone of both aging and cancer prevention.

The knee's anterior cruciate ligament is intracapsular but extrasynovial — it lies within the joint capsule but outside the synovial cavity, which is why it lacks the blood supply needed for effective natural healing after rupture. Surgical reconstruction using a graft (hamstring or patellar tendon) is therefore required for functional recovery in active individuals.

Estrogen receptors α and β are nuclear hormone receptors that, when bound to estrogen, translocate to the nucleus and act as transcription factors regulating hundreds of gene targets. They also have rapid non-genomic effects at the cell membrane. Tissue-specific expression of ERα vs ERβ determines the organ's response: ERα predominates in uterus and breast; ERβ in ovary, prostate, lung, and brain.

The spleen's white pulp contains lymphoid tissue organized around central arterioles as periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) of T cells and adjacent B cell follicles. The red pulp consists of sinusoids and splenic cords where old red cells are trapped and destroyed by macrophages. The marginal zone between them filters blood-borne antigens and mounts rapid antibody responses.

Caloric restriction — reducing food intake by 20–40% without malnutrition — extends lifespan in organisms from yeast to mice, partly by activating SIRT1 deacetylase and AMPK pathways that mimic low-energy states, promote autophagy, and reduce IGF-1 signaling. Whether it extends human lifespan is unknown, but the CALERIE trial showed it reduces multiple aging biomarkers.

The skin acts as a neuroendocrine organ, producing neurohormones in response to UV light. UV-B drives cutaneous synthesis of vitamin D3; UV-A and stress trigger production of β-endorphin and corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) from keratinocytes, which activate μ-opioid receptors — a possible mechanism for the relaxing, mildly addictive effect of sun exposure.

The human body contains roughly 30–40 trillion bacteria (mostly in the colon) and a comparable or greater number of bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) — the so-called virome. The gut virome, largely unexplored, may influence host immunity and microbiome composition and has been linked to inflammatory bowel disease.

Stem cells in hair follicle bulges give rise to the cells of the outer root sheath and regenerate the follicle with each hair cycle. They can also migrate into the epidermis after wounding to help re-epithelialize the wound surface. Their niche signals — from dermal papilla cells below — are essential for triggering follicle regeneration and are the focus of hair loss therapy research.

The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is a master growth regulator that senses nutrients, growth factors, and energy status. When nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 drives protein synthesis and cell growth; when starved, mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy. Because mTOR is overactivated in many cancers, rapamycin and its analogs are used as immunosuppressants and anticancer drugs.

Aquaporins are membrane channels that allow rapid passive transport of water across cell membranes. AQP2 in the kidney collecting duct is regulated by ADH: hormone-triggered signaling inserts AQP2 channels into the apical membrane within minutes, enabling rapid concentration of urine. AQP4 in astrocytes regulates brain water homeostasis and contributes to glymphatic flow.

Ion channels are gated protein pores in cell membranes that allow selective passive flow of ions down their electrochemical gradients. The voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7, expressed in peripheral nociceptors, is critical for pain sensation: people with loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A (which encodes Nav1.7) are congenitally insensitive to pain, making Nav1.7 a top target for non-opioid analgesic development.

The refractory period of a neuron after an action potential (typically 1–3 ms) is caused by inactivation of sodium channels (absolute refractory — no new AP possible) followed by prolonged potassium channel opening (relative refractory — larger stimulus needed). This period sets the maximum firing rate (~1,000 Hz) and ensures action potentials propagate in only one direction.

Retinal ganglion cells are the output neurons of the retina, sending visual signals along the optic nerve to the brain. Among the ~20 functional types, melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) are key for non-image-forming vision: setting circadian rhythms via the SCN, triggering the pupillary light reflex, and mediating light aversion.

Transthyretin (TTR) is a plasma protein that transports thyroxine and vitamin A (as retinol-binding protein complex). With age, TTR can misfold and aggregate into amyloid fibrils that deposit in the heart and nerves, causing transthyretin amyloidosis — a disease increasingly recognized as a cause of heart failure in older adults, now treatable with RNA-silencing drugs (patisiran, inclisiran).

The Pacinian corpuscle, a large encapsulated mechanoreceptor in deep skin and viscera, is among the fastest-adapting sensory receptors in the body — it responds to rapid vibration (200–300 Hz) and accelerations but ignores static pressure. Its onion-like lamellae dissipate sustained pressure, leaving only transient mechanical changes to bend the inner axon.

The pineal gland's melatonin output is suppressed by light not through the visual cortex but directly via a retino-hypothalamic tract to the SCN, which then inhibits the paraventricular nucleus, the spinal cord intermediolateral column, the superior cervical ganglion, and finally the pineal gland itself. This five-neuron multi-relay pathway explains why even low-level nocturnal light can suppress melatonin.

Sirtuins (SIRT1–7) are NAD+-dependent deacetylases and ADP-ribosyltransferases that regulate genome stability, metabolism, and aging. SIRT1 deacetylates p53, FOXO transcription factors, and histones to promote stress resistance and longevity; SIRT3 in mitochondria protects against oxidative stress; and all sirtuins are activated when NAD+ levels rise (as during caloric restriction or exercise).

The human cornea is the only tissue in the body that is completely avascular — it receives oxygen directly from the atmosphere and nutrients from the aqueous humor and tear film. This lack of blood vessels is essential for maintaining optical clarity.

Cartilage is also avascular and relies entirely on diffusion for nutrient supply, which is why cartilage heals so slowly after injury. The chondrocytes embedded within the cartilage matrix must survive without a direct blood supply.
The human body produces about 1–1.5 liters of saliva each day, which contains amylase to begin starch digestion, lysozyme as an antibacterial agent, and mucin to lubricate food for swallowing.

Brown adipose tissue (BAT) generates heat through non-shivering thermogenesis by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation via UCP1 (thermogenin). Activated by cold and norepinephrine, BAT burns calories to maintain body temperature and is now recognized as metabolically active in adult humans.

The human gut contains approximately 100 trillion microorganisms — roughly equal in number to the total cells in the body — collectively weighing around 1–2 kg. This gut microbiome plays critical roles in digestion, immune regulation, and even mood via the gut-brain axis.

The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the human body, comprising about one quarter of a person's height. It can withstand compressive forces of up to 1,700–2,500 newtons during normal walking.

The stapedius is the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body, measuring only about 1 mm in length. It attaches to the stapes bone of the middle ear and contracts reflexively to dampen loud sounds, protecting the inner ear from acoustic trauma.
Human fingernails grow at approximately 3–4 mm per month, while toenails grow about 1.5 mm per month. Nails on the dominant hand and on longer fingers tend to grow faster due to increased blood flow.

The liver is the only internal organ capable of complete regeneration — it can regrow to its full functional size even after up to 70% of its mass is removed surgically. This remarkable capacity is driven by hepatocyte proliferation triggered by cytokines and growth factors.

During REM sleep, the brain is nearly as active as when awake, and the body experiences temporary muscle paralysis (atonia) to prevent acting out dreams. This paralysis is mediated by GABA and glycine inhibiting spinal motor neurons.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human eye can distinguish approximately 10 million different colors, owing to three types of cone photoreceptors (S, M, L) sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths of light. Color perception is further refined by opponent color processing in the retina and visual cortex.

The spleen acts as a blood filter and reservoir, removing aged or damaged red blood cells and storing about one-third of the body's platelets. During heavy exercise or severe hemorrhage, the spleen contracts to release its blood reserve into circulation.

Humans are born with about 270 bones, but many fuse during childhood and adolescence, leaving the adult skeleton with 206 bones. The last bones to fully fuse are typically the clavicles and the vertebral growth plates, completing around age 25.

The appendix was long thought vestigial, but research suggests it serves as a 'safe house' for beneficial gut bacteria, repopulating the colon after infections like cholera or dysentery. It also contains lymphoid tissue involved in immune surveillance.

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and consists of two numbers: systolic pressure (when the heart contracts) over diastolic pressure (when the heart relaxes). A normal reading is below 120/80 mmHg; sustained readings above 130/80 mmHg are classified as hypertension.

The human body contains about 5 liters of blood on average, which is pumped by the heart approximately 70 times per minute, circulating the entire blood volume once per minute at rest. Over a lifetime, the heart beats more than 2.5 billion times.

The lymphatic system drains approximately 2–4 liters of interstitial fluid back into the bloodstream each day, preventing edema. Unlike the circulatory system, it has no pump — lymph flow depends on skeletal muscle contractions and breathing.

Keratinocytes make up approximately 90% of the epidermis. They produce keratin, a fibrous structural protein that gives skin its protective barrier properties, and they progressively flatten and die as they migrate from the stratum basale to the stratum corneum over about 2–4 weeks.

The human bladder can comfortably hold about 300–400 mL of urine before the urge to urinate becomes strong, and it can stretch to hold up to 600–800 mL at maximum capacity. The wall contains transitional epithelium (urothelium) that allows this dramatic change in volume.

Each kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons — the functional filtration units. Together, the kidneys filter about 180 liters of blood plasma per day, producing only 1–2 liters of urine after 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: Taste buds are not only found on the tongue — they also exist in the throat, epiglottis, soft palate, and upper esophagus. The average adult has 2,000–8,000 taste buds, each containing 50–100 taste receptor cells that regenerate every 10–14 days.

The human pancreas is both an exocrine and endocrine gland. As an exocrine gland it secretes about 1.5 liters of digestive enzymes into the duodenum daily; as an endocrine gland its islets of Langerhans secrete insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin into the bloodstream to regulate blood sugar.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: Approximately 2% of the human genome encodes proteins; the remaining 98% was once dismissed as 'junk DNA.' Research now shows much of it contains regulatory elements, enhancers, non-coding RNA genes, and structural regions critical for chromosome stability.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human eye moves in saccades — rapid, jerky movements between fixation points — rather than smooth sweeps. During reading, saccades occur 3–5 times per second, and the visual system suppresses perception during these movements (saccadic suppression) to prevent the world from appearing blurry.

Myelin sheaths around axons increase nerve conduction velocity dramatically — from about 1 m/s in unmyelinated fibers up to 120 m/s in the largest myelinated fibers. Myelin works by allowing electrical signals to 'jump' between nodes of Ranvier in a process called saltatory conduction.

The human gut is sometimes called the 'second brain' because it contains the enteric nervous system — a network of about 500 million neurons lining the gastrointestinal tract. This system can regulate digestion independently of the brain and communicates bidirectionally with the central nervous system via the vagus nerve.

Sweat glands come in two types: eccrine glands (distributed over most of the body surface) produce watery sweat for thermoregulation, while apocrine glands (concentrated in armpits and groin) produce thicker, protein-rich secretions that bacteria metabolize into body odor.

The human spine has four natural curves (cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, sacral kyphosis) that act as a spring to absorb impact and distribute the weight of the head and torso. These curves develop during infancy when babies begin holding their heads up and learning to walk.

The immune system's T cells 'learn' which antigens to attack in the thymus during fetal development and early childhood. T cells that strongly react to self-antigens are eliminated through a process called negative selection, preventing autoimmune diseases.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: The human foot contains 26 bones, 33 joints, and more than 100 muscles, tendons, and ligaments. The arched structure of the foot distributes body weight efficiently and acts as a spring during walking and running, storing and releasing elastic energy.

Oxytocin, produced in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary, promotes social bonding, trust, and maternal behaviors. It is released during childbirth, breastfeeding, hugging, and orgasm, earning it the nickname 'the love hormone.'

The human hand has 27 bones — 8 carpal (wrist) bones, 5 metacarpals, and 14 phalanges. The opposable thumb, controlled by 9 separate muscles, enables the precision grip that distinguishes humans from most other animals.

Cortisol, the primary stress hormone, follows a diurnal rhythm: it peaks sharply within 30–45 minutes of waking (the cortisol awakening response) and gradually declines throughout the day. This morning surge prepares the body for the metabolic demands of the day.

The heart's electrical conduction system begins in the sinoatrial (SA) node — the natural pacemaker — generating roughly 60–100 impulses per minute. The signal travels to the atrioventricular (AV) node, then through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to coordinate ventricular contraction.

Human breast milk contains over 200 distinct oligosaccharides (HMOs) that act as prebiotics, selectively feeding beneficial Bifidobacterium in the infant gut. These sugars are not digested by the infant directly but shape a microbiome that protects against infection and programs the immune system.

The inner ear contains the cochlea, which is coiled 2.5 turns and contains approximately 15,000–16,000 hair cells that transduce sound vibrations into nerve signals. High-frequency sounds activate hair cells near the base of the cochlea, while low frequencies activate those near the apex — a property called tonotopy.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human stomach produces hydrochloric acid with a pH of approximately 1.5–3.5 — acidic enough to dissolve razor blades. The stomach lining is protected by a thick layer of mucus and bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid at the epithelial surface.

Endorphins — the body's endogenous opioids — are released during exercise, laughter, and excitement. They bind to the same receptors as morphine and heroin, producing feelings of euphoria and pain relief; this is responsible for the so-called 'runner's high.'

The human body has approximately 650 skeletal muscles, which account for about 40% of total body weight in men and 35% in women. Skeletal muscle is the largest metabolically active tissue and is the primary site of glucose disposal after a meal.

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, preventing most molecules in the blood from entering the brain. Only small, lipid-soluble molecules and those with specific transporters can cross, which is why developing drugs for the brain is extremely challenging.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: Approximately 8% of the human genome is derived from ancient viral infections — these endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) integrated into germline DNA millions of years ago. Some ERV sequences have been co-opted for biological functions, including placenta formation and immune regulation.

The human body loses about 30,000–40,000 skin cells every hour — roughly 600,000 per day — as the outermost layer of the epidermis is continuously shed. The entire outer layer of skin is replaced approximately every 2–4 weeks.

Adiponectin, a hormone secreted exclusively by fat cells (adipocytes), paradoxically increases insulin sensitivity and has anti-inflammatory effects. Obese individuals have lower adiponectin levels, contributing to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.

The human larynx (voice box) produces sound when exhaled air causes the vocal folds to vibrate. The fundamental frequency of the voice is determined by tension in the vocal folds: adult males average ~120 Hz and adult females ~210 Hz, while infants cry at around 400–600 Hz.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Bone is a living tissue that is continuously remodeled by osteoclasts (which resorb bone) and osteoblasts (which form new bone). The entire adult skeleton is replaced approximately every 10 years through this coupled process of resorption and formation.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human brain generates roughly 20 watts of electrical power — enough to light a dim light bulb. This power supports the firing of approximately 86 billion neurons and their 100 trillion synaptic connections.

The human body produces about 200 billion red blood cells every day to replace those that die after approximately 120 days in circulation. This production takes place in the red bone marrow of flat bones like the sternum, ribs, pelvis, and vertebrae.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Humans have two copies of most genes — one inherited from each parent — and approximately 5–10 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that differ between any two people. This genetic variation accounts for differences in disease susceptibility, drug response, and physical traits.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The gallbladder concentrates and stores bile produced by the liver, releasing it into the small intestine when fat-containing food arrives. Bile emulsifies fats into tiny droplets, vastly increasing the surface area available for lipase enzymes to digest them.

The human lung has an internal surface area of approximately 70 square meters — roughly the size of a tennis court — packed into a chest cavity of only about 6 liters. This enormous surface area is created by around 500 million tiny air sacs called alveoli.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is the largest cranial nerve and provides sensory innervation to the face, scalp, teeth, sinuses, and meninges. It is also the nerve involved in trigeminal neuralgia — one of the most painful conditions known, causing sudden, severe facial pain.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human body contains enough carbon to make about 900 pencils, enough iron to make a 3-inch nail, and enough fat to make 7 bars of soap. Oxygen is the most abundant element by mass, constituting about 65% of body weight.

Telomeres are protective caps on chromosome ends made of TTAGGG repeats. They shorten with each cell division; when they become critically short, the cell enters replicative senescence or apoptosis. Telomerase, an enzyme that lengthens telomeres, is highly active in stem cells and cancer cells.

The human body can detect touch through four main types of mechanoreceptors: Meissner's corpuscles (light touch, texture), Merkel's discs (sustained pressure, edges), Ruffini endings (skin stretch), and Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure, vibration). Each provides unique information processed by the somatosensory cortex.

Approximately 25% of adults carry Staphylococcus aureus harmlessly in their nasal passages — a state called asymptomatic carriage. This colonization is a major risk factor for hospital-acquired staph infections, since the nasal flora can spread to wounds and catheters.

The human body has roughly 10,000 taste receptor cells per taste bud, and taste buds are replaced entirely every 10–14 days. This rapid turnover is why cancer chemotherapy patients, whose rapidly dividing cells are targeted, frequently experience altered taste perception.

The human eye performs about 100,000 micro-movements per day, including micro-saccades, drifts, and tremors — even when trying to fixate steadily on a point. These tiny movements prevent visual fading (Troxler fading) by continuously refreshing the stimulation of retinal receptors.

Human sweat contains dermcidin, an antimicrobial peptide that kills bacteria on the skin surface. This innate immune defense is particularly effective against Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli, supplementing the physical barrier function of the skin.

The human body contains about 1.2–1.5 kg of calcium, 99% of which is stored in bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite crystals. The remaining 1% circulates in blood and is essential for muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and blood clotting.

The hypothalamus, a pea-sized region at the base of the brain, regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and the release of pituitary hormones. It acts as the master regulator linking the nervous system to the endocrine system.

The human immune system recognizes foreign antigens through T cell receptors and B cell receptors, which are generated by a process of V(D)J recombination that can theoretically produce over 10^18 unique receptor combinations — far more than enough to recognize every known pathogen.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: A sneeze can travel at speeds of up to 160 km/h (100 mph) and propel up to 40,000 droplets up to 8 meters. The sneeze reflex is coordinated by the trigeminal nerve sensing nasal irritation and the brainstem triggering a deep inhalation followed by rapid exhalation.

The olfactory epithelium in the nasal cavity contains about 6 million specialized olfactory receptor neurons, each expressing only one of the approximately 400 functional olfactory receptor genes. Unlike most neurons, olfactory receptor neurons are regularly replaced from stem cells throughout life.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human body's total DNA, if stretched end to end, would reach from Earth to Pluto and back about 17 times. Each of the approximately 37 trillion cells contains about 2 meters of DNA, tightly coiled around histone proteins into chromatin.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The placenta is a remarkable temporary organ that develops during pregnancy to supply nutrients and oxygen to the fetus while removing waste. It also produces hormones like hCG, progesterone, and estrogen that maintain the pregnancy and prepare the body for labor.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The average human blinks about 15–20 times per minute, or roughly 10,000 times a day. Each blink lasts about 150–400 milliseconds and serves to spread the tear film evenly across the eye surface, preventing drying and clearing debris.

The human small intestine averages 6–7 meters in length and is lined with finger-like projections called villi, each covered by microscopic microvilli (forming the brush border). These structures increase absorptive surface area to approximately 250 square meters.

Interstitial fluid — the fluid bathing cells outside the bloodstream — constitutes about 15% of body weight and is the immediate environment from which cells take nutrients and into which they excrete waste. The composition of interstitial fluid is tightly regulated to mirror the ionic composition of plasma.

The human immune system produces antibodies (immunoglobulins) in five classes: IgG (most abundant in blood), IgA (predominant in secretions like saliva and breast milk), IgM (first antibody made in a new infection), IgE (triggers allergic responses), and IgD (function still not fully understood).

Ghrelin, produced primarily in the stomach, is the main hunger-stimulating hormone. It rises sharply before meals and falls after eating. Ghrelin also stimulates growth hormone release and promotes fat storage, linking appetite with long-term energy balance.

The human body temperature is regulated by the hypothalamus around a set point of 37°C (98.6°F). A fever occurs when pyrogens (such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides or cytokines like IL-6) raise this set point, making the body produce and conserve more heat to fight infection.

The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is the longest cranial nerve, running from the brainstem to the abdomen and innervating the heart, lungs, and most digestive organs. It carries about 80% afferent (sensory) fibers — meaning the gut sends far more signals to the brain than vice versa.

The human body replaces its entire complement of platelets approximately every 8–10 days. Platelets are small anucleate cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow; they are essential for blood clotting and wound repair.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Amygdala-based fear memories are formed faster and are more durable than other memories, due to the release of norepinephrine and cortisol during stress, which enhance synaptic plasticity. This evolutionary advantage helps humans remember and avoid life-threatening situations.

The human body has two adrenal glands (one on top of each kidney), each with two distinct zones: the outer cortex secretes steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones), and the inner medulla secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) as part of the fight-or-flight response.

The human body's total blood vessel length — including arteries, veins, and capillaries — is estimated at about 100,000 km (60,000 miles), enough to encircle Earth more than twice. Most of this length consists of microscopic capillaries.

The human brain's default mode network (DMN) — including the medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex — is most active during mind-wandering, self-referential thought, and daydreaming, and deactivates when attention is directed outward. Disruption of DMN connectivity is seen in Alzheimer's disease and depression.

The human liver performs over 500 distinct metabolic functions, including synthesizing clotting factors and albumin, detoxifying ammonia to urea, metabolizing drugs, storing glycogen and vitamins A/D/B12, and producing bile. It processes virtually all blood from the intestines via the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation.

The corneal endothelium — the single innermost cell layer of the cornea — does not regenerate after injury in adults. A minimum density of about 500 cells/mm² is needed to keep the cornea clear; below this, the cornea swells and vision becomes blurred, requiring a corneal transplant.
