The human body contains approximately 3 grams of iron, about 70% of which is incorporated into hemoglobin in red blood cells and myoglobin in muscles. The body has no active mechanism to excrete excess iron; instead, it tightly regulates intestinal absorption via the hormone hepcidin.

The human cerebellum contains more than half of all the neurons in the brain — approximately 50 billion — despite being only about 10% of the brain's volume. It coordinates balance, fine motor control, and is increasingly linked to cognitive and emotional processing.

Humans can detect pain because of nociceptors — specialized free nerve endings that respond to tissue damage or potentially harmful stimuli (heat, cold, chemicals, pressure). Pain signals travel to the spinal cord via fast A-delta fibers (sharp, initial pain) and slow C fibers (burning, aching pain).

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: Melanin in the skin is produced by melanocytes and comes in two forms: eumelanin (brown/black) and pheomelanin (red/yellow). All humans have roughly the same number of melanocytes, but skin color varies based on the type and quantity of melanin produced.

The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle, accounting for about 70–80% of the work of breathing at rest. When it contracts, it flattens and descends, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity and causing air to rush into the lungs.

The retina is technically an extension of the central nervous system — it develops from the same embryonic tissue as the brain. The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) performs daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments, clearing about 10% of rod outer segment volume per day.

The human body undergoes circadian fluctuations in virtually every physiological parameter: core temperature peaks in the late afternoon, immune cell activity peaks at night, grip strength and athletic performance peak in the early evening, and pain sensitivity follows a 24-hour cycle.

The human body generates enough heat through metabolic processes to boil 0.5 liters of water every hour. The body loses this heat primarily through radiation (40%), evaporation (27%), convection (27%), and conduction (5%) to maintain a stable core temperature.

The eardrum (tympanic membrane) vibrates in response to sound waves and transmits these vibrations to three tiny ossicles: the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup). The ossicles amplify sound about 22-fold before transmitting it to the fluid-filled cochlea.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Complement proteins in the blood form an innate immune system that can directly lyse bacteria by inserting the membrane attack complex (MAC) into bacterial cell membranes. The complement cascade also opsonizes bacteria (coating them to enhance phagocytosis) and triggers inflammation.

The human trachea bifurcates at the carina into the left and right main bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left — which is why aspirated objects (like a peanut) more commonly end up in the right lung.

The average human produces about 25,000 quarts of saliva in a lifetime — enough to fill two swimming pools. Saliva begins digesting starch via salivary amylase, moistens food to form a bolus, and contains antibacterial compounds that protect the teeth and oral mucosa.

Proprioception — the sense of body position and movement — depends on specialized mechanoreceptors called proprioceptors in muscles (muscle spindles), tendons (Golgi tendon organs), and joints. This sense allows you to touch your nose with eyes closed and is critical for coordinated movement.

Human hair grows at approximately 15 cm (6 inches) per year on the scalp. Each hair follicle cycles through three phases: anagen (active growth, 2–7 years), catagen (transition, 2–3 weeks), and telogen (resting/shedding, 3 months). At any time, about 85–90% of scalp hairs are in anagen.

The human body can store only about 400–500 grams of glycogen — roughly 1,600–2,000 calories of carbohydrate energy — split between the liver (100 g) and muscles (300–400 g). This limited store is why marathon runners 'hit the wall' around mile 20 when glycogen is depleted.

Surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes in the alveoli, reduces surface tension and prevents alveoli from collapsing on exhalation. Premature infants born before 34 weeks often lack sufficient surfactant, leading to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), which can be treated with exogenous surfactant.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human brain's neuroplasticity — its ability to reorganize by forming new synaptic connections — persists throughout life, though it is greatest during early childhood sensitive periods. After a stroke, unaffected brain regions can sometimes take over functions of damaged areas through this mechanism.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human spinal cord contains about 13.5 million neurons and is the main highway for motor commands going down from the brain and sensory information going up. At each vertebral level, anterior (motor) and posterior (sensory) nerve roots merge to form spinal nerves that supply specific body regions called dermatomes.

The human embryo develops a tail during weeks 4–8 of gestation that is subsequently reabsorbed; a remnant, the coccyx, persists in adults. Occasionally, infants are born with a vestigial tail — a true atavism — which is always surgically removed.

A single mitochondrion contains its own circular DNA (mtDNA), encoding 37 genes — a vestige of the ancient bacterial ancestor that was engulfed by a eukaryotic cell about 1.5 billion years ago. mtDNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother and is used in forensic analysis and ancestry testing.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body makes about 0.5–1 liter of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) per day, continuously cycling it through the ventricles and around the brain and spinal cord. CSF cushions the brain, removes metabolic waste, and provides a stable ionic environment; its reabsorption occurs mainly through arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses.

Autophagy — literally 'self-eating' — is a cellular housekeeping process by which cells degrade and recycle damaged organelles, misfolded proteins, and pathogens in lysosomes. It is upregulated during fasting and caloric restriction and is linked to longevity; its discovery earned Yoshinori Ohsumi the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The human knee is the largest and most complex joint in the body, stabilized by four major ligaments (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL) and two crescent-shaped cartilage pads called menisci. It must absorb forces up to 8 times body weight during running.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: Aquaporins are protein channels in cell membranes that allow water molecules to pass through at rates of up to 3 billion water molecules per second per channel. In the kidney, aquaporin-2 in collecting duct cells is regulated by antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) to control water reabsorption and urine concentration.

Humans are the only known animals that cry emotional tears — tears shed in response to emotions rather than merely for eye lubrication or foreign body removal. Emotional tears contain higher levels of prolactin, ACTH, and leucine-enkephalin (an endorphin) compared to irritant-triggered tears.

Gluconeogenesis — the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors like lactate, amino acids, and glycerol — occurs primarily in the liver (and to a lesser extent in the kidneys and intestines). It is essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting, supplying the brain with glucose when dietary carbohydrates are unavailable.

The reticuloendothelial system (mononuclear phagocyte system) consists of monocytes and macrophages distributed throughout the body. Kupffer cells in the liver, microglia in the brain, Langerhans cells in the skin, and alveolar macrophages in the lungs all belong to this system, providing tissue-resident immune surveillance.

The human tongue contains 8 muscles — 4 intrinsic (changing shape) and 4 extrinsic (moving the tongue in space). It is one of the strongest muscles relative to its size and is essential for speaking, chewing, swallowing, and tasting.

The placental syncytiotrophoblast is a giant multinucleate cell layer that directly contacts maternal blood in the intervillous space. It absorbs glucose and amino acids, secretes hCG and progesterone, and constitutes an immune barrier that prevents rejection of the genetically foreign fetus.

Mast cells are tissue-resident immune cells loaded with histamine-containing granules. When activated by allergens binding to IgE on their surface, they rapidly degranulate, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause the redness, swelling, and itching of allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: The human scalp contains approximately 100,000–150,000 hair follicles, and it is normal to lose 50–100 hairs per day as part of the natural hair growth cycle. Hair appears to keep growing after death because the skin dehydrates and retracts, making existing hair more visible — it is not actually growing.

The human stomach can stretch from about 75 mL when empty to approximately 1 liter after a typical meal and up to 4 liters when maximally distended. This capacity is enabled by rugae — folds in the stomach lining — that flatten as the stomach fills.

The human auditory system can detect sounds across a frequency range of approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. With age, the upper limit progressively drops — a phenomenon called presbycusis — because outer hair cells in the basal cochlea (responsible for high-frequency detection) deteriorate first.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, with a diameter of about 2–3 cm at its widest point. It must withstand peak blood pressures exceeding 120 mmHg with every heartbeat, which over a lifetime amounts to billions of pressure pulses — making aortic aneurysm a serious age-related risk.

The human body has approximately 30 different types of collagen — the most abundant structural protein in the body, accounting for about 30% of total protein mass. Type I collagen is the main component of bones, tendons, and skin; type II is found in cartilage; type IV forms basement membranes.

The human embryo passes through a pharyngeal arch stage in which it briefly has gill-like structures (pharyngeal arches) that later develop into jaw, ear, and neck structures. These are not functional gills but reflect the shared embryonic toolkit of all vertebrates.

The human brain contains a specialized structure called the hippocampus that is critical for forming new episodic (autobiographical) memories. Patient H.M., who had both hippocampi surgically removed in 1953, became unable to form any new long-term memories, a condition called anterograde amnesia.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: Nitric oxide (NO), a gas produced by endothelial cells lining blood vessels, is a potent vasodilator that relaxes smooth muscle in arterial walls. It is how nitroglycerin relieves angina (nitroglycerin is converted to NO) and how sildenafil (Viagra) works (by blocking the enzyme that breaks down NO's signaling molecule, cGMP).

Humans have a vestigial palmaris longus muscle in the forearm that is absent in about 14% of the population with no functional deficit. Surgeons commonly harvest its tendon for tendon grafts because its absence causes no harm, making it an ideal donor site.

The human body maintains blood glucose within a narrow range of approximately 70–100 mg/dL (3.9–5.6 mmol/L) through a tight hormonal balance between insulin (which lowers glucose) and glucagon (which raises glucose). Sustained glucose above 126 mg/dL fasting is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: Epigenetic marks — including DNA methylation and histone modifications — can be passed from parent to child and from one generation to the next (transgenerational epigenetic inheritance). Notably, famine exposure in grandparents has been linked to metabolic effects in grandchildren in studies of the Dutch Hunger Winter.

The human ear can detect sounds as quiet as 0 dB SPL — equivalent to the movement of an air molecule by about the diameter of a hydrogen atom. The pain threshold is around 120–130 dB, so the human auditory range spans a factor of one trillion in sound intensity.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human immune system's innate arm uses pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs) to detect conserved microbial signatures called pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). TLR4, for example, recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) on gram-negative bacteria and triggers the inflammatory cascade.

A yawn lasts on average about 6 seconds, and yawning is contagious in humans and other social animals. The most accepted theory is that yawning cools the brain — it coincides with deep breathing that draws cooler air over sinus blood vessels, and it is most common when brain temperature rises.

The human kidney's juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) acts as a blood pressure sensor: when blood pressure drops, juxtaglomerular cells release renin, triggering the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). This cascade ultimately causes sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction to restore blood pressure.

Human breast cancer begins most often in the ductal epithelium; the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes encode proteins that repair double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination. Women with pathogenic BRCA1/2 mutations have a lifetime breast cancer risk of 40–80% compared to the general population risk of ~12%.

The human fovea — the central 1.5 mm of the retina — contains the highest density of cone photoreceptors and provides the sharpest color vision. When you look directly at something, you are projecting its image onto the fovea; peripheral vision is dominated by rod photoreceptors optimized for low-light and motion detection.

Hiccups are caused by involuntary spasms of the diaphragm, followed by abrupt closure of the vocal cords — it is the sound of the glottis snapping shut. Hiccups have no known physiological purpose in adults, though some researchers hypothesize they are a vestigial reflex inherited from gill-breathing ancestors.

Stem cells in the bone marrow — hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) — give rise to every type of blood cell through a hierarchical process of differentiation. A single HSC can theoretically reconstitute the entire blood system, which is the basis for bone marrow transplantation to treat leukemia and other blood disorders.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human ear contains the smallest bones in the body: the malleus (9 mg), incus (25 mg), and stapes (2.5 mg). Together, these three ossicles weigh less than a raindrop yet are essential for transmitting sound vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The blood-testis barrier (BTB) isolates developing sperm cells from the immune system in the testes. Because sperm are produced after the immune system learns 'self' during fetal development, the immune system would attack them as foreign without this barrier.

The muscular walls of the heart are nourished by the coronary arteries — not directly from the blood inside the chambers. The left coronary artery and right coronary artery branch off the aorta immediately above the aortic valve, and blockage of these vessels causes a heart attack.

The hormone leptin is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and signals satiety to the hypothalamus. Individuals with leptin deficiency or leptin receptor mutations develop severe early-onset obesity; however, most obese people have high leptin levels but are leptin-resistant, a situation analogous to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.

Human chromosomes are maintained by a specialized form of DNA replication at telomeres. Without telomerase activity, telomeres shorten by 50–200 base pairs per cell division; in most adult somatic cells, this limits the number of times a cell can divide (the Hayflick limit), generally 50–70 divisions.

Swallowing is a complex reflex involving over 30 pairs of muscles coordinated by the swallowing center in the medulla oblongata. The entire process of moving food from the mouth to the stomach takes 8–20 seconds, and the epiglottis flips down to cover the trachea within 0.3 seconds to prevent aspiration.

The human body has two kidneys, each shaped like a bean and about the size of a fist. A person can live normally with just one kidney — living kidney donors typically show no significant long-term health consequences, with their remaining kidney compensating by growing larger and increasing its filtration rate.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: The human immune system's B cells produce antibodies in a process that deliberately mutates the antibody-encoding genes (somatic hypermutation) in germinal centers of lymph nodes. The cells with the strongest antigen binding are selected for survival — an evolutionary process within the body called affinity maturation.

The human skin is the largest organ of the body by surface area (~1.8 m²) and by weight (~11 kg, or 16% of body weight). It performs multiple vital functions: acting as a physical barrier, regulating temperature, synthesizing vitamin D, providing immune surveillance, and housing sensory receptors.

The stretch reflex (myotatic reflex) is the fastest reflex in the human body, operating at a latency of about 25–50 ms. It occurs when a muscle spindle detects a rapid stretch and sends a signal via Ia afferent fibers directly to an alpha motor neuron in the spinal cord, bypassing the brain — the knee-jerk reflex is the classic example.

Platelets contain dense granules (storing ADP, ATP, serotonin, and calcium) and alpha granules (storing von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and platelet factor 4). Upon activation by vessel injury, they rapidly degranulate to recruit more platelets and promote coagulation.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human brain's white matter consists of myelinated axon tracts connecting different brain regions. The largest is the corpus callosum — a thick bundle of approximately 200–250 million axons linking the left and right cerebral hemispheres, enabling interhemispheric communication.

Human embryogenesis is guided by Hox genes — a conserved family of transcription factors that determine the anterior-posterior body axis. Fruit flies (Drosophila) share homologous Hox genes with humans, underscoring the deep evolutionary conservation of body plan specification across 600 million years.

The sinoatrial (SA) node can increase the heart rate dramatically during exercise or stress via sympathetic innervation and epinephrine — from resting 70 bpm to over 200 bpm in trained athletes. Each heartbeat initiated by the SA node takes about 0.8 seconds at rest: 0.4 s for atrial contraction and filling, 0.3 s for ventricular contraction, and 0.1 s for the brief pause.

The human genome has 23 pairs of chromosomes — 22 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome pair (XX in females, XY in males). The Y chromosome contains only about 55 protein-coding genes compared to the ~800 on the X chromosome, and it has been shrinking evolutionarily for the past 200 million years.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body mounts an acute-phase response to infection or injury, during which the liver rapidly increases production of proteins like C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, and complement components. CRP levels can rise up to 1,000-fold within 24–48 hours and are used clinically as a marker of inflammation.

The human lens of the eye can change its curvature to focus on objects at different distances — a process called accommodation. The ciliary muscle contracts to release tension on the lens, letting it become more spherical for near vision. This ability progressively declines with age (presbyopia), typically requiring reading glasses after age 45.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced by mitochondria during energy metabolism cause oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids — a key mechanism of aging. Antioxidant enzymes like superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and glutathione peroxidase neutralize ROS, and their activity correlates with lifespan across species.

The human body normally maintains pH of arterial blood between 7.35 and 7.45 — a remarkably narrow range, given that pH 7 is neutral. This is regulated by three systems: chemical buffers (bicarbonate), respiratory adjustment (CO2 exhalation), and renal adjustment (bicarbonate/H+ excretion), each operating on different timescales.

Human night vision is mediated almost entirely by rods, which contain the photopigment rhodopsin. Rhodopsin requires about 20–30 minutes in the dark to fully dark-adapt as rhodopsin regenerates; however, a brief exposure to bright light bleaches it and destroys dark adaptation in seconds.

The human gut lining renews itself completely every 4–5 days — making intestinal epithelial cells among the shortest-lived cells in the body. This rapid turnover, driven by intestinal stem cells in crypts, allows the gut to repair damage from digestion, pathogens, and chemotherapy.

The human immune system contains immunological memory: after a first infection or vaccination, long-lived memory B and T cells persist for decades. These cells respond faster and more powerfully to the same antigen on re-exposure, which is the fundamental mechanism underlying vaccine protection.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: The human uterus — when not pregnant — is about the size and shape of an inverted pear, weighing about 70–80 grams. During pregnancy, it expands to accommodate a full-term fetus and placenta, increasing up to 20-fold in weight to about 1,100 grams (1.1 kg), then returns to near-normal size within 6–8 weeks after delivery.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human pituitary gland, often called the 'master gland,' is about the size of a pea (0.5 g) and sits at the base of the brain in the sella turcica. Its anterior lobe produces six hormones (GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, PRL) that regulate growth, thyroid function, adrenal function, and reproduction.

Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the persistent strengthening of synapses based on recent activity and is widely considered the cellular basis of learning and memory. LTP requires NMDA receptor activation (which acts as a coincidence detector) and results in insertion of more AMPA receptors at the synapse.

Human bone marrow produces about 10 billion white blood cells (leukocytes) daily under normal conditions. This rate can increase up to tenfold during infections when the body demands more neutrophils to fight bacteria, driven by cytokines like G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor).

The human immune system uses a process called MHC (major histocompatibility complex) presentation to alert cytotoxic T cells to viral infection. Virally infected cells display viral peptide fragments on MHC class I molecules, allowing CD8+ T cells to recognize and kill infected cells before the virus spreads.

Human sweat is 99% water, with small amounts of sodium, chloride, potassium, urea, and lactate. Cystic fibrosis causes abnormally high sodium and chloride concentrations in sweat — a finding used in the diagnostic sweat chloride test — because the CFTR protein that normally reabsorbs chloride in sweat ducts is dysfunctional.

The human thyroid gland produces three hormones: thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3), and calcitonin. T3 and T4 regulate the metabolic rate of virtually every cell in the body; calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity. An iodine-deficient diet leads to goiter as the thyroid enlarges in an effort to trap more iodine.

Every human cell (except red blood cells and platelets) contains the full complement of approximately 20,000 protein-coding genes, but each cell type expresses only a specific subset. A liver cell and a neuron have the same DNA but behave completely differently because of differential gene expression controlled by transcription factors and epigenetic marks.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human cough reflex can generate expiratory airflow velocities exceeding 500 mph and can propel respiratory droplets up to 6 meters. It is triggered by sensory nerve endings in the larynx and trachea and is coordinated by the cough center in the brainstem.

The human sense of balance (vestibular system) is housed in the inner ear, in three semicircular canals oriented in three perpendicular planes. These canals detect rotational acceleration, while the otolith organs (utricle and saccule) sense linear acceleration and the direction of gravity.

The human immune system's regulatory T cells (Tregs) suppress excessive immune responses to prevent autoimmunity and allergy. They are identified by expression of the FOXP3 transcription factor; mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX syndrome — a devastating autoimmune disease affecting multiple organs.

The human body can survive without food for several weeks but only about 3–4 days without water. Dehydration of just 2% of body weight reduces cognitive performance; at 10% dehydration, organ dysfunction begins; and at 15–25% dehydration, death can occur.

The human brain contains a specialized region — the fusiform face area (FFA) in the temporal lobe — that is preferentially activated by faces. Damage to this region causes prosopagnosia, an inability to recognize faces even of close family members, while still being able to recognize other objects.

The human thoracic duct is the main lymphatic vessel, draining lymph from the legs, abdomen, and left side of the body into the left subclavian vein. It carries about 100 mL of lymph per hour and is a major route by which dietary fat (as chylomicrons) enters the bloodstream after absorption from the intestine.

Osteocalcin, produced exclusively by bone-forming osteoblasts, is not just a structural protein — it also functions as a hormone, signaling muscles during exercise, regulating insulin secretion from the pancreas, and promoting memory and cognition. This discovery revealed that bone is a metabolically active endocrine organ.

The human central nervous system has 12 pairs of cranial nerves, numbered I–XII, that emerge directly from the brain and serve the head, neck, and most thoracoabdominal organs. Among them, the olfactory nerve (CN I) is the only cranial nerve whose fibers regenerate throughout adult life.

The human fetal heart begins beating at approximately 22 days after fertilization — before the mother even knows she is pregnant. The fetal circulation is unique: oxygenated blood from the placenta bypasses the non-functioning fetal lungs via the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale, both of which close at birth.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the human body, connecting the calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) to the heel bone. It must withstand forces of 7–12 times body weight during running and jumping, yet it has poor blood supply, which is why Achilles tendon injuries heal slowly.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: Nerve growth factor (NGF), discovered by Rita Levi-Montalcini (Nobel 1986), is essential for the survival and growth of sympathetic and sensory neurons during development. In adults, NGF continues to support peripheral nerve maintenance and is implicated in pain sensitization in chronic inflammatory conditions.

The average adult human head weighs about 4.5–5 kg (10–11 lbs). The cervical spine and surrounding neck muscles must constantly support this weight, and forward head posture (as in looking at a phone) multiplies the effective load — at 60 degrees forward tilt, the effective load on the neck rises to approximately 27 kg (60 lbs).

The human immune system can remember pathogens for a lifetime through long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow that continuously secrete protective antibodies. Studies of measles survivors show protective antibody titers persisting for 50+ years after a single infection.

The human small intestine is lined with enterocytes that live for only 3–5 days before being shed into the gut lumen. They are continuously replaced by daughter cells from intestinal stem cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn, making the intestinal epithelium one of the most rapidly self-renewing tissues in the body.

The human lung's right side has three lobes (upper, middle, lower) while the left lung has only two (upper, lower) to accommodate the heart, which sits slightly to the left of center in the thorax. The left lung also has a notch called the cardiac notch where the heart presses against it.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human body contains approximately 40 grams of ATP at any one time, yet the body turns over its own weight in ATP every day — roughly 40 kg for a resting adult. This turnover is possible because ADP is continuously recycled back to ATP by mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

Exosomes are tiny vesicles (30–150 nm) shed by virtually every cell in the body and found in blood, urine, saliva, and breast milk. They carry proteins, lipids, and microRNAs to neighboring and distant cells, mediating intercellular communication and playing roles in cancer metastasis, immune regulation, and tissue repair.

The human body produces approximately 800 mL of bile per day. Bile is synthesized from cholesterol in hepatocytes, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and then released into the duodenum after eating. Bile recycling — the enterohepatic circulation — means each bile salt molecule is recycled 4–12 times per day.

The human eye's blind spot — where the optic nerve exits the retina — has no photoreceptors and creates a gap in the visual field. The brain fills in this 'scotoma' seamlessly using information from the surrounding retinal area and the other eye, so most people never notice it without a specific test.

Mitochondria generate approximately 90% of the cell's usable energy (as ATP) through oxidative phosphorylation. The inner mitochondrial membrane is highly folded into cristae to maximize surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase complexes.

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the master circadian clock — a bilateral cluster of about 20,000 neurons that keeps time through interlocking transcription-translation feedback loops involving the genes CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY. The cycle repeats every ~24 hours and is entrained daily by light via the retinohypothalamic tract.

The human body's largest single nerve is the sciatic nerve, roughly the diameter of a thumb at its widest point. It arises from the L4–S3 nerve roots, runs through the gluteal region and down the back of the leg, innervating the entire lower leg and foot. Compression of the sciatic nerve causes sciatica — pain radiating down the leg.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human newborn's brain at birth is only about 25% of its adult size, but the number of neurons is approximately the same as in adulthood — neurons are already largely formed at birth. Most postnatal brain growth comes from myelination, synapse formation, and glial cell proliferation.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibers are highly oxidative, fatigue-resistant, and red (due to abundant myoglobin and mitochondria) — ideal for endurance activities. Type II (fast-twitch) fibers are glycolytic, generate more force rapidly, but fatigue quickly — suited for sprinting and power movements.

The human intestinal microbiome produces a significant portion of vitamin K2 (menaquinone), biotin, and folate — essential nutrients that humans cannot synthesize themselves. Disruption of the gut microbiome by antibiotics can therefore impair these vitamin supplies.

Astrocytes are the most abundant type of glial cell in the brain, outnumbering neurons. They perform a vast number of functions: maintaining the blood-brain barrier, supplying neurons with lactate as fuel, modulating synaptic transmission by taking up neurotransmitters, and regulating ionic homeostasis in the extracellular space.

The human colon absorbs approximately 1.5 liters of water per day from the ~2 liters of chyme that enter it from the small intestine, reducing this volume to the 100–200 mL of water excreted in stool. The colon also harbors the densest microbial community in the body, with up to 10^11 bacteria per gram of feces.

Cartilaginous intervertebral discs — which act as shock absorbers between vertebrae — are the largest avascular structures in the body, up to 6 cm in diameter. They rely entirely on diffusion from adjacent vertebral end plates for nutrition, and they lose hydration with age, which is why people are slightly shorter in the evening than in the morning.

The human brain uses the glymphatic system — discovered in 2013 — to clear metabolic waste, including amyloid-beta and tau proteins, from the interstitium during sleep. Cerebrospinal fluid flows along periarterial spaces, flushes the interstitium, and drains waste via perivenous spaces, a process greatly enhanced during deep non-REM sleep.

The human body generates approximately 1–3 million new red blood cells per second to replace the same number dying, in a process regulated by erythropoietin (EPO) produced by peritubular fibroblasts in the kidney. High altitude stimulates more EPO production because lower oxygen partial pressures trigger the HIF pathway.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Human fingers are sensitive enough to detect ridges as small as 13 nanometers high — finer than many microstructures. This extraordinary tactile acuity is due to Merkel's discs concentrated at the fingertips and amplified by fingerprint ridges that act as vibration amplifiers.

The human body's somatic mutation rate — the rate at which new mutations accumulate in non-germline cells — is approximately 1–2 mutations per cell division. Over a lifetime, most cells accumulate hundreds to thousands of somatic mutations; cancer occurs when critical driver mutations in oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes accumulate in a single cell.

The human intestinal lining contains specialized M cells (microfold cells) overlying Peyer's patches — clusters of lymphoid tissue in the small intestine. M cells sample antigens from the gut lumen and present them to immune cells below, allowing the immune system to monitor gut contents and mount mucosal immune responses.

The human kidney's glomerulus filters blood at a rate of approximately 125 mL/min (glomerular filtration rate, GFR). This value is used clinically to assess kidney function — a GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for 3 months indicates chronic kidney disease.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter involved in reward, motivation, motor control, and working memory. It is released by neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra; degeneration of the latter causes the movement disorder Parkinson's disease, characterized by tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human body's tallest vertebra is the C2 (axis), which features a unique bony projection called the dens (odontoid process) that articulates with C1 (atlas). This joint allows the head-nodding motion (atlanto-occipital) and the 'no' rotation (atlantoaxial) that together give the head most of its range of motion.

The human immune system's natural killer (NK) cells do not require antigen presentation to kill target cells — they detect the absence of MHC class I (a 'missing self' signal) and signs of cellular stress. This makes them effective against tumor cells and virally infected cells that downregulate MHC I to evade cytotoxic T cells.

The human body's total surface area of the capillary bed is estimated at about 6,000 m² — larger than a soccer field. At any given moment, about 5% of the total blood volume is in the capillaries, where gas, nutrient, and waste exchange with the interstitial fluid occurs.

The human fetus's eyelids are fused shut from week 10 to week 26 of gestation. When the retina begins to differentiate around week 26, the eyes start briefly opening and can detect light (though there is little light to detect in the womb), and rudimentary visual circuitry begins forming.

Serotonin (5-HT) is not just a brain neurotransmitter — approximately 90–95% of the body's total serotonin is produced in enterochromaffin cells of the gut, where it regulates intestinal motility. Many antidepressants (SSRIs) that block serotonin reuptake also cause gastrointestinal side effects because of this gut abundance.

The human immune response to a vaccine or infection takes 1–2 weeks to produce a protective antibody response (primary response), but a second exposure triggers memory B cells to produce much higher antibody levels within 2–3 days (secondary response). This anamnestic response can be 100–1,000 times stronger than the primary response.

The human pancreatic beta cells contain an estimated 10,000–15,000 secretory granules per cell, each containing a dense core of crystallized insulin complexed with zinc. Upon glucose stimulation, these granules fuse with the plasma membrane and release insulin through a Ca²⁺-dependent exocytosis process.

The human body has approximately 72 km (45 miles) of nerves. A single neuron can have an axon up to 1 meter long — the sciatic nerve's axons, running from the lower spine to the foot, are among the longest single cells in the human body.

Human red blood cells lack a nucleus and mitochondria, making them unable to divide or respire aerobically. This adaptation maximizes their capacity to carry hemoglobin and oxygen, but it also means they rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis for energy and must be replaced every ~120 days.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human spleen recycles iron from old red blood cells: its macrophages engulf aged erythrocytes, extract heme, break it down to biliverdin and bilirubin, and release iron for transport via transferrin back to the bone marrow. Jaundice occurs when bilirubin accumulates in the blood faster than the liver can conjugate and excrete it.

The human intestinal microbiome produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) — primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate — by fermenting dietary fiber. Butyrate is the primary energy source for colonocytes (cells lining the colon) and has anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer effects, which is one reason high-fiber diets are protective against colon cancer.

Human embryonic development is initiated by a sperm fertilizing an egg to form a zygote with 46 chromosomes. The first cell division occurs about 30 hours after fertilization, and by day 5 the embryo is a blastocyst of ~100 cells that implants into the uterine wall on day 6–10.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human eye can detect a single photon in optimal dark-adapted conditions — a sensitivity close to the theoretical physical limit. The scotopic (rod) visual system achieves this through convergence: up to 100 rods pool their signals onto a single retinal ganglion cell, amplifying the signal at the cost of spatial resolution.

The human palms and soles have no hair follicles and no sebaceous glands — which is why they do not get acne and why the skin there is thicker and more resistant to friction. These regions do have the highest density of eccrine sweat glands, which play a role in grip during activity and emotional sweating.

The human body's coagulation cascade involves two pathways — intrinsic (contact activation) and extrinsic (tissue factor) — that converge on thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Fibrin forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells to create a stable clot; clotting factors are numbered I–XIII, with no factor VI.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Human stem cells in hair follicles are also responsible for regenerating the epidermis after wounding. These bulge-region stem cells can migrate out of the follicle during wound healing and differentiate into keratinocytes to re-cover the wound surface — a discovery that has implications for treating severe burns.

The human large intestine (colon) is about 1.5 meters long and has four segments: ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. Its primary role is water and electrolyte absorption; it does not significantly contribute to nutrient absorption, which is handled almost entirely by the small intestine.

The human immune system's dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells, acting as messengers between the innate and adaptive immune systems. After engulfing a pathogen in a tissue, they migrate to lymph nodes and present antigen fragments on MHC molecules to prime naïve T cells, initiating a specific adaptive immune response.

Aldosterone, the main mineralocorticoid, is produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex and acts on the kidney's collecting duct to increase sodium reabsorption (and potassium excretion). This retains water and raises blood pressure; it is the final effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

The human brain's basal ganglia — a collection of nuclei including the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, and subthalamic nucleus — play a critical role in selecting and initiating voluntary movement and in procedural learning. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine loss in the striatum disrupts basal ganglia circuits, causing motor dysfunction.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human knee joint has approximately 60–80 mL of synovial fluid under normal conditions. This viscous fluid, secreted by the synovial membrane, lubricates the joint (reducing friction to near zero), nourishes the avascular cartilage, and absorbs mechanical shock. Inflammation causes excess fluid production (joint effusion).

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human stomach has three layers of smooth muscle — longitudinal, circular, and oblique — which create the churning motion that mixes food with gastric acid and enzymes, breaking it into chyme. This trituration is so effective that it can grind tablets and hard food particles into particles smaller than 1 mm.

The human body's lymph nodes contain germinal centers where B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation to produce increasingly potent antibodies during an immune response. Swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) during infection reflect this intense proliferative activity.

Human nasal passages warm, humidify, and filter inhaled air before it reaches the lungs. Turbinate bones (nasal conchae) create turbulent airflow to maximize contact with the mucosa; cilia beat mucus laden with trapped particles towards the throat for swallowing, in a process called mucociliary clearance.

The human body produces approximately 50–70 billion cells that die by apoptosis (programmed cell death) every day. Apoptosis is a controlled, orderly process in which cells shrink, DNA is fragmented, and membrane blebs form, without triggering inflammation — unlike necrosis (uncontrolled cell death), which causes tissue damage.

The human body's major histocompatibility complex (MHC) — known in humans as the HLA system — is the most polymorphic set of genes in the human genome. Different HLA alleles influence resistance and susceptibility to infectious diseases, autoimmune conditions, and the success of organ transplantation.

The human retina contains approximately 6 million cone cells (for color and daylight vision) concentrated in the fovea, and approximately 120 million rod cells (for low-light and peripheral vision) distributed over the rest of the retina. Both types of photoreceptors synapse onto bipolar and ganglion cells that transmit signals to the brain.

Human tears contain lysozyme, lactoferrin, immunoglobulin A (IgA), and defensins — all antimicrobial agents that protect the eye from infection. Lysozyme in tears cleaves the cell walls of gram-positive bacteria; its concentration in tears is among the highest of any body fluid.

Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding behavior is cooperative — binding one O2 molecule increases the affinity for subsequent molecules, producing a sigmoidal oxygen-dissociation curve. This property, arising from the allosteric conformational shift from tense (T) to relaxed (R) state upon oxygen binding, allows hemoglobin to load O2 efficiently in lungs and release it in tissues.

The human body's total protein content is approximately 10–12 kg in a 70 kg adult. Proteins serve as structural components, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and transport molecules; they are made of 20 standard amino acids, 9 of which are essential because the body cannot synthesize them and they must be obtained from diet.

Human neonates are born with the ability to swim reflexively if placed face-down in water — a reflex called the diving reflex, which also involves bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction to conserve oxygen. This reflex diminishes after about 6 months of age as the nervous system matures.

The human body's total lipid content ranges from about 15–30% of body weight, stored predominantly as triglycerides in adipose tissue. Each gram of fat stores 9 kilocalories — more than twice the energy density of carbohydrate or protein — making fat the body's primary long-term energy reservoir.

The human fetus generates heat primarily through non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT), with deposits around the neck and between the shoulder blades. Premature infants have less BAT and greater surface-area-to-volume ratio, making thermoregulation challenging and requiring incubators.

The human middle ear is connected to the back of the throat by the Eustachian tube, which equalizes air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. When cabin pressure changes in an airplane or at altitude, yawning or swallowing opens the tube's valve, allowing pressure equalization and relieving ear pain.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human body's fastest healing tissue is the oral mucosa — mouth wounds typically heal in 7–10 days compared to 2–4 weeks for skin wounds of similar size. This rapid healing is attributed to high local concentrations of growth factors in saliva, a rich blood supply, and a moist wound environment.

The human brain weighs about 1.3–1.4 kg and contains approximately 86 billion neurons connected by an estimated 100 trillion synapses. The number of possible unique synaptic configurations has been estimated to exceed the number of atoms in the observable universe.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human heart pumps blood through two circuits in series: the pulmonary circulation (right heart → lungs → left heart) and the systemic circulation (left heart → body → right heart). The left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right because it must generate higher pressure to drive blood around the entire body.

Xenotransplantation research has revealed that pigs are the most promising source of organs for human transplantation because pig organs are similar in size, anatomy, and physiology to human organs. Genetically engineered pigs with human complement-regulatory genes reduce the hyperacute rejection that destroys pig organs within minutes in humans.

The human body's largest lymphoid organ is the spleen, but the largest collection of lymphoid tissue overall is the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), which includes Peyer's patches, mesenteric lymph nodes, and isolated lymphoid follicles. GALT contains more immune cells than all other lymphoid organs combined.

Human scalp hair grows in a mosaic pattern where individual follicles cycle asynchronously, preventing all hairs from shedding simultaneously. Some animals (like mink) have synchronous cycling and shed their coat all at once — a dramatic phenomenon called molting. The asynchronous pattern in humans ensures continual coverage.

The human inner ear also plays a role in immune privilege — it is largely protected from systemic immune responses because an inflammatory response in the cochlea would damage the delicate hair cells and cause permanent hearing loss. The endolymph is tightly sealed from the immune system by tight junctions, similar to the blood-brain barrier.

The human brain's prefrontal cortex (PFC) is the last brain region to fully mature, completing development around age 25. The PFC governs planning, decision-making, impulse control, and social behavior — which is why adolescents show greater risk-taking and emotional reactivity before its maturation is complete.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Mental Health

text: The human kidney conserves water by generating a high osmolality gradient in the renal medulla — up to 1,200 mOsm/kg, about four times the osmolality of blood. This is achieved through a counter-current multiplier in the loop of Henle and counter-current exchange in the vasa recta blood vessels.

Muscle contraction occurs through the sliding filament mechanism: myosin thick filaments use ATP hydrolysis to 'walk' along actin thin filaments, pulling the ends of the sarcomere together and shortening the muscle fiber. The troponin-tropomyosin system controls this by gating access to actin's myosin-binding sites based on intracellular calcium levels.

The human body's immune system communicates through cytokines — small signaling proteins that coordinate immune responses. There are hundreds of known cytokines, including interleukins (IL-1 through IL-40+), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and interferons (IFN). Dysregulated cytokine release, called a 'cytokine storm,' can be life-threatening, as seen in severe COVID-19.

Human fingertip skin ridges (fingerprints) are unique to each individual and even to each identical twin, because their fine details are shaped by random developmental forces during fetal growth, not genetics alone. Even a single finger has a pattern complexity estimated at about 35 bits of unique information.

The human body can produce vitamin D when ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation from sunlight converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin into pre-vitamin D3, which is then isomerized to vitamin D3 and hydroxylated twice in the liver and kidney into active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). About 15–30 minutes of midday sun exposure on bare skin produces approximately 10,000–25,000 IU of vitamin D.

The human cornea has the highest density of pain-sensing nerve endings of any tissue in the body — approximately 300–600 times denser than skin. A 1 mm corneal abrasion is therefore exquisitely painful. This high sensitivity serves as an early warning system to protect the eye from injury.

Human blood type is determined by antigens on the surface of red blood cells. The ABO system involves antigens A and B (or both, or neither) on RBCs. The Rh system adds the D antigen; Rh-negative mothers carrying Rh-positive fetuses can develop antibodies that cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn if untreated with Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM).

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human tonsils — palatine, lingual, pharyngeal (adenoids), and tubal — form a ring of lymphoid tissue at the entrance to the throat called Waldeyer's ring. They are the first line of immune defense against inhaled and ingested pathogens, sampling them to initiate adaptive immune responses.

The human body coordinates movement through the corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract) — a bundle of about 1 million axons descending from the motor cortex through the brainstem to the spinal cord. Most fibers cross (decussate) in the medulla, which is why left brain injuries affect the right side of the body.

The human fetus swallows amniotic fluid starting around week 12, contributing to the development of the gastrointestinal tract and providing nutrients and antibodies. By term, the fetus swallows about 500–1,000 mL of amniotic fluid per day. This fluid is produced by the kidneys and lungs and constantly recycled.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human adrenal cortex synthesizes more than 50 different steroid hormones from cholesterol. The three functional zones produce mineralocorticoids (zona glomerulosa), glucocorticoids (zona fasciculata), and sex steroids (zona reticularis). Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is life-threatening because all three hormone classes are absent.

Tight junctions between cells — made of claudins, occludins, and junction adhesion molecules — create selective barriers that regulate the paracellular passage of ions and molecules. Their tightness varies by tissue: kidney proximal tubule tight junctions are leaky (allowing reabsorption), while brain endothelial tight junctions are extremely restrictive (forming the blood-brain barrier).

The human body contains roughly 37 trillion cells in total. Contrary to a common myth, bacteria in and on the human body do not outnumber human cells 10:1; the current best estimate is a ratio close to 1:1, with about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells.

The human body's circadian rhythm influences drug metabolism — a field called chronopharmacology. Many drugs work better or have fewer side effects when taken at specific times of day because drug-metabolizing enzymes, transporters, and target proteins fluctuate with the circadian clock. Cancer chemotherapy timed to circadian rhythms can reduce toxicity while maintaining efficacy.

The human zona pellucida — the glycoprotein shell surrounding the egg — contains ZP3, which acts as a species-specific sperm receptor. After a single sperm fertilizes the egg, the zona undergoes a rapid 'zona reaction' — calcium-triggered exocytosis of cortical granules that modify ZP3 and prevent polyspermy.

Human bone is a composite material: organic collagen fibers provide tensile strength and flexibility, while inorganic hydroxyapatite crystals provide compressive strength and hardness. This two-component structure makes bone much tougher than either component alone — neither pure collagen (too flexible) nor pure mineral (too brittle) would serve as well.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human body has a portal circulation — a venous system that drains one capillary bed into another before returning to the heart. The hepatic portal system carries nutrient-rich blood from the intestines directly to the liver for processing; the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system delivers releasing hormones directly to the anterior pituitary.

The human body contains about 25 grams of magnesium, 60% of which is stored in bones. Magnesium is a cofactor for more than 300 enzymatic reactions, including ATP synthesis, DNA replication, and protein synthesis. It also serves as a natural calcium channel blocker, regulating nerve and muscle excitability.

The Müller cells of the retina are specialized radial glial cells that span the full thickness of the retina. They act as optical fibers, channeling light directly from the retinal surface to the photoreceptors beneath the blood vessels and ganglion cells, maintaining image quality by reducing light scatter.

The human appendicular skeleton — comprising the arms, legs, pelvis, and shoulder girdle — is connected to the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and allows locomotion and manipulation. The pectoral and pelvic girdles are the major articulation points between appendicular and axial skeleton.

A human hair strand can support approximately 100 grams of weight, and a full head of hair (about 100,000 hairs) could theoretically support 10,000 kg (about 10 tonnes). The hair shaft is composed of three layers: the cuticle (outer scales), cortex (pigmented keratin fibers), and medulla (inner pith, present only in thick hairs).

The human immune system's complement system can be activated through three pathways: classical (antibody-antigen complexes), lectin (mannose-binding lectin recognizing sugar patterns on pathogens), and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis amplified on microbial surfaces). All three converge at C3 and produce the membrane attack complex.

Human sperm cells are the smallest cells in the human body — about 5 micrometers in the head, with a 50 micrometer tail. They are among the few cell types with a haploid (n=23) genome and are specialized for a single purpose: swimming to and fertilizing an egg. Each ejaculate contains ~200–500 million sperm.

The human immune response to influenza infection generates memory T and B cells, but influenza virus mutates rapidly (antigenic drift) so each year's strain may differ enough from previous ones to partially evade immune memory. This is why annual influenza vaccination is necessary, formulated each year to match predicted circulating strains.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: The human body stores approximately 150–160 grams of glycogen in the liver and releases it as glucose between meals to maintain blood glucose. After about 12–16 hours of fasting, liver glycogen is depleted and gluconeogenesis must sustain blood glucose; the brain gradually adapts to using ketone bodies when glucose becomes insufficient.

The human appendix reaches its maximum lymphoid tissue content during childhood (ages 10–20) and then gradually atrophies with age. In infants and children, it is relatively larger and more active immunologically, which may partly explain why appendicitis is most common in young adults.

The human ear's cochlear amplifier — powered by electromotility of outer hair cells through the protein prestin — amplifies basilar membrane vibrations up to 1,000-fold, sharpening frequency selectivity and boosting sensitivity. Loss of outer hair cells (from noise, ototoxic drugs, or aging) causes permanent sensorineural hearing loss.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Human bones are not solid — their interior consists of spongy (trabecular) bone with a honeycomb structure that maximizes strength while minimizing weight. The spaces within trabecular bone are filled with red or yellow marrow; cortical (compact) bone forms the dense outer shell.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human body's major veins contain one-way valves — especially in the limbs — that prevent backflow of blood against gravity. Incompetent valves cause varicose veins, where blood pools in the superficial leg veins. The calf muscle acts as a 'second heart,' pumping venous blood back toward the heart during walking.

The human body secretes over 50 known hormones from endocrine glands and peripheral tissues. Among them, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), secreted by the liver in response to growth hormone, is the main mediator of somatic growth during childhood, stimulating protein synthesis and cell proliferation throughout the body.

The human body's sense of pain uses two parallel pathways: the spinothalamic tract (transmitting pain and temperature) and the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway (transmitting fine touch, proprioception, and vibration). Selective injury to one pathway can abolish pain while preserving touch — as in Brown-Séquard syndrome from a hemisection of the spinal cord.

The human gut microbiome is disrupted by antibiotic use, which kills beneficial bacteria and allows opportunistic pathogens like Clostridioides difficile to flourish, causing antibiotic-associated colitis. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) — transferring stool from a healthy donor — restores a healthy microbiome and cures recurrent C. diff in over 90% of cases.

The human salivary glands — parotid, submandibular, and sublingual — together produce 0.5–1.5 liters of saliva per day. Saliva is 99.5% water but the remaining 0.5% is biologically active, containing amylase, lipase, mucin, IgA, lactoferrin, lysozyme, and electrolytes.

Human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are pluripotent — they can differentiate into any of the ~200 cell types in the human body. They are derived from the inner cell mass of blastocysts. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), discovered by Shinya Yamanaka (Nobel 2012), can be generated from adult cells by introducing four transcription factors, bypassing the need for embryos.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

text: The human heart's Frank-Starling mechanism ensures that cardiac output matches venous return: the more the heart fills with blood (preload), the greater the force of contraction and the more blood ejected. This intrinsic property means that if the right heart pumps more blood, the left heart automatically pumps more blood too.

Human tears produced during emotional crying have been shown to contain high levels of leucine-enkephalin, an endogenous opioid, and prolactin. Some researchers hypothesize that shedding tears during emotional distress provides a neurochemical benefit by releasing these compounds, contributing to the calming effect often reported after crying.

The human immune system generates approximately 10 billion new lymphocytes per day. However, in the thymus, more than 95% of T cells generated fail selection (either they don't recognize self-MHC or they react too strongly to self-antigens) and are eliminated — leaving only a highly selected, useful repertoire.

The human body has a specialized sweat response during emotional stress or fear called 'cold sweat' — produced by palms, soles, and armpits under sympathetic nervous system stimulation without the body temperature elevation that accompanies heat-related sweating. This response is evolutionarily linked to the fight-or-flight response.

The human body's largest artery (aorta) and largest vein (superior/inferior vena cava) both connect to the heart. The aorta has a diameter of 2–3 cm; the vena cavae are slightly wider at 2–3.5 cm. The aorta contains elastic fibers that stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining blood flow between heartbeats.

Phagocytosis — the engulfment and destruction of pathogens by immune cells — is mediated by pseudopods of actin filaments that surround the target, forming a phagosome. Lysosomes then fuse with the phagosome to deliver digestive enzymes, reactive oxygen species, and antimicrobial peptides that kill the pathogen.

The human nasal cavity has a 'nasal cycle' — alternating congestion and decongestion of the two nasal passages roughly every 2–4 hours — controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Most people are unaware of this because both sides together provide adequate airflow, but it becomes obvious during a cold when both sides congest simultaneously.

The human placenta produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) starting about 10 days after fertilization, which maintains the corpus luteum and progesterone production until the placenta takes over hormone production at ~10 weeks. Pregnancy tests detect hCG in urine or blood; levels double approximately every 48 hours in early pregnancy.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human body's neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (50–70% of total leukocytes) and the first responders to bacterial infection. They survive only 6–12 hours in circulation and 1–2 days in tissue before undergoing apoptosis. The pus in an infected wound is largely composed of dead neutrophils.

The human somatosensory cortex contains a 'homunculus' — a distorted map of the body where regions with the highest touch sensitivity (hands, lips, tongue) occupy disproportionately large cortical areas relative to their physical size. This cortical magnification reflects the much higher density of sensory receptors in these areas.

The human liver metabolizes ethanol (alcohol) primarily through two enzymes: alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) converts ethanol to acetaldehyde, and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) converts acetaldehyde to acetate. Acetaldehyde is highly toxic and responsible for many of the negative effects of alcohol; genetic variants in ALDH2 that impair acetaldehyde clearance cause the 'Asian flush' reaction.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism

text: The human body's thoracic cage (12 pairs of ribs, sternum, and thoracic vertebrae) protects the heart and lungs and plays an active role in breathing. During inspiration, the external intercostal muscles and diaphragm increase thoracic volume; during expiration, elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall passively deflates them at rest.

The human kidney has a unique ability to sense low oxygen — hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) stabilizes when oxygen falls and drives transcription of erythropoietin to stimulate RBC production. At high altitude, this pathway is activated within hours, and RBC production increases within days, improving oxygen delivery.

The human immune system generates natural killer T (NKT) cells that bridge innate and adaptive immunity by recognizing lipid antigens presented on CD1d molecules — not peptide antigens on MHC, as conventional T cells do. NKT cells are particularly important in responses to certain bacteria (like Borrelia and Salmonella) and tumor surveillance.

The human gut releases over 20 different hormones including GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), GIP, PYY, and CCK after meals. These gut hormones signal satiety to the brain, regulate insulin secretion, slow gastric emptying, and control overall energy intake. GLP-1 receptor agonists (such as semaglutide) mimic these signals and are highly effective weight-loss drugs.

The human skeletal muscle fiber contains bundles of myofibrils, each of which is made of repeating sarcomeres — the basic contractile units. Each sarcomere is ~2.2 micrometers long at rest and can shorten to ~1.5 micrometers upon full contraction. A single muscle fiber may be 30 cm long but only 50–100 micrometers wide.

The human body's microbiome can be disrupted during birth: vaginally delivered babies acquire their initial microbiome primarily from the mother's vaginal and fecal flora (Lactobacillus-dominated), while cesarean-born babies are initially colonized by skin and hospital environmental bacteria. This difference may have long-term health consequences for immune programming.

The human ear's pitch perception follows Ohm's acoustic law: the ear performs a real-time Fourier analysis, separating complex sound waves into their component pure tones. This is carried out by the tonotopic map of the basilar membrane in the cochlea, which acts as a biological frequency analyzer.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human brain's Broca's area (left inferior frontal gyrus) is essential for speech production and grammatical processing. Damage here causes Broca's aphasia — patients understand language but speak in halting, effortful phrases. Wernicke's area (left posterior superior temporal gyrus) handles language comprehension; its damage causes fluent but nonsensical speech.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human parathyroid glands — four tiny glands behind the thyroid — produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), the primary regulator of calcium homeostasis. When blood calcium drops, PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the kidney, activates vitamin D to increase gut calcium absorption, and stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone.

Human skin color across populations is an adaptation primarily to UV radiation levels. In equatorial regions, dark skin (high eumelanin) protects against UV-induced folate degradation and DNA damage; in high-latitude regions, lighter skin (less melanin) allows sufficient UV penetration for vitamin D synthesis during weaker sunlight.

The human brain contains specialized 'grid cells' in the entorhinal cortex that fire in a hexagonal lattice pattern as an animal moves through space, acting as a coordinate system for spatial navigation. Combined with hippocampal place cells, they form the brain's GPS. Moser and O'Keefe were awarded the 2014 Nobel Prize for these discoveries.

The human body's nervous system is divided into the somatic (voluntary control of skeletal muscle, sensory reception) and autonomic (involuntary control of smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands) nervous systems. The autonomic system has two main branches: sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest), which generally antagonize each other.

The human body loses approximately 2–2.5 liters of water per day through urine (~1.5 L), perspiration (~0.5 L), respiration (~0.3 L), and feces (~0.1 L). This must be replaced by drinking (~1.5 L) and eating (~0.7 L), plus ~0.3 L from metabolic water produced when cells burn carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

Human red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape that maximizes their surface area-to-volume ratio, facilitating rapid oxygen and CO2 exchange. They lack a nucleus and contain about 270 million hemoglobin molecules each, capable of carrying up to 1.08 billion oxygen molecules per cell.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human body's immune system contains about 2 trillion lymphocytes, more than half of which are stored in lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, thymus) rather than circulating in blood. The total mass of the immune system is approximately 0.9–1.5 kg — comparable to the size of the brain.

Human hair color is determined by the ratio of eumelanin (dark) to pheomelanin (light/red) in the cortex. Red hair results from a high proportion of pheomelanin due to variants in the MC1R gene. Gray hair occurs when melanocytes in hair follicles are depleted with age, producing unpigmented hair.

The human skeleton serves not only as a structural framework but also as an endocrine organ. Osteoblast-derived osteocalcin functions as a hormone that promotes muscle uptake of glucose during exercise, improves memory and cognition, and increases testosterone production — revealing unexpected connections between bone and whole-body physiology.

The human body has a specialized network of pain-modulating neurons in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain. The PAG releases endogenous opioids and activates descending pain-inhibitory pathways (including the raphe nucleus serotoninergic neurons and locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons) that suppress pain at the spinal cord level — the basis of 'mind over pain.'

The human testes are located outside the body in the scrotum because sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires temperatures 2–4°C below core body temperature. The cremaster muscle raises or lowers the testes to maintain this temperature; prolonged elevated scrotal temperature (as in fever or tight clothing) can temporarily impair sperm quality.

The human body's eosinophils — white blood cells that make up 1–4% of circulating leukocytes — are specialized against multicellular parasites (helminths) too large to be phagocytosed. They attack parasites by degranulating toxic proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil peroxidase). Their numbers rise dramatically during parasitic infections and allergic diseases.

The human body's largest endocrine gland is the thyroid, weighing about 25 grams in adults. It wraps around the trachea just below the larynx and is divided into two lobes connected by an isthmus. Its follicular cells produce thyroid hormones stored as thyroglobulin within follicles — a unique form of extracellular hormone storage.

Human pain sensitization — where the nervous system amplifies pain signals — involves two mechanisms: peripheral sensitization (inflamed tissue releases prostaglandins and bradykinin that lower the threshold of nociceptors) and central sensitization (increased synaptic efficacy in the spinal cord dorsal horn). Chronic pain often involves persistent central sensitization.

The human diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5 — 'three, four, five keeps the diaphragm alive'). Damage to the cervical spinal cord above C3 paralyzes both phrenic nerves, causing respiratory failure and requiring mechanical ventilation.

The human placenta contains two separate circulations that never mix: fetal blood in villous capillaries and maternal blood in the intervillous space. Substances cross by simple diffusion (O2, CO2), facilitated transport (glucose), active transport (amino acids, iron), or receptor-mediated endocytosis (IgG antibodies), depending on the molecule.

Human tears have three layers: a mucin layer (anchoring tears to the cornea), an aqueous layer (containing antibacterial proteins and nutrients), and an outer lipid layer (produced by Meibomian glands, preventing evaporation). Dysfunction of any layer contributes to dry eye disease, which affects an estimated 344 million people worldwide.

The human body's smooth muscle — found in blood vessels, the gut, airways, and the uterus — is involuntary and lacks the striations of skeletal muscle. It contracts more slowly than skeletal muscle but can sustain contractions for extended periods with less energy. The uterus is the strongest smooth muscle in the body during labor.

Chylomicrons are the largest lipoproteins in the blood — up to 1,000 nm in diameter — assembled in intestinal cells to transport dietary fat through lymph into the bloodstream. Their apolipoprotein B-48 coat allows them to be recognized by lipoprotein lipase in capillary walls, which extracts triglycerides for storage or energy use.

The human spinal cord has 31 pairs of spinal nerves organized into 5 regions: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Because the spinal cord ends at L1–L2 (the conus medullaris) while the vertebral column extends further, the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots form a horse-tail of nerves called the cauda equina.

Nitric oxide (NO) produced by neurons in the central and peripheral nervous system acts as an unconventional neurotransmitter — it is a gas, not stored in vesicles, and diffuses freely across cell membranes in all directions from its point of synthesis. In the gut, it is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter relaxing smooth muscle.

Human embryonic development follows a cephalocaudal gradient: structures of the head develop earlier and more rapidly than those of the trunk and limbs. This is reflected in the disproportionately large head of the fetus (50% of crown-rump length at 8 weeks) compared to the adult (14% of total height).

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human immune system's NK cells kill target cells by releasing perforin (which punches holes in the target cell membrane) and granzymes (serine proteases that enter through the perforin pores and trigger caspase-mediated apoptosis). This same killing mechanism is used by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells.

The human esophagus is approximately 25 cm long and has both voluntary (upper) and involuntary (lower) muscular control. Peristaltic waves generated by enteric neurons propel food from the pharynx to the stomach in about 8–10 seconds. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) prevents acid reflux; its dysfunction causes GERD.

Human sebum — produced by sebaceous glands — is a complex mixture of triglycerides, wax esters, squalene, and free fatty acids that lubricates and waterproofs skin and hair. At puberty, androgens dramatically increase sebum production; excess sebum and follicular plugging are the primary triggers for acne vulgaris.

The human cerebral cortex has a surface area of approximately 2,500 cm² (about the size of a pillowcase) but is crammed into the skull by extensive folding into gyri (ridges) and sulci (grooves). Only about one-third of the cortical surface is visible externally; the rest is buried in sulci.

The human immune system's interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β) are produced by virus-infected cells within hours of infection and trigger an antiviral state in neighboring cells by upregulating hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). These ISGs degrade viral RNA, inhibit protein synthesis, and upregulate MHC class I molecules to alert T cells.

The human stomach lining contains three types of secretory cells: parietal cells (produce HCl and intrinsic factor), chief cells (produce pepsinogen, the precursor of pepsin), and mucous cells (produce protective mucus and bicarbonate). Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum; its absence causes pernicious anemia.

Human height is determined by approximately 700 genetic loci, each contributing tiny effects, plus significant environmental factors (chiefly nutrition). Twin studies show that genetics accounts for about 80% of height variation in populations with adequate nutrition. The global average adult male height has increased by ~10 cm over the past century.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human kidney produces calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) — the active form of vitamin D — by hydroxylating 25-hydroxyvitamin D using the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. This final activation step is regulated by PTH and phosphate levels; defects in the kidney enzyme cause vitamin D-dependent rickets, leading to soft, deformed bones.

The human body has approximately 3 million eccrine sweat glands distributed across the skin surface, with the highest density on palms and soles (~600 glands/cm²). During intense exercise or extreme heat, the body can produce up to 10–14 liters of sweat per day, with peak rates of about 2–3 liters per hour.

The human immune system's myeloid cells include neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, basophils, mast cells, and dendritic cells — all derived from a common myeloid progenitor in the bone marrow.
