Monocytes circulate in blood and migrate into tissues where they differentiate into macrophages or dendritic cells.

The human knee joint has two menisci — medial and lateral — that are C-shaped fibrocartilage discs distributing load across the joint surface. They absorb up to 70% of the compressive force on the knee. Meniscal tears are the most common knee injury in athletes, and the medial meniscus tears more often because it is less mobile.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human immune system produces IgA antibodies in dimeric form held together by a J-chain and secretory component, making secretory IgA (sIgA) resistant to proteolytic digestion in the gut lumen. sIgA coats and neutralizes pathogens, preventing their attachment to gut epithelial cells — the main antibody defense at mucosal surfaces.

Angiogenesis — the formation of new blood vessels from pre-existing ones — is tightly regulated by a balance between pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF, FGF, angiopoietins) and anti-angiogenic factors (thrombospondin, endostatin). Tumors hijack angiogenesis to supply themselves with nutrients; anti-VEGF drugs (bevacizumab) starve tumors by blocking this process.

The human pancreas has both alpha cells (producing glucagon) and beta cells (producing insulin) organized in clusters called islets of Langerhans, which are embedded in the exocrine pancreatic tissue. These islets also contain delta cells (producing somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon) and PP cells (producing pancreatic polypeptide).

The human ear can localize sounds in the horizontal plane by detecting interaural time differences (ITD) as small as 10 microseconds and interaural level differences (ILD). These cues are processed by the superior olivary complex in the brainstem. Vertical localization relies on the shape of the outer ear (pinna) that differentially filters sounds from above and below.

Human fetal hemoglobin (HbF) contains two alpha and two gamma subunits, with a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA). This difference is essential for the fetus to extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta. HbF is gradually replaced by HbA during the first year of life.

Human skin's dermis contains elastic fibers made of elastin protein, which allow the skin to stretch and recoil. Elastic fiber production declines with age and UV exposure; this, combined with reduced collagen synthesis, causes skin to lose elasticity and form wrinkles. The dermis also contains fibroblasts that continuously remodel the extracellular matrix.

Human hearts develop from the mesoderm in the embryo around day 18–19, making the heart one of the first organs to form and function. By gestational week 8, the four-chambered heart structure is largely complete, including the atrioventricular valves — earlier than almost any other organ system.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human body can sense five basic tastes: sweet (sugars, saccharin), salty (NaCl), sour (acids), bitter (toxins, alkaloids), and umami (glutamate, savory). A sixth taste — fat taste (oleogustus) — was proposed in 2015. Each is detected by specific taste receptor proteins on taste receptor cells.

The human immune system can differentiate between danger signals from damaged self-tissue (damage-associated molecular patterns, DAMPs) and pathogen signals (PAMPs) using overlapping but distinct pattern recognition receptors. DAMPs like HMGB1, HSPs, and ATP released from dying cells alert the immune system to sterile injury, triggering inflammation without infection.

Human bones grow in length at cartilaginous growth plates (physes) near the ends of long bones. Chondrocytes in the growth plate proliferate, enlarge, mineralize, and are replaced by bone. When sex hormone levels rise at puberty, growth plates close and linear growth stops — typically by age 14–16 in girls and 16–18 in boys.

The human body contains about 25 trillion red blood cells at any time. If all of a person's red blood cells were laid flat and side by side, they would cover approximately 2,000 square meters — about half an acre.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human brain's anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is activated both by physical pain and by social pain (rejection, ostracism, grief). Brain imaging shows that social exclusion activates the same neural circuits as physical pain, suggesting that 'social pain' is not merely a metaphor but involves genuine overlap with the pain-processing system.

The human body's lymphocytes patrol the body continuously: T cells recirculate every 12–24 hours through blood, lymph nodes, and tissues. A naïve T cell that has never encountered its antigen circulates for years awaiting activation. Once activated by antigen, it undergoes clonal expansion and can divide 10–15 times over 3–5 days, generating thousands of identical effector cells.

Human breast milk contains lactoferrin, a glycoprotein that binds iron with high affinity, preventing its use by bacteria (bacteriostasis). Unlike iron in formula, the iron in human milk is highly bioavailable because lactoferrin-bound iron is absorbed via specific receptors in the infant gut, not competing with bacterial iron-acquisition systems.

The human glomerulonephritis illustrates a key immune mechanism: immune complexes (antibody-antigen aggregates) depositing in glomerular capillaries activate complement and attract neutrophils, causing inflammation that destroys the filtration apparatus. Diseases like lupus nephritis and IgA nephropathy (the world's most common glomerulonephritis) involve this immune complex pathway.

The human body contains about 110 grams of phosphorus (as phosphate) after calcium the most abundant mineral, over 85% stored in bones as hydroxyapatite. Phosphate is also critical for energy transfer (ATP), DNA/RNA backbone structure, and cell signaling via protein phosphorylation.

Human immune cells use neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) — web-like meshes of DNA, histones, and antimicrobial proteins expelled by dying neutrophils — to trap and kill extracellular bacteria and fungi. NETs are a relatively recently discovered immune defense (2004); excessive NET formation contributes to organ damage in sepsis and autoimmune diseases.

The human knee's anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) prevents the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur and resists rotational forces. ACL injuries most commonly occur via non-contact mechanisms — sudden stopping, pivoting, or landing — and are 3–5 times more frequent in female athletes compared to males, partly due to anatomical and hormonal differences.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human body produces reactive nitrogen species (RNS) alongside reactive oxygen species (ROS) as part of the oxidative burst in macrophages and neutrophils. Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is upregulated in activated macrophages to produce large amounts of NO, which reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite — a potent antimicrobial agent.

Human walking requires the precise coordination of over 200 muscles. The gait cycle consists of a stance phase (60% of the cycle, when the foot is on the ground) and a swing phase (40%, when the foot is airborne). The center of mass follows an inverted pendulum trajectory, exchanging kinetic and potential energy to minimize metabolic cost.

The human tongue is covered with papillae — small bumps housing taste buds. Fungiform papillae (scattered randomly across the tongue tip and edges) each contain 3–5 taste buds; circumvallate (vallate) papillae (8–12 large papillae at the back of the tongue) are densely packed with hundreds of taste buds each and are where bitter taste is most strongly perceived.

The human immune system possesses approximately 1 billion unique B cell clones — each with a different antigen receptor — circulating in the blood and lymphoid organs at any time. When a foreign antigen enters the body, it selects and activates the rare B cells whose receptors match it, causing clonal expansion of just that specific specificity.

The human pupil diameter ranges from about 1.5 mm in bright light to 8–9 mm in complete darkness — an area ratio of about 30-fold. This pupillary response is mediated by two sets of iris muscles: the sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, constricts) and the dilator pupillae (sympathetic, dilates).

Human wound healing proceeds through four overlapping phases: hemostasis (clot formation within minutes), inflammation (neutrophil and macrophage recruitment, days 1–4), proliferation (fibroblast collagen synthesis, days 4–21), and remodeling (scar maturation, months to years). The final scar contains type I collagen but lacks the normal basket-weave organization, making it weaker.

The human body's gut-associated immune system must simultaneously tolerate harmless food proteins and commensal bacteria while defending against pathogens. This tolerance is enforced by regulatory T cells, secretory IgA, and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β). Breakdown of this balance underlies food allergies, celiac disease, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Human DNA replication is semi-conservative — each new double helix consists of one original strand and one newly synthesized strand. The entire human genome (~3.2 billion base pairs per haploid set) is replicated in roughly 6–8 hours, initiated at approximately 30,000–50,000 origins of replication simultaneously, as no single origin could copy the entire genome in time.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue making it part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and is richly supplied with IgA-producing B cells. Appendectomy does not appear to cause significant immunological deficits, suggesting functional redundancy with other lymphoid tissues.

Human infants are born with a large amount of cartilage in their skeleton that progressively ossifies (converts to bone). The carpal (wrist) bones are entirely cartilaginous at birth and ossify one at a time between ages 1–9; their appearance on X-rays has historically been used to assess a child's 'bone age' and skeletal maturity.

The human body's sensory system uses a labeled line code: each sensory neuron responds to a specific modality (touch, pain, temperature), and the brain infers the nature of the stimulus from which neurons are active. This is why stimulating pain fibers electrically always produces pain, even if the physical stimulus was something else.

The human eye's lens grows throughout life — unlike most tissues, it never stops adding new fiber cells around its outer margin. Old fiber cells remain at the center (nucleus) indefinitely, which is why the lens nucleus gradually hardens with age. This lifelong accumulation of cells is why cataracts (lens clouding) are inevitable if one lives long enough.

The human body's major energy currency — ATP — is produced in three main ways: substrate-level phosphorylation (in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle), oxidative phosphorylation (in mitochondria via the electron transport chain), and the creatine phosphate system (in muscle, providing immediate ATP for the first 10 seconds of intense exercise).

The human immune system's cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize viral peptides displayed on MHC class I of infected cells and kill them within minutes through perforin/granzyme delivery. A single cytotoxic T cell can serially kill multiple target cells without being destroyed itself — a process called serial killing.

Human bone density peaks in the late 20s to early 30s and then gradually declines with age. Women lose bone density faster in the years immediately following menopause due to reduced estrogen, which normally inhibits osteoclast activity. Osteoporosis results when bone resorption exceeds formation, leading to fracture risk.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human immune response to cancer involves tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) — immune cells that migrate into tumors and can kill cancer cells. The presence and density of TILs correlates strongly with prognosis in many cancers; checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4 drugs) works by removing brakes on these TILs.

Human muscles can only pull, never push — they generate force only by contracting (shortening). Therefore, joints are typically controlled by pairs of antagonistic muscles: a flexor (bends the joint) opposed by an extensor (straightens it). The biceps flexes the elbow; the triceps extends it.

The human spleen's white pulp contains germinal centers similar to lymph nodes, where T and B cells interact in adaptive immune responses to blood-borne antigens. The red pulp filters blood, removes old and abnormal red blood cells, and stores platelets. People without a spleen (asplenia) are especially susceptible to infections by encapsulated bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The human body synthesizes cholesterol endogenously at a rate of about 1 gram per day, primarily in the liver. Cholesterol is the precursor for steroid hormones, vitamin D, and bile acids, and is an essential component of all cell membranes. The HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) reduce cardiovascular risk by blocking the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.

The human body's insula (insular cortex) integrates internal body signals (interoception) with emotional processing and is activated by disgust, empathy, pain, craving, and social emotions. It creates the sense of body ownership and contributes to 'gut feelings.' Insula damage impairs the ability to recognize facial expressions of disgust.

Human fetal red blood cells are produced first in the yolk sac (~weeks 3–8), then in the fetal liver (~weeks 6–22), and finally in the bone marrow (~weeks 12 onwards), which becomes the primary hematopoietic organ by birth. This progressive shift from primitive to definitive hematopoiesis parallels the switch from embryonic to fetal to adult hemoglobin.

The human liver detoxifies ammonia — a byproduct of amino acid catabolism — by converting it to urea in the urea cycle. Urea is then excreted by the kidneys. Liver failure disrupts this process, causing ammonia to accumulate in the blood (hyperammonemia), which is neurotoxic and causes hepatic encephalopathy.

The human body experiences a phenomenon called 'referred pain,' where pain originating in an internal organ is perceived as coming from a distant body surface area. Heart attacks cause pain referred to the left arm and jaw; gallbladder inflammation refers to the right shoulder. This occurs because visceral and somatic afferent fibers converge on the same spinal cord neurons.

Intestinal peristalsis is driven by two types of movement in the small intestine: segmentation (non-propulsive mixing contractions that occur 12–16 times per minute in the duodenum) and peristaltic waves that propel chyme towards the colon. Between meals, the migrating motor complex sweeps residual contents and bacteria from the small intestine every 90–120 minutes.

The human body has ~7,000 different proteins circulating in blood plasma at any given time. The most abundant is albumin (~40–50 g/L), which maintains oncotic pressure, transports fatty acids and drugs, and buffers pH. Low albumin levels indicate liver disease or malnutrition and allow tissue edema to develop.

Human stem cells in the bone marrow niches are maintained in a quiescent (dormant) state by signals from supporting stromal cells, including CXCL12, SCF (stem cell factor), and low oxygen tension. This quiescence protects stem cells from DNA damage and exhaustion while ensuring a long-lived reservoir for lifelong blood cell production.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human body's autonomic nervous system regulates heart rate through the concept of cardiac vagal tone: the vagus nerve normally suppresses heart rate via acetylcholine. Heart rate variability (HRV) — the variation in time between heartbeats — reflects this tonic vagal control and is used as a marker of cardiovascular and autonomic health; higher HRV correlates with better fitness and resilience.

Human TRPV1 receptors — ion channels expressed on nociceptors — are activated by capsaicin (the hot compound in chili peppers) and also by temperatures above 43°C. This is why capsaicin feels 'hot' even though no heat is present. Topical capsaicin depletes substance P from nerve endings over repeated application, eventually reducing pain sensation.

The human body's omentum — a fat-laden apron of peritoneum hanging from the stomach and large intestine — is a major site of immune cell storage, containing large numbers of macrophages, B cells, and T cells. It migrates to sites of intra-abdominal infection and injury, earning it the nickname 'the policeman of the abdomen.'

Human aging is associated with a phenomenon called inflammaging — a chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammatory state that develops with age. It is driven by accumulation of senescent cells secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines (the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, SASP), microbiome changes, and leakage of mitochondrial DNA. Inflammaging contributes to cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases.

The human ear's outer ear (pinna) is unique to each individual — twins have different ear shapes — and earprints have been proposed as a forensic identification method. The pinna's complex ridges and folds collect and direct sound into the ear canal while providing spectral cues for vertical and front/back sound localization.

The human body's portal triad — the structural unit of the liver — consists of a portal arteriole, a portal venule, and a bile duct. Blood flows from the portal triad inward through liver sinusoids past hepatocytes (which process it) to the central vein. This centripetal flow means hepatocytes near the portal triad receive more oxygen and are specialized differently from those near the central vein.

The human body's complement system proteins circulate as inactive precursors (zymogens) in plasma at a combined concentration of about 3 mg/mL. When activated, each step amplifies dramatically — a single triggering event can generate millions of membrane attack complexes. This amplification also makes uncontrolled complement activation dangerous; multiple regulatory proteins (C1-INH, factor H, CD59) prevent autoactivation.

The human brain's limbic system — including the hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate cortex, and septal nuclei — regulates emotion, memory, and motivation. The amygdala's role in fear conditioning is among the best-studied neural circuits: fear associations are formed at amygdala synapses via LTP and are remarkably durable, persisting even after the association becomes irrelevant (extinction is formed in the prefrontal cortex, not erasure of the original memory).

The human body's reticulocytes — immature red blood cells — are released from the bone marrow still containing residual ribosomes (giving them their name from the reticular network of ribosomal RNA visible under special staining). They mature to fully functional erythrocytes within 24–48 hours of entering the bloodstream. Elevated reticulocyte counts indicate accelerated RBC production.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Human bone marrow contains both hematopoietic cells (blood-forming) and stromal cells that support them, including mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) that can differentiate into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes. With aging, the ratio of red (active) to yellow (fatty) marrow shifts toward yellow marrow, reducing hematopoietic reserve.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human gut produces cholecystokinin (CCK) when fats and proteins enter the small intestine. CCK simultaneously triggers gallbladder contraction (releasing bile), pancreatic enzyme secretion, and satiety signals to the brain via the vagus nerve — integrating digestive and appetite-regulatory functions in a single hormone.

The human eye uses optical aberrations inherent in its structure (spherical aberration, chromatic aberration, coma) that are minimized by the pupil constricting in bright light. The pupil acts as a natural aperture stop: smaller pupils reduce aberrations and increase depth of focus, sharpening near vision — which is why people with presbyopia can sometimes read better in bright light.

The human body's major glycoprotein on the red blood cell surface is glycophorin A, which carries the MN blood group antigens and is heavily sialylated (negatively charged). This negative charge helps keep red blood cells from sticking to each other and to blood vessel walls — a form of passive anti-thrombotic protection.

Human skin contains Langerhans cells — dendritic cells of the epidermis — that serve as sentinels of the immune system. They constantly sample antigens from the skin surface and migrate to lymph nodes when activated to present antigens to T cells. They are particularly important in contact hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., poison ivy rash).

The human body's largest autonomic ganglion is the coeliac (celiac) ganglion, a pre-vertebral ganglion sitting in front of the aorta at the level of T12–L1. It receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the splanchnic nerves and provides sympathetic innervation to most abdominal organs. The celiac plexus block, used for cancer pain relief, targets this ganglion.

Human photoreceptors undergo a daily cycle of outer segment renewal — approximately 10% of the rod outer segment disk membranes are shed each morning just after light onset and phagocytosed by the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Failure of RPE phagocytosis leads to accumulation of shed discs and photoreceptor degeneration as seen in some forms of retinitis pigmentosa.

The human microbiome's fungal component (mycobiome) includes Candida species as the most common commensal fungi, residing in the gut, mouth, and vagina without causing harm in healthy people. When the bacterial microbiome is disrupted (by antibiotics) or immune defenses weaken, Candida can overgrow and cause infections ranging from oral thrush to life-threatening systemic candidiasis.

The human sinus cavities (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid) are air-filled spaces within the skull bones that reduce skull weight, produce mucus, humidify inhaled air, and contribute to voice resonance. Because they drain through narrow ostia (openings), they are prone to congestion and sinusitis when mucosa swells during colds.

The human body uses vitamin K as an essential cofactor for carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S, activating them. Warfarin, a commonly used blood thinner, works by blocking vitamin K recycling, thereby reducing the activity of all these factors and prolonging clotting time.

Human touch receptors in the lips (especially perioral region) achieve two-point discrimination thresholds as fine as 2 mm — among the smallest in the body. This exquisite sensitivity is why babies explore objects with their mouths, why kiss stimulation is intensely pleasurable, and why dentists can detect filling irregularities of just micrometers with the tongue.

The human body's most abundant protein, collagen, has a distinctive triple-helix structure made of three polypeptide chains wound around each other. Every third amino acid must be glycine (the smallest amino acid) to fit inside the helix. Vitamin C (ascorbate) is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues that stabilize the helix; its deficiency causes scurvy, leading to weak connective tissue.

The human body's skin microbiome on normal, healthy skin is dominated by Staphylococcus epidermidis — a bacterium that actively competes with and inhibits S. aureus and other pathogens by producing bacteriocins and glycerol fermentation products. Disrupting the skin microbiome (e.g., with excessive washing or antibiotics) can paradoxically increase susceptibility to skin infections.

Human lung surfactant is a mixture of phospholipids (~80%), neutral lipids (~10%), and proteins (~10%), including the surfactant proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D. SP-A and SP-D are collectins with immune functions — they agglutinate bacteria, enhance phagocytosis, and regulate inflammation in the alveolar space.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human genome contains approximately 98 million base pairs of simple sequence repeats (microsatellites and minisatellites). These repeat sequences differ in length between individuals and form the basis of DNA fingerprinting (forensic profiling) — comparing repeat lengths at 20 locations can uniquely identify any individual except identical twins.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human body's cerebellum contributes to cognitive and emotional functions beyond motor control. Cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (Schmahmann's syndrome), caused by cerebellar damage, produces deficits in executive function, spatial cognition, language, and affect regulation — suggesting the cerebellum modulates thinking as precisely as it modulates movement.

The human body produces erythropoietin (EPO) primarily in the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney cortex. EPO binds to its receptor on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, promoting their survival, proliferation, and differentiation into red blood cells. Synthetic EPO is used medically to treat anemia of chronic kidney disease and is famously abused by endurance athletes.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Human neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) serves two entirely different functions depending on the receptor: at nicotinic ACh receptors (on skeletal muscle and ganglia), it produces fast excitation by opening ion channels; at muscarinic ACh receptors (on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands), it acts via G proteins producing slower, diverse effects (slowing the heart, increasing gut motility, stimulating secretion).

The human immune system uses clonal ignorance as a form of peripheral tolerance: potentially autoreactive lymphocytes that escape thymic deletion may exist in the periphery but fail to encounter their self-antigen (sequestered behind barriers like the blood-brain barrier or blood-testis barrier). Breaking this ignorance through inflammation or trauma can trigger autoimmune attack on these previously protected tissues.

The human body's fasciae — sheets and bands of connective tissue encasing muscles, organs, and nerves — are not inert wrappers but mechanically active structures rich in fibroblasts and sensory nerves. Fascia transmits mechanical forces across the body and is increasingly recognized as a sensory organ involved in proprioception and possibly myofascial pain syndromes.

The human skull consists of 22 bones: 8 cranial bones forming the neurocranium (protecting the brain) and 14 facial bones. In newborns, the cranial bones are separated by fibrous fontanelles (soft spots) that allow the skull to flex during birth and expand as the brain grows. The anterior fontanelle typically closes by 18–24 months of age.

Human muscle memory is not stored in the muscles but in the motor cortex and cerebellum. Repeated practice drives synaptic strengthening and myelination of neural circuits controlling specific motor sequences, allowing them to run faster, more automatically, and with less conscious effort — which is why expert musicians or athletes can perform complex sequences without thinking.

The human body's cardiac pacemaker cells in the SA node have an unusual property called funny current (If) — a mixed Na+/K+ current that flows inward during diastole, slowly depolarizing the cell toward threshold and generating the next action potential automatically. Ivabradine, a drug that selectively blocks If, slows heart rate without affecting contractility.

Human color vision has a subtle asymmetry: there are ~6 million cones in the fovea, but only ~3,000 S-cones (sensitive to short/blue wavelengths) — just 5% of all cones — compared to roughly equal numbers of L and M cones. Blue-cone photopigment matures later in infancy, explaining why newborns may not discriminate blue-yellow color contrasts as well as red-green.

The human kidney uses the countercurrent mechanism to concentrate urine using two key transporters: the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb (site of action of loop diuretics like furosemide) and aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct (regulated by ADH). Blocking either impairs concentration and dramatically increases urine volume.

Human platelet-rich plasma (PRP) contains high concentrations of growth factors including PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, and IGF-1, all released from platelet alpha granules upon activation. PRP injections are used clinically to promote healing in tendons, ligaments, and osteoarthritic joints — though evidence for efficacy varies by condition.

The human body's largest endocrine gland by weight is actually the small intestine — it contains more than 20 different types of enteroendocrine cells distributed among the billions of epithelial cells, collectively making it the largest source of hormones in the body. These gut hormones regulate appetite, gastric motility, insulin secretion, and pancreatic function.

Human tears evaporate at a rate of approximately 0.06 µL/min/cm² of ocular surface. The mucin layer secreted by conjunctival goblet cells anchors the aqueous tear film to the hydrophobic corneal surface; without it, the aqueous layer would bead up and not spread, leaving dry patches. Reduced goblet cell density is a hallmark of severe dry eye disease.

The human immune system can tolerate the 10–100 trillion commensal microbes in the gut through active regulation rather than passive ignorance. Regulatory T cells induced in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, secretory IgA that neutralizes bacteria without inflammation, and IL-10 produced by macrophages work together to prevent a perpetual inflammatory response to the microbiome.

Human muscle fibers can hypertrophy (increase in size) in response to resistance exercise through two mechanisms: myofibrillar hypertrophy (increased myosin and actin content, improving force production) and sarcoplasmic hypertrophy (increased volume of the cell's fluid and glycogen stores, improving endurance). Satellite cells — muscle stem cells — fuse to growing fibers, adding myonuclei to support the larger cell volume.

Human embryos develop three sets of kidneys in sequence: pronephros (appears week 3, vestigial and non-functional), mesonephros (weeks 4–8, contributes to reproductive structures), and metanephros (beginning week 5, becomes the permanent kidney). The final kidney ascends from the pelvis to its adult position in the abdomen during fetal development.

source.name: NIH Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

text: The human body's hair follicle dermal papilla — a cluster of mesenchymal cells at the base of the follicle — is the master regulator of hair growth. It communicates with follicle stem cells via WNT, BMP, and FGF signaling to initiate anagen (growth) and can be transplanted to induce new hair growth, which is the basis of hair transplant surgery.

Human vision uses two neural pathways from the retina to the cortex: the magnocellular (M) pathway carries fast, coarse motion and depth information to the dorsal 'where/how' stream; the parvocellular (P) pathway carries slow, fine-grained color and form information to the ventral 'what' stream. Selective damage to either stream produces striking dissociations between motion perception and object recognition.

The human body's bile acid pool consists of about 4–6 grams of bile acids that cycle through the enterohepatic circulation 6–10 times per day. Primary bile acids (cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol; secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid) are formed by gut bacterial modification.

The human body responds to a 5-km run by increasing BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) in the hippocampus. BDNF promotes neurogenesis (new neuron formation), synaptic plasticity, and neuron survival — which is why regular aerobic exercise improves memory and reduces the risk of depression and neurodegenerative disease.

Human skin produces antimicrobial peptides called defensins and cathelicidins that kill bacteria, fungi, and enveloped viruses by disrupting their membranes. Beta-defensins are constitutively expressed; alpha-defensins are released by neutrophils. These peptides are part of the skin's immediate innate defense against infection.

The human body's cardiac output at rest is about 5 liters per minute but can increase to 20–25 liters per minute during maximal exercise in untrained individuals — and up to 40 liters per minute in elite endurance athletes. This increase is achieved by raising both heart rate and stroke volume (via the Frank-Starling mechanism and catecholamine stimulation).

The human immune system has a specialized subset of T cells called follicular helper T cells (Tfh) that reside in germinal centers of lymph nodes and provide critical signals (CD40L, IL-21) to B cells to support antibody class switching, somatic hypermutation, and memory B cell generation. Without Tfh cells, antibody responses are weak and short-lived.

Human skeletal growth during childhood follows a predictable tempo controlled by growth hormone and IGF-1, which are secreted in pulses — primarily during deep sleep. This is why adequate sleep is essential for children's growth and why the first deep sleep cycle of the night has the largest growth hormone pulse.

Human DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) — the most dangerous form of DNA damage — are repaired by two main pathways: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ, error-prone, active in all cell cycle phases) and homologous recombination (HR, high-fidelity, active only in S and G2 phases when a sister chromatid template is available). Defects in HR cause the BRCA mutation-associated cancer predisposition.

The human brain's neurons communicate at chemical synapses by releasing neurotransmitters from vesicles into the synaptic cleft (20–40 nm wide). Neurotransmitter action is terminated by reuptake transporters (e.g., the serotonin transporter blocked by SSRIs), enzymatic degradation (e.g., acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh), or diffusion away from the synapse.

Human fingernails are made of compacted dead keratinocytes layered in a structure that is harder than skin keratin due to a high content of disulfide bonds between cysteine residues in hard keratin. Nails protect the fingertip, enhance precision grip, and serve as tools for scratching — but importantly they allow the fingertip's sensory receptors to detect finer textures by acting as a counter-pressure plate.

The human immune system uses opsonization to enhance phagocytosis: coating pathogens with IgG antibodies and complement fragment C3b marks them for destruction. Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) express Fc receptors (binding IgG) and complement receptors (binding C3b), enabling them to recognize and engulf opsonized targets efficiently.

Human bone marrow transplantation (BMT) replaces a patient's blood-forming stem cells with donor stem cells. Before BMT, the patient undergoes myeloablative conditioning (high-dose chemotherapy ± radiation) to destroy their bone marrow and immune system. The primary complication is graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), where donor T cells attack the recipient's tissues.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human body's gut permeability is tightly regulated by tight junctions between enterocytes. When these junctions are disrupted — by certain bacteria, gluten in susceptible individuals, stress, or alcohol — luminal contents including bacteria-derived LPS can enter the bloodstream, triggering systemic inflammation and metabolic endotoxemia linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Human binocular vision gives depth perception (stereopsis) by comparing the slightly different images captured by each eye (retinal disparity). The brain's visual cortex contains neurons that respond selectively to specific depths — a property called binocular disparity tuning. The maximum depth that can be discriminated by stereopsis is about 200 meters.

The human urinary system produces about 1–1.5 liters of urine per day under normal conditions, but this can vary from as little as 0.5 liters (in severe dehydration) to 10–20 liters (in the absence of ADH, as in diabetes insipidus). Urine composition reflects the kidney's regulation of fluid, electrolyte, acid-base, and nitrogen balance.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

text: Human cardiac muscle (myocardium) differs from skeletal muscle in several ways: it is involuntary, branched, connected by gap junctions (intercalated discs) that allow electrical impulses to spread rapidly through the entire myocardium as a syncytium, and it has a long refractory period (~250 ms) preventing tetanic contraction that would stop the pumping action.

Human vision contains a temporal resolution limit: the 'flicker fusion frequency' at which separate flashes appear as continuous light is about 60 Hz under photopic (daylight) conditions and lower under scotopic conditions. Cinema relies on this — films played at 24–30 frames per second appear as smooth motion because the eye cannot resolve the individual frames.

The human gut can perform mucosal healing after injury via a rapid restitution process: surviving epithelial cells flatten and migrate to cover denuded areas within minutes to hours, before proliferation can replace lost cells. This migration is driven by EGF (epidermal growth factor), TGF-alpha, and prostaglandins and does not require cell division.

Human pain transmission can be modulated at the spinal cord level via gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965): large-diameter Aβ fibers (carrying touch) can inhibit pain transmission by activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn. This explains why rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain — touch signals compete with pain signals.

The human kidney's proximal tubule reabsorbs approximately 65–70% of the filtered sodium, water, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate. SGLT2 transporters in the proximal tubule co-transport glucose with sodium; SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins), a class of diabetes drugs, block this transporter, causing glycosuria and weight loss while also reducing cardiovascular and kidney disease risk.

The human body can synthesize all purines (adenine and guanine, for DNA and RNA) de novo from simple precursors, but pyrimidine synthesis requires carbamoyl phosphate — a regulated step in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Both pathways also have salvage routes that recycle purines and pyrimidines from degraded nucleic acids, which is more energetically efficient.

Human macrophages exhibit remarkable plasticity: classical activation (M1) by IFN-γ and LPS produces a pro-inflammatory phenotype (high TNF-α, IL-12, ROS) optimized to kill bacteria; alternative activation (M2) by IL-4 and IL-13 produces an anti-inflammatory, pro-tissue-repair phenotype (high IL-10, arginase). These distinct macrophage states reflect the dual role of macrophages in fighting infection versus healing.

The human genome contains approximately 500 RNA genes encoding ribosomal RNA (rRNA) — all clustered in the nucleolus at the acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22). The nucleolus is the most prominent structure in the nucleus and is a dedicated ribosome factory, assembling ~10 million ribosomes per day in rapidly dividing cells.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Human baroreceptors — stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the carotid sinus and aortic arch — monitor blood pressure beat by beat and reflexively regulate heart rate and vascular tone via the brainstem. When blood pressure rises, baroreceptors increase firing, triggering parasympathetic activation and sympathetic withdrawal to reduce heart rate and dilate vessels — the baroreceptor reflex.

The human brain's reward circuit centers on the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum), which receives dopamine signals from the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Pleasurable stimuli — food, sex, social connection, novelty — trigger dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, reinforcing the behavior. Addictive substances hijack this circuit by causing massive, sustained dopamine surges.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Drug Abuse

text: Human skin is the primary site of production for over 29 known neuropeptides, including substance P, CGRP, and VIP. These neuropeptides are released from sensory nerve endings in skin and can modulate local immune responses, vascular tone, and itch — creating a neuro-immuno-cutaneous communication system that links the nervous system and skin immunity.

The human retinal vasculature is organized into three distinct capillary networks (superficial, intermediate, deep) that supply the inner retina. The outer retina (photoreceptors and RPE) is avascular and nourished by the choriocapillaris of the choroid beneath. Diabetic retinopathy damages the inner retinal capillaries, while age-related macular degeneration often involves abnormal choroidal neovascularization.

Human sweat contains trace amounts of pheromone-like compounds including androstenone and androstenol derived from testosterone metabolism. While no dedicated vomeronasal organ is functional in adult humans, some olfactory receptors in the main nasal epithelium can detect these compounds, and studies suggest they subtly influence social and sexual behavior.

The human cerebral cortex is organized into six layers (I–VI) of distinct neuron types, from superficial to deep. Layer IV is the main input layer (receiving thalamic projections); layers II–III form cortico-cortical connections; layers V–VI send output to the brainstem, spinal cord, and thalamus. This laminar organization is a fundamental unit of neocortical processing.

Human lungs contain alveolar macrophages — the first line of immune defense in the airways — that patrol the alveolar surface, engulfing inhaled particles, bacteria, and dead cells. They are remarkably long-lived (months to years) compared to blood monocytes and are maintained locally by self-renewal rather than constant replenishment from the blood.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: Human mitochondria can fuse and divide (mitochondrial dynamics) as part of a quality control process: healthy mitochondria fuse to share contents and compensate for damage; damaged mitochondria fragment and are selectively removed by mitophagy (a form of selective autophagy). Defects in mitochondrial dynamics underlie several neurodegenerative diseases.

The human body uses a lipid raft model of membrane organization: certain sphingolipids and cholesterol cluster into ordered membrane domains called lipid rafts that concentrate specific signaling proteins (like GPI-anchored proteins and tyrosine kinases). These rafts facilitate efficient signal transduction and are also exploited by some viruses and bacteria to enter cells.

Human newborns have relatively elevated hematocrit (45–65%) compared to adults (~40–45%) because high fetal hemoglobin in utero offloads less oxygen in peripheral tissues, and extra red cells compensate. After birth, as adult hemoglobin rises and fetal hemoglobin declines, red blood cell production slows and the hematocrit drops to a nadir around 8–12 weeks ('physiological anemia of infancy').

The human body's pain-inhibiting system includes the periaqueductal gray (PAG) that, when stimulated, activates serotonergic and noradrenergic neurons that inhibit pain transmission in the spinal dorsal horn. This descending inhibition is why electrical stimulation of the PAG can provide profound analgesia — a discovery that led to spinal cord stimulation and deep brain stimulation for chronic pain.

Human adult neurogenesis — the production of new neurons in the adult brain — robustly occurs in two regions: the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles (producing interneurons that migrate to the olfactory bulb) and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (producing granule cells). The functional significance of adult hippocampal neurogenesis is linked to pattern separation in memory.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human lens protein crystallin has no turnover — the crystallin molecules present in the lens nucleus at birth remain there for an entire lifetime. This extraordinary longevity is possible because the lens fiber cells that form the nucleus destroy their organelles (including the nucleus itself) during differentiation, preventing any normal protein turnover. Protein aggregation and modification over decades leads to age-related nuclear cataracts.

The human body's hepatic stellate cells (formerly called Ito cells) normally store 80% of the body's vitamin A as retinyl esters in lipid droplets. When the liver is injured (by alcohol, hepatitis, or fat), these cells activate into myofibroblasts that produce excess collagen, leading to liver fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis. Reversing stellate cell activation is a key goal in anti-fibrotic therapy.

Human bone contains hydroxyapatite crystals oriented parallel to collagen fibers, giving bone its directional mechanical properties. Cortical bone is strongest in compression (resisting being crushed) along the long axis — the dominant loading direction during standing and walking — which is why osteoporotic vertebral fractures are typically compressive collapses.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human immune system's type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) respond to epithelial-derived alarmins (IL-25, IL-33, TSLP) by producing IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 — the same cytokines produced by Th2 cells. ILC2s are pivotal in orchestrating allergic inflammation in asthma and atopic dermatitis before adaptive immune cells are recruited.

Human mitosis divides a single cell into two genetically identical daughter cells through four phases: prophase (chromosome condensation), metaphase (chromosome alignment at the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), and telophase (nuclear envelope reformation). The entire process takes about 1 hour, after which cytokinesis physically divides the cytoplasm.

Human smell is the only sense whose primary projections bypass the thalamus and connect directly to the limbic system (amygdala and piriform cortex). This direct connection explains why smells are uniquely powerful triggers of vivid emotional memories — a phenomenon described by Proust — compared to sights and sounds, which are processed through the thalamus first.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: The human immune system contains cells that can recognize lipid antigens — a form of antigen not presented on classical MHC molecules. CD1 proteins (non-classical MHC-like molecules) present lipid and glycolipid antigens to specialized T cells including NKT cells. This pathway is important in immunity to mycobacteria (like M. tuberculosis) whose cell walls are lipid-rich.

The human stomach's chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which is activated to pepsin by the acidic gastric environment (pH <4). Pepsin is a protease that begins protein digestion by cleaving peptide bonds. Gastric lipase from chief cells also begins fat digestion, accounting for about 10–30% of total fat digestion.

Human cardiac troponin I and troponin T are released into the bloodstream when cardiac muscle cells die. Highly sensitive troponin assays can detect myocardial injury within 1–3 hours of a heart attack, making them the gold standard biomarkers for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction. Levels peak at 12–24 hours and return to normal over 10–14 days.

Human blastocyst implantation involves the outer trophoblast cells invading the uterine decidua in an event analogous to tumor invasion: trophoblasts express metalloproteinases to degrade extracellular matrix and downregulate MHC class I (except HLA-C, -E, -G) to evade uterine NK cells. HLA-G expressed on trophoblasts specifically inhibits uterine NK cells and promotes vascular remodeling.

Human skin produces a lipid called squalene in sebum, which is ozonated by air pollution into squalene peroxides that trigger skin inflammation and are linked to acne and atopic dermatitis. Conversely, squalene itself has anti-cancer properties and is used as an adjuvant in vaccines to boost immune responses.

The human intestine's migrating motor complex (MMC) — often called 'the housekeeper' — is a cyclical electromechanical pattern that sweeps undigested residue and bacteria from the small intestine to the colon every 90–120 minutes during fasting. Eating interrupts the MMC and replaces it with the fed motor pattern. Disruption of the MMC underlies small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).

Human muscle cramps occur when a motor unit fires repetitively and uncontrollably, causing sustained painful muscle contraction. They are more common during or after exercise, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance (especially low magnesium, calcium, or potassium). The fastest relief is passive stretching, which activates Golgi tendon organs that inhibit the cramping motor neurons.

The human immune system's IFN-gamma (type II interferon) is produced by activated T cells and NK cells — not by virus-infected somatic cells — and serves to activate macrophages for enhanced killing of intracellular pathogens. It upregulates MHC class II expression on macrophages and dendritic cells, enabling them to present antigens to CD4+ T cells more effectively.

Human adipose tissue secretes dozens of bioactive proteins called adipokines, including leptin, adiponectin, TNF-α, IL-6, and resistin. In obesity, adipose tissue becomes inflamed, with macrophage infiltration and elevated pro-inflammatory adipokine production contributing to insulin resistance, cardiovascular risk, and cancer susceptibility.

The human body's cochlea performs a mechanical frequency analysis because the basilar membrane's physical properties vary along its length: it is narrow and stiff at the base (resonating at ~20,000 Hz) and wide and flexible at the apex (resonating at ~20 Hz). Von Békésy won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering this traveling wave mechanism.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Human pluripotent cells in the inner cell mass of the blastocyst (days 4–5 post-fertilization) are maintained in a pluripotent state by the transcription factors OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG, which form an interconnected regulatory network. These same factors were identified by Yamanaka as the reprogramming cocktail that converts adult cells back to a pluripotent state (iPSCs).

Human muscle fascia contains mechanoreceptors that can sense deformation and send signals to the CNS via Ruffini endings and interstitial free nerve endings. The density of sensory innervation in thoracolumbar fascia is comparable to the joint capsule, supporting a role for fascial proprioception in coordinating trunk stability and postural control.

The human body's venous blood from the lower limbs is actively propelled against gravity by the calf muscle pump: during walking, contraction of the gastrocnemius and soleus compresses the deep calf veins, expelling up to 60% of their blood volume upward toward the heart per step. Prolonged inactivity (bed rest, long flights) removes this pump and promotes deep vein thrombosis.

Human innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are tissue-resident lymphocytes that lack antigen-specific receptors but can rapidly produce large quantities of cytokines in response to tissue damage or infection signals. The three groups — ILC1 (IFN-γ), ILC2 (IL-4/5/13), and ILC3 (IL-17/22) — mirror the cytokine profiles of Th1, Th2, and Th17 CD4+ T cells.

Human cerebral blood flow (CBF) is maintained remarkably constant through cerebrovascular autoregulation over a wide range of mean arterial pressures (50–150 mmHg). When perfusion pressure drops, cerebral arterioles dilate; when it rises, they constrict. This protects the brain from underperfusion during hypotension and hemorrhagic damage during hypertension.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

text: The human knee's patellar tendon — connecting the kneecap to the tibia — transmits force from the quadriceps muscle to extend the leg. It has the highest tensile strength of any tendon in the body (up to 17 kN), but its blood supply is poor, contributing to patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee') in athletes who subject it to repetitive high loads.

source.name: NIH National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases

text: The human body's adipose tissue releases free fatty acids (FFAs) during fasting and exercise through lipolysis — the enzymatic hydrolysis of triglycerides by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) and adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL). Glucagon, cortisol, and epinephrine stimulate lipolysis; insulin strongly inhibits it. FFAs provide fuel for muscle, heart, and liver during fasting.

The human immune response generates trained immunity — a form of innate memory in which monocytes and macrophages exposed to a pathogen (like BCG vaccine or beta-glucan) undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enhances their responses to subsequent unrelated infections for months. Unlike adaptive memory, trained immunity is non-specific but provides a broad boost to innate defense.

Human ribs are connected to the sternum by costal cartilages, which remain flexible and allow the rib cage to expand during breathing. The 7 true ribs (1–7) connect directly to the sternum via their own cartilage; ribs 8–10 (false ribs) connect indirectly via shared cartilage; ribs 11–12 (floating ribs) have no anterior attachment. This arrangement balances protection with respiratory flexibility.

The human body's enteric glial cells — the glia of the enteric nervous system — are analogous to astrocytes of the brain and perform similar functions: supporting enteric neurons, maintaining mucosal barrier integrity, and modulating motility and immune responses. They communicate with mucosal immune cells and are increasingly recognized as key integrators of gut physiology.

Human lungs have a unique dual circulation: the pulmonary arteries deliver deoxygenated blood for gas exchange, while the bronchial arteries (branches of the aorta) supply oxygenated blood to nourish the bronchi, trachea, and connective tissue. The pulmonary capillary transit time is only ~0.75 seconds at rest — just enough for full oxygen equilibration across the thin alveolar membrane.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human body's main iron storage protein, ferritin, can hold up to 4,500 iron atoms per molecule within its hollow protein shell. Serum ferritin level is the most reliable clinical indicator of total body iron stores: low ferritin indicates iron deficiency; elevated ferritin may indicate iron overload (hemochromatosis), inflammation, or liver disease.

Human mitochondrial ATP synthesis uses a chemiosmotic mechanism: protons are pumped across the inner mitochondrial membrane by complexes I, III, and IV of the electron transport chain, creating a proton motive force. ATP synthase (complex V) uses this proton gradient to phosphorylate ADP, rotating its rotor subunit — a molecular motor turning at ~100 revolutions per second.

Human skin's Merkel cells — located in the basal epidermis at touch domes — are the only non-neuronal cells in the skin that form direct synaptic connections with slow-adapting type I (SAI) mechanosensory neurons. They were traditionally thought to be specialized transducers but are now known to act as neuroendocrine cells releasing peptides and ATP to modulate sensory neuron firing.

Human cartilage lacks not only blood vessels but also lymphatic vessels and nerve supply. This explains why cartilage damage is painless until it exposes the subchondral bone beneath (which has nerve supply), why infections in cartilage are very rare (no lymphocytes reach it), and why early-stage joint diseases like osteoarthritis are often silent until advanced.

The human hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is the central stress response system. Psychological or physical stressors trigger CRH release from the hypothalamus → ACTH from the anterior pituitary → cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Cortisol then suppresses further CRH and ACTH release through negative feedback, self-limiting the stress response.

Human immune surveillance against cancer is carried out partly by NK cells recognizing 'missing self' (reduced MHC I), partly by CD8+ T cells recognizing tumor neoantigens (mutant peptides presented on MHC I), and partly by γδ T cells recognizing stress ligands. Cancers escape immune surveillance through mechanisms including MHC I downregulation, PD-L1 upregulation, and creating an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

The human gallbladder can concentrate bile up to 10-fold by actively absorbing water and electrolytes across its wall. Cholesterol gallstones form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol (due to excess secretion or reduced bile acids), which precipitates as cholesterol crystals. Eighty percent of gallstones are cholesterol stones; the remainder are pigment stones from bilirubin.

Human proprioception enables joint position sense accurate to within 1–2 degrees at the knee and shoulder under normal conditions. Joint replacement surgery reduces this proprioceptive acuity because the prosthesis lacks the mechanoreceptors of the native joint capsule — which is one reason physical therapy and re-learning movement patterns is important after joint replacement.

Human cells contain approximately 1.5–2 meters of DNA, which must be compacted 10,000-fold to fit into a 6-micrometer nucleus. This is achieved through successive levels of folding: DNA wraps around nucleosomes (histone octamers) forming a 10 nm 'beads on a string' structure, which coils into 30 nm chromatin fibers, and further into loops, domains, and eventually condensed chromosomes during mitosis.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: Human nociceptors (pain-sensing neurons) release substance P and CGRP from their peripheral terminals when activated by tissue damage, causing neurogenic inflammation: vasodilation, plasma extravasation, and mast cell degranulation. This local tissue response amplifies the inflammatory signal and is exploited by capsaicin and CGRP antagonists as therapeutic targets for migraine and pain.

The human immune system's plasma cells — the antibody-secreting terminally differentiated B cells — can produce up to 10,000 antibody molecules per second. Long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow continue secreting protective antibodies for decades without restimulation, providing lasting humoral immunity after infection or vaccination.

Human ear wax (cerumen) is produced by specialized apocrine glands in the outer ear canal and serves as a natural self-cleaning agent. It has antimicrobial, antifungal, and insect-repelling properties. The ear canal epithelium migrates outward from the eardrum at the same rate as fingernail growth (~1.5 mm/month), carrying old wax and debris toward the outer ear.

source.name: NIH National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

text: Human DNA polymerases proofread newly synthesized DNA by using their 3'→5' exonuclease activity to remove incorrectly incorporated bases. This proofreading reduces the error rate of replication from ~10⁻⁵ to ~10⁻⁷ per base. Subsequent mismatch repair (MMR) reduces it further to ~10⁻⁹ — meaning approximately 1 error per billion bases, or about 3 errors per genome replication.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

text: The human spleen's marginal zone B cells are specialized for rapid responses to blood-borne encapsulated bacteria (like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae). They produce IgM antibodies without needing T cell help — a T cell-independent response. This is why patients without a spleen must be vaccinated against these bacteria and are at risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis.

The human body generates heat through shivering thermogenesis in cold conditions by activating spinal cord pattern generators that cause rapid involuntary muscle oscillations (~10 Hz), increasing metabolic heat production by up to 5-fold. This is metabolically costly, and the body tries to reduce it by using non-shivering thermogenesis in BAT (brown adipose tissue) first.

Human optic nerves contain about 1.2 million axons each — far fewer than the ~130 million photoreceptors they serve — because of extensive convergence and processing within the retina before signals are sent to the brain. This convergence allows the retina to perform significant computation (contrast enhancement, motion detection, edge detection) before visual information even leaves the eye.

Human blood plasma contains von Willebrand factor (vWF) — a large multimeric glycoprotein that bridges damaged subendothelial collagen and platelet glycoprotein Ib, initiating platelet adhesion. vWF also stabilizes factor VIII in circulation; its deficiency causes von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder affecting ~1% of the population.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

text: The human immune system deploys a specialized compartment called the bone marrow niche for long-term memory: long-lived plasma cells migrate to survival niches in the bone marrow stroma where CXCL12, IL-6, and APRIL from stromal and megakaryocyte cells maintain their survival and antibody secretion for decades — the cellular basis of vaccine-induced lifetime immunity.

The human brain's thalamus is the relay center for most sensory information reaching the cortex, with the exception of olfaction. The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) relays visual signals; the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) relays auditory signals; the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) relays somatosensory signals from the body. The thalamus also regulates consciousness and sleep via its connections with the brainstem reticular activating system.

Human intrafusal muscle fibers (within muscle spindles) contain two types of sensory endings: primary endings (Ia afferents) that respond to both the rate of muscle stretch and the static stretch, and secondary endings (II afferents) that respond mainly to static stretch. Gamma motor neurons regulate spindle sensitivity by adjusting intrafusal fiber tension, maintaining spindle sensitivity across the entire range of muscle lengths.

The human immune system contains memory stem T cells (Tscm) — a long-lived subset with self-renewal capacity that persist for decades and can regenerate the entire memory T cell pool. Their discovery suggests that some T cell memory may be truly lifelong. Tscm cells express markers of naive T cells (CCR7, CD62L) but have antigen-specific memory, combining the best properties of both.

Human aging is associated with immunosenescence — a decline in immune function that makes older adults more susceptible to infections, less responsive to vaccines, and more prone to cancer. Immunosenescence includes thymic involution (reducing naïve T cell output), accumulation of exhausted and senescent immune cells, and chronic low-grade inflammation (inflammaging) that impairs effective immune responses.

The human body — its atoms, cells, tissues, organs, and systems — is the product of nearly 4 billion years of evolution. About 99% of the human genome is identical to that of chimpanzees, ~85% to mice, ~60% to fruit flies, and ~31% to yeast. Every gene we use to make a heart, a brain, or an immune cell has evolutionary precedents stretching back to the earliest eukaryotes.

text: Human brown adipose tissue (BAT) is activated by sympathetic innervation releasing norepinephrine, which binds beta-3 adrenergic receptors on brown adipocytes to trigger lipolysis and UCP1-mediated uncoupled respiration. Cold exposure for even 2–3 hours per day can activate and increase BAT mass in adults, improving metabolic health and insulin sensitivity.

The human knee's menisci are not just passive shock absorbers — they also transmit axial load, provide stability, aid in synovial fluid distribution for lubrication and nutrition, and contribute to proprioception via mechanoreceptors embedded in their outer zones. Total meniscectomy removes these functions and accelerates cartilage degeneration, which is why surgeons now prefer meniscus repair over removal.

text: Human dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta are particularly vulnerable to oxidative stress because they contain high concentrations of neuromelanin (a dark pigment formed by dopamine oxidation), have long, highly branched axonal arbors requiring enormous mitochondrial support, and have low intrinsic antioxidant capacity — factors that together explain their selective degeneration in Parkinson's disease.

text: Human skeletal muscle can increase its oxidative capacity through exercise training by increasing mitochondrial density (biogenesis) via activation of PGC-1α, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. A single bout of endurance exercise triggers PGC-1α activity; consistent training over weeks to months results in 50–100% increases in mitochondrial content in trained muscle.

Human enamel — the outer layer of teeth — is the hardest substance produced by the human body, with a Vickers hardness of ~300–450 HV, comparable to some metals. It is composed of ~96% hydroxyapatite crystals by weight and contains no living cells after completion, which is why teeth cannot heal themselves once enamel is damaged.

text: The human immune system's Th17 cells produce IL-17A and IL-17F, which stimulate epithelial cells and stromal cells to release chemokines that recruit neutrophils to sites of extracellular bacterial and fungal infection. Th17 cells are also major players in autoimmune diseases like psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and multiple sclerosis — which is why IL-17 blockers (secukinumab, ixekizumab) are effective treatments.

The human body's most abundant structural protein collagen has a unique amino acid composition: every third residue is glycine (Gly-X-Y triplet), with proline and hydroxyproline frequently in the X and Y positions. The triple helix's extraordinary tensile strength comes from the interchain hydrogen bonding between these hydroxyproline residues, which is why vitamin C deficiency (required for proline hydroxylation) causes the connective tissue failure seen in scurvy.

Human sensory adaptation occurs when continuously stimulated sensory receptors reduce their firing rate over time. Fast-adapting receptors (Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles) respond only to changing stimuli — explaining why you stop feeling your clothes within minutes of putting them on. Slow-adapting receptors (Merkel's discs, Ruffini endings) continue firing for as long as the stimulus persists.

The human body's complete proteome — all proteins expressed across all cell types — is estimated to contain over 1 million distinct protein forms (proteoforms), arising from ~20,000 protein-coding genes through alternative splicing (generating ~100,000 distinct mRNAs), post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination, etc.), and proteolytic processing. This enormous molecular complexity underlies the richness of human biology.
